The Test, Decoded

Know the target before you study. Every fact here comes from your module's past papers, the professor's walkthrough slides, or his own words in the class recordings.

Logistics

  • Friday 14 August 2026 · 2:30 PM, exam hall booked 2:30–5:00 — he tends to start ~15 minutes after the official time so latecomers make it, which means arriving at 2:30 sharp buys you free reading time. 2 hours of writing, done by ~4:45.
  • Closed book. No notes; the paper itself bans non-sanctioned tools (“ChatGPT, phone, etc”) under the university's assessment policy.
  • Handwritten prose + diagrams. No coding. His words: “the test is not coding.” (The March 2026 sitting he shared a sample from was submitted digitally as slides — formats have varied between sittings, but the three questions and their mark split have not. Yours is handwritten; prepare for prose you can produce at ~20 words a minute.)
  • 40 marks. He told this cohort the test carries 40%, citing the national rule that a masters final assessment must be 40%; his older Module Overview slide still shows the earlier split (Simulation 40 / Report 30 / Class Test 30), so treat 40% as the live figure and confirm in the module guide. Either way the framing is the same: assignment marks run high, so “the test is the one that basically determines your overall.”
  • Logistics come from class recordings and may have shifted — always trust the latest official announcement over this page.
His own announcement, on tape

“Friday, next Friday, 14th… I have it booked for 2:30 to 5 o'clock.”

The paper's fixed anatomy

On the recent papers: a cover page (module code, cohort, date, duration) → a 1–2 page scenario, always a scheduling, routing or allocation problem → usually a bulleted constraints list, and on the newest paper an explicit “In addition to the above, please consider” block that is a free plan for your answer → three questions.

Older papers vary: 2111 PT, 2208, 2307, 2308 PT, 2402 and 2410 have no cover page and open straight on the instructions, and only 2601 FT prints a literal “please consider” list (2506 calls it “Constraints and Considerations”, 2208 “the following considerations”). If Friday's paper has no hint block, the constraints bullets inside the scenario are doing that job — mine them the same way.

QWording (near-verbatim, it barely changes)Marks
Q1“Explain in detail the process of encoding, decoding and the representation of the solution as a chromosome” — for a genetic algorithm solving the scenario. Both 2026 papers add required sub-bullets underneath, and the April 2026 full-time list ends with “how the genetic operators will be applied” — three sentences on crossover + mutation that fit your encoding.15
Q2“Discuss in detail how fitness and validity will be determined. Explain the components of the fitness / objective function in detail.”15
Q3“Outline how encoding/decoding, evaluation and implementation would differ if you used a different computational intelligence optimisation algorithm.”10

Q1 + Q2 = 75% of the marks, and on every paper but one they are about a GA — the exception is 2308 PT, whose Q1 reads “you may opt for any CIO approach”, so if Friday's stem says that, you are free to answer with any CI algorithm you can encode. Q3 is where ACO / AIS / PSO appear — outline depth only.

That Q3 row is a paraphrase — the paper's own wording is longer, and you should recognise it on sight. Every sitting from February 2024 onwards opens Q3 with the identical clause — six consecutive papers, codes 2402, 2408, 2410, 2506 and both 2026 versions — and it reaches back further still, to the oldest paper in the archive: “Provide an outline explanation of how addressing the above would differ (both in terms of encoding/decoding and implementation) if you were to opt for another …”.

That unbroken run is why you should expect it on Friday. Three phrases in it are load-bearing. “Outline explanation” fixes the depth — breadth, not a second full design. “How addressing the above would differ” anchors the answer to your own Q1 and Q2 script rather than to a textbook: the thing being compared is your answer, which is exactly why saying what stays the same scores. “Both in terms of encoding/decoding and implementation” names two of your three headings outright.

What changes between sittings is only the tail. Four archived papers (codes 2111 PT, 2402, 2408, 2410) name the algorithm for you — “…opt for another either ACO or AIS to address the above problem”, clumsy grammar and all; paper 2506 left it wide open with “…another optimisation algorithm”; and both 2026 papers say “…another CI optimisation algorithm” and then hand you your three Q3 headings: “your answer should consider encoding and representation, evaluation strategy, and practical implementation considerations”.

April 2026 went one further and bolted the scenario onto the end — “as well as how the algorithm will be designed to encourage building clustering while simultaneously discouraging peak window travel for both students and staff”. Prepare for all three cases: told which algorithm to use, told nothing, or told to design its machinery around the scenario's own soft goals.

Three papers older than that run word Q3 differently, and it costs you nothing to recognise them: 2208 asked for “an alternative strategy by outlining how the above optimisation problem can be solved using a either ACO or PSO based solution”, and 2307 for “Briefly outline either (a) how Ants in an ACO algorithm or (b) Cells in AIS, would go about constructing a solution” — both of those want the general outline only, with no comparison to your GA, so they are a strictly easier version of the same task.

Add those two to the four above and six of the ten archived papers restrict your Q3 algorithm to a two-item menu — free choice is the recent exception, not the rule, and every menu ever printed has included ACO. The one true outlier is paper 2308 PT, whose Q3 asked instead how DEAP (the Python library the labs use to build GAs) would implement your encoding; that one cannot come back in a closed-book handwritten paper where, in his words, “the test is not coding.”

The sub-bullets are the mark scheme in disguise — copy them as your headings

Both 2026 papers print, underneath each question, the list of things the answer must cover. Do not read that list as friendly advice. Read it as the rows the marker will tick, and write each line into your script as an underlined heading with the answer under it. Here they are, quoted from April 2026's paper exactly as printed — the ragged capitalisation is the paper's, not a slip.

QThe printed sub-bullets — use them, word for word, as your headings
Q1The structure of the chromosome · The meaning of each gene · How key scenario requirements are represented · How a chromosome is decoded · The data required to support encoding and decoding · How the genetic operators will be applied
Q2distinguish between hard constraints and soft constraints · explain how invalid solutions are detected and handled · Describe each component of the fitness/objective function · Justify penalty weights and prioritisation mechanisms
Q3encoding and representation · evaluation strategy · practical implementation considerations

Thirteen headings, handed to you before you write a word. Lay the script out under those exact labels and you cannot lose a row to “the examiner could not find it”, which is the way marks quietly vanish on a fast read. Notice too how neatly they match the mark scheme below: Q1's six bullets are the 3 · 4 · 4 · 2 · 2 rows in the paper's own language, and Q3's three are the three headings the whole site drills you on.

Two of the Q2 bullets are unusually easy to answer thinly, so answer them thickly: for “justify penalty weights and prioritisation mechanisms”, say what each weight buys — which trade-off it forces, and what would go wrong at half or double its value — not merely what number it is; and if the fairness bullet is on your paper, point at two separate mechanisms rather than one, a workload-spread or balance term and an explicit priority weight, because “fairness and priority” is two asks in one line.

Provenance and the small print. The bullets above are verbatim from the April 2026 full-time paper. The part-time / ODL version of the same sitting differs in three places: its Q1 names the entities instead of talking generally (“How exams, time slots, halls, and invigilators are represented”, “How a chromosome is decoded into a complete timetable”) and drops the genetic-operators bullet, while its Q2 adds a fifth line, “Explain how fairness and priority are incorporated” — so on a people-scheduling scenario, budget a paragraph on fairness.

Papers before 2026 print the three questions bare, with no sub-bullets at all. Treat the list as likely rather than guaranteed: if your paper prints them, follow them slavishly; if it does not, write those same headings anyway, because they are what the mark scheme rewards either way.

Hold that table against his own words further down this page — “you can pick up half those marks… just by giving a bit of an outline of PSO. The rest of the marks, those five marks, are an outline of how we apply it.” The rows are the same ten marks cut a different way.

The named algorithm (2), the implementation differences (2) and the judgement sentence (1) are the general half: a compact outline of the algorithm itself. Write it even though the examiner plainly knows how the algorithm works — he is marking whether you do, and those are the cheapest marks on the paper.

How the key decision is represented in this scenario (3) and what happens to evaluation (2) are the applied half. Five and five. The internal split moves by a mark between deck versions and papers, so don't budget against it — cover both halves and every version adds up. His full-mark recipe also wants similarities as well as differences: Lesson 11's two-column table is the checklist for that.

Two Q3 wrinkles from past papers. First, being told which algorithm to use is the historical norm, not a freak event: six of the ten archived papers hand you a two-item menu instead of a free choice. Four of them (codes 2111 PT, 2402, 2408 and 2410) say “…opt for another either ACO or AIS to address the above problem”; 2208 says “…using a either ACO or PSO based solution”; and 2307 asks the same thing in the narrower form “Briefly outline either (a) how Ants in an ACO algorithm or (b) Cells in AIS, would go about constructing a solution”.

Only the three most recent papers — 2506 and both 2026 versions, the ones closest to Friday — leave the choice open. So be ready to be told which, and note that every menu ever printed contains ACO: that is the one alternative you cannot afford to arrive without. If the paper names a pair, answer from that pair — writing PSO into a question that said “either ACO or AIS” is off-question and puts the 2-mark “a sensible algorithm is named” row at risk for no gain.

Second, the newest paper asked you to design the algorithm's mechanics around the scenario's own soft goals (e.g. “encourage building clustering, discourage peak-window travel”) — always tie your alternative's machinery to the scenario's named objectives, not just generic theory.

His Q3 sketch, two days before your test (12 Aug). On the whiteboard he wrote the question as “Q3: Compare with another CI approach (ACO)” and split the answer exactly in two: “Part A — differences GA vs ACO” (his first row: GA has populations of solutions, ACO a population of 'agents') and “Part B — how ACO will be applied”.

Part B he drew as a chain of nodes “taken from the scenario (ie wards, slots, etc)” with a column of options at each node, and the sentence that carries the marks: “we can apply rules (ie filtering of options) as the ant moves from node to node.” That is the structure to reproduce tomorrow — the full recipe with sentence templates is on How to Write Answers.

The only pacing rule his deck actually prints is for Q3: “Ten marks in a two-hour paper is roughly 30 minutes of writing. Do not overrun — Q1 and Q2 are worth more.” (His revised deck puts it as “Ten marks is about 30 minutes of writing. Three short paragraphs under three headings is enough.”) Scaling that to about three minutes a mark is our arithmetic, not a rule he states — and it is worth doing, because it shows there is no slack: 40 marks × 3 minutes is 120 minutes of pure writing with no reading and no checking.

This plan trims five minutes off each of Q1 and Q2 and ten off Q3 — exactly the twenty minutes the reading block and the final check cost you. There is no spare time in it. Q3 only gets its full thirty if you come out of Q2 early; if you do, take the minutes, because Q3's marks are the cheapest on the paper.

Lesson 1 · ~15 min

What Is Computational Intelligence Optimisation?

You've never attended a class. That's fine — here is the entire big picture, honestly explained.

Lesson 1 on one slide
  • Optimisation = pick the best arrangement out of astronomically many: 20 parcels = 20! ≈ 2.4 quintillion routes ≈ 77,000 years at a million checks a second.
  • So the goal changes: not the perfect answer — a very good answer, quickly.
  • CI copies nature's search: try a population of candidates, keep what scores well, vary it, repeat.
  • Five branches on his board — EA · Swarm · Neural Nets · Fuzzy · AIS; this module runs on EA + Swarm.
  • Any CI algorithm needs exactly two things from you: an encoding (write a candidate down) and a fitness function (score it).
  • No-Free-Lunch: no algorithm is universally best — you justify by fit to this scenario, never by crowning a winner.
Tomorrow this buys you: the opening paragraph of every answer (good-answer-quickly + the search-space number) and Q3's closing judgement sentence.

Optimisation, in plain language

Optimisation = making something better: time, money, efficiency, fairness. You have many possible ways to do something (schedules, routes, allocations) and you want a good one — ideally the best, realistically an excellent one found in reasonable time.

Some problems are small enough to solve exactly with maths or brute force. But real problems — timetabling a university, routing vehicles, rostering staff — have astronomically many possible solutions. Checking them all would outlast the universe.

Conventional exact methods — calculus (differentiate, set to zero, solve) and linear programming are the two his slide names — choke: they need a precise mathematical model, they examine one solution at a time, and they degrade badly as the problem grows. That's the gap this module fills.

Start with the puzzle the module itself starts with, because it hands you the number to quote in the hall

You run a delivery company in Kuala Lumpur. You have one van and 20 parcels to deliver in a single day, and the only thing you choose is the order the driver visits the 20 addresses in, so that the round finishes as quickly as possible. No compatibility rules, no capacities — just an order.

That problem has over 2 quintillion possible routes: exactly 2,432,902,008,176,640,000 of them, which is 20 factorial (20 × 19 × 18 × … × 1). A computer checking one million routes every second would need roughly 77,000 years to try them all.

Buying a faster machine does not rescue you: ten times the speed still leaves 7,700 years, and adding a twenty-first parcel multiplies the whole thing by 21 again. So the goal quietly changes, and this is the sentence the rest of the module rests on — you do not need the perfect answer, you need a very good answer, quickly. Write that trade-off explicitly in your opening line and you have justified a CI method before you have named one.

The phrase you will use constantly is search space

The set of every arrangement the problem lets you write down — good and bad, legal and illegal. One point in that space is one complete answer, never a fragment: if you are placing 40 exams into 20 time slots, a point is a whole timetable with all 40 exams placed. Optimising means finding the point with the best score.

What makes it hard is that the space comes with no map — you cannot look down on it and spot the peak. You can only stand at one point, score it, and step to something nearby. Everything else in this module — chromosomes, fitness functions, mutation, swarms — is machinery for taking useful steps through a space far too large to walk.

Each of those four gets a lesson to itself from Lesson 3 onwards, and every term used anywhere on this site has a one-line entry in the glossary on the Practice page. Nothing here assumes you already know them.

The trick: copy nature

Computational Intelligence (CI) is a family of algorithms inspired by how nature solves hard problems without a mathematician in charge. Evolution breeds better animals; ant colonies find shortest paths; bird flocks converge on food. None of them enumerate every option — they search cleverly: try a population of candidate solutions, keep what works, vary it, repeat.

The CI family tree

The Week 1 lecture slide, titled “Four major branches of CI”, names four — and says the module “focuses mainly on Evolutionary Algorithms and Swarm Intelligence”. His own Lecture 1 whiteboard opens with five, written across the top of the board as “CI: EA, FL, NN, SI, AIS”, so treat all five branch names below as his; the fifth is spelled out here because past papers name it.

The examples in brackets are partly his and partly filled out here, so treat the branch names as his and the example lists as a superset:

  • Evolutionary Algorithms (EA) — inspired by Darwinian evolution. His examples: Genetic Algorithms (GA), Genetic Programming, Differential Evolution. The GA is the star of this module. (Evolutionary Strategies are not on the slide, but he wrote them on the Lab 1 whiteboard alongside Differential Evolution and Genetic Programming — all three are safe to name.)

  • Swarm Intelligence (SI) — inspired by the group behaviour of animals. His examples: PSO (Particle Swarm Optimisation — bird flocks), ACO (Ant Colony Optimisation — ant trails), and Bee/Firefly algorithms. Bee Colony Optimisation (BCO) and the Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) are the bee methods you will meet in Lesson 11. His Lab 1 whiteboard lists five under Swarm Intelligence — PSO, ACO, ABC, GWO, AHA — where GWO is the Grey Wolf Optimiser and AHA the Artificial Hummingbird Algorithm.

    Those last two are named on his board rather than taught anywhere in the module, so naming them back is safe and correctly attributed; just do not build a Q3 answer on one, because you were never shown its mechanics.

  • Neural Networks — inspired by the human brain; used widely in machine learning and pattern recognition. A CI branch, but not what this test is about.
  • Fuzzy Systems — human reasoning with vague terms (“hot”, “warm”, “a bit cold”), i.e. handling uncertainty. Also not what this test is about.
  • Artificial Immune Systems (AIS) — the fifth branch on his Lecture 1 whiteboard, and in the Week 1 reading, though not on the four-branch slide. Mimics your immune system: clonal selection — generate diverse candidate detectors, clone and mutate the best ones, remember the good ones for next time. His Week 1 slides do mention immune systems in passing as a nature-inspired mechanism (“recognising and adapting to new threats… distinguish friend from foe”). Worth knowing by name: past papers phrase Q3 as “ACO or AIS”, so this one line is cheap breadth insurance.

Why should copying biology beat guessing?

Ask the honest question before you accept any of this. Because evolution is not guessing — it is a ratchet assembled from three parts.

  • Variationthrows up candidates slightly different from what you already had.
  • Selectiondiscards most of them and keeps the ones that scored well.
  • Inheritancemeans the survivors are what the next round varies.

Any single round is nearly worthless: a random tweak to a schedule is usually neutral or harmful. But because losses are thrown away and gains are carried forward, small improvements accumulate, and after a few hundred rounds the population holds a solution that no single random guess would ever have produced in the lifetime of the universe.

That is the conceptual payload of this whole module: pure randomness is hopeless, pure greed gets stuck, and randomness filtered by a score and passed on is neither.

Why does copying nature work? Because these mechanisms are general-purpose search strategies: they need no formula for the problem, only a way to score a candidate solution. That makes them ideal when the problem is messy, discrete, and full of constraints — exactly the problems in your test scenarios.

And why want a general-purpose optimiser at all, instead of a clever method built for your one problem?

Because a bespoke method dies the moment the problem moves: add a rule, add a machine, change a policy, and the maths must be rederived from scratch. A CI algorithm asks you for exactly two things — a way to write a candidate down (the encoding) and a way to score it (the fitness function). Change the rules and you change the score, not the algorithm.

That is also why Q1 and Q2 — 30 of the 40 marks — ask you to design the encoding and the fitness function rather than to run the algorithm. It does not mean the algorithm is a free ride you can skip.

Q3 is worth 10 marks and every one of them is algorithm-specific, marked in two roughly equal halves: about five for a general outline of how your chosen alternative algorithm actually works, and about five for applying it to the scenario in front of you — how it would encode and decode a solution, how its evaluation differs, what parameters it needs, and a closing comparative judgement against the GA. Lessons 9–11 exist to give you that outline; Lesson 12 shows you how to apply it.

One honest caveat, and it comes with a name worth quoting

The No-Free-Lunch theorem (Wolpert & Macready, 1997) proves that averaged over all possible problems every search algorithm performs identically — if algorithm A beats B on some problems, B beats A on the rest. So general-purpose does not mean better-at-everything, and no optimiser is universally best.

What that buys you is the sentence Q3 is actually asking for: you justify an algorithm by matching its machinery to this scenario's structure, never by crowning it the strongest.

CI ≠ AI, in one line

AI is the broader field; CI is a toolkit inside it — the nature-inspired corner — and his phrase for what it is good at is that CI methods “handle uncertainty, incomplete information, and noisy data”. Two further contrasts off the same slide, each worth a sentence in answers:

  • conventional exact methods are deterministic (same input ⇒ same output, every run) while CI methods are stochastic (they use randomness, so two runs can differ);
  • and where exact methods struggle as the problem grows, CI scales much better to large problems.

Where this actually runs

CI is not a classroom curiosity, and one sentence naming real deployments makes an opening paragraph sound informed rather than recited. Your lecturer's own list:

  • Logistics and deliveryroute planning for Grab, Lalamove, DHL and FedEx
  • Manufacturingscheduling factory machines and supply chains
  • Financeportfolio optimisation, fraud detection and trading strategies
  • Healthcaredesigning treatment plans, scheduling staff, drug discovery
  • Engineeringdesigning aircraft wings, antennas and car parts
  • Energyoptimising power grids and renewable placement
  • GamesAI opponents and procedurally generated content
  • and machine learning itselftuning the settings of other AI models

Do not memorise the list; notice the pattern in it. Every entry is a problem where you must pick one arrangement out of an enormous number, where the rules are messy and interlocking, and where a very good answer found today is worth more than a perfect answer found next year. Your test scenario will be one more member of that family — and in this module it is always the first kind, scheduling and allocation.

What this module actually assesses

Not maths proofs. Not coding (in the test). The skill is translation: take a messy real-world brief and translate it into a form a CI algorithm can search — then explain how the algorithm evaluates and improves candidate solutions.

That translation has two halves, and the module's own learning outcome names both:

  • Encodingis writing a candidate solution down as a string of symbols the algorithm can copy, cut and mutate;
  • Decodingis the rule that turns that string back into the real object — an actual berth plan, an actual timetable — so it can be scored.

Q1 asks for both by name, and a gene layout with no decoder answers half the question. Lesson 3 builds the pair.

Mental model to keep: a CI algorithm is a blind cook. It cannot see the recipe book (the problem structure). It can only taste dishes (score solutions) and remix what tasted good. Your job in the test: design the dish format (encoding), the tasting rules (fitness), and describe an alternative cook. Which cooks are on the menu depends on the paper: older papers say “either ACO or AIS”, one says “either ACO or PSO”, the newest simply says “another CI optimisation algorithm”. Safe answers in every case are PSO, ACO, AIS or simulated annealing — Lessons 9–12 give you each one.

Week one, first mention of the test, ten weeks out

“Don't worry, worry later.”

Lesson 2 · ~20 min

Anatomy of an Optimisation Problem

Every scenario in every past paper decomposes into the same three ingredients. Learn to spot them and half of Q1 writes itself.

Lesson 2 on one slide
  • Every scenario = three ingredients: decision variables (what you choose) · objectives (how a choice is scored) · constraints (what must hold).
  • Decisions come in five flavours: continuous · integer · categorical · binary · sequence — test scenarios live on the last three, and binary hides in sentences that sound like costs (“pays a fee each time a building is opened”).
  • Objective = fitness function: two names, one thing — a rule turning one complete candidate into one number.
  • Maximising X is the same problem as minimising −X — direction is a free choice.
  • Formal skeleton, once: minimise f(x) subject to h(x)=0, g(x)≤0 — and a hard rule bent into g gives you the penalty for free: max(0, g).
Tomorrow this buys you: Q1's 3 problem-understanding marks (name every decision) and the hard/soft sort that opens Q2.

The three ingredients

The warm-up example the module uses is a grocery run, and it is worth stating in full before the table because every column below refers to it. You walk into a supermarket with RM100 (Malaysian ringgit) and a shelf of items, each with a price and a nutritional value. You must come out with a basket for the week.

What you get to choose is which items go in, and how much of each — already two different kinds of decision, a yes/no per item and a quantity; what you are trying to achieve is a nutritious, varied basket you will actually enjoy eating; what you may not do is spend over RM100, or come home with no protein and no vegetables. Trivial as a shopping trip, identical in structure to every scenario in every past paper.

IngredientQuestion it answersIn the grocery run
1. Decision variablesWhat are you actually choosing?Which grocery items go in the basket, and how much of each
2. Objective(s)How do you score a choice?Maximise nutrition, variety and enjoyment for the week
3. ConstraintsWhat must / must not hold?Total cost ≤ RM100; basket must include protein and vegetables

Decision variables are the most important

In the test, every decision the scenario leaves open — which hall, which time slot, which staff member, whether a building is even opened — must eventually live inside your chromosome (the encoded solution string — Lesson 3). Miss one and you have capped your own mark: the walkthrough deck's Q1 rubric gives 3 of the 15 marks for “problem understanding — you identify the real decisions (who, order, when)”, and a chromosome that cannot express a decision the scenario asks you to make cannot be rescued by anything you write afterwards.

Decision variables come in five flavours, and running a fresh scenario past the list is the cheapest way to stop missing one — which matters because Q1's first mark row is 3 marks for identifying the real decisions.

  • Continuousa number anywhere on a smooth range — the temperature setting on a machine, the price of a product.
  • Integera whole number — how many staff to hire, how many trucks to send.
  • Categoricalone choice from a fixed list — which supplier, which exam hall, which yard section.
  • Binarya true/false switch — “include this item?”, “open this building for tonight's session?”.
  • Sequence or orderingthe order things happen in — which city to visit next, which ship is unloaded first.

Test scenarios are dominated by the last three, and the one most often missed is binary, because on/off decisions hide inside sentences that sound like costs (“the university pays a fee each time a building is opened” is a decision, not a price list). Each flavour has a matching chromosome shape waiting in Lesson 4 — categorical becomes integer genes, binary becomes bits, ordering becomes a permutation — so naming the flavour has already done half of your encoding argument.

One word swap to make now, because the exam paper makes it

The objective is the thing you are trying to make bigger or smaller — profit, accuracy, energy generated if you are maximising; cost, time, error, fuel, waste if you are minimising. In computational intelligence that same quantity is almost always called the fitness function, a name borrowed straight from biology, where an organism's fitness is how well it survives and breeds.

They are two names for one thing: a rule that takes one complete candidate solution and returns a single number saying how good it is. Q2 on your paper says “the components of the fitness / objective function” with a slash for exactly that reason, and every lesson from here on says fitness function.

Whichever direction the scenario points, note that maximising X is the same problem as minimising −X — framing is a free choice, not a different problem, and Lesson 8 shows you how to use that to get every component of a weighted sum pointing the same way.

Writing the problem down formally (the notation, once)

You will never be asked to prove anything, but ten minutes on the standard notation buys you the ability to write constraints as one-line equations instead of paragraphs — and Q2 pays 3 marks for separating hard from soft and giving a checkable test for each hard constraint. The textbook form is: minimise fi(x) for i = 1…M, subject to hj(x) = 0 for j = 1…J, and gk(x) ≤ 0 for k = 1…K, where x = (x₁, x₂, …, xd) is the design vector — simply the list of your decision variables, one slot per decision, which is the same list that will become your chromosome in Lesson 4. Read it slowly.

An f is a score you want small; the textbook calls the f's the objective functions or cost functions, and M = 1 means single-objective while M > 1 means multi-objective. An h is a rule of the form “this must come out exactly zero”. A g is a rule of the form “this must not go above zero”.

J and K are just how many of each you have. Almost every hard rule in a scheduling brief bends into a g: yard section A of the port holds 200 containers, so g₁ = (containers stacked in A) − 200 ≤ 0. And that pays off twice, because the penalty you will add to fitness for breaking that rule in Lesson 7 is literally max(0, g₁) — zero while the rule holds, and equal to the overflow when it does not. One symbol, two jobs.

Kinds of problems (vocabulary you'll reuse in answers)

  • Continuous vs discrete — choosing amounts (a temperature) vs choosing among options (which hall). Test scenarios are discrete, sometimes with continuous costs on top.
  • Single- vs multi-objective — one score vs several conflicting goals (cost and fairness and speed). Test scenarios are naturally multi-objective; you choose whether to combine goals into one score (a weighted sum — multiply each goal by a weight you pick and add them into a single number) or keep them separate and report the whole set of best trade-offs, where improving one goal necessarily worsens another (the Pareto front — Lesson 9).
  • Constrained vs unconstrained — without constraints, optimisation is trivial: just pick the extreme value. Constraints are what make it a real problem — and test scenarios are heavily constrained; that's where marks hide.
  • Static vs dynamic — the test's problems are static (data doesn't change mid-solve), worth one line as an assumption.

Static versus dynamic, spelled out, because it is worth an assumption line in Q1 and a critical-awareness line in Q2. A static problem holds still while you solve it: all the data is fixed at the moment you start and nothing arrives or changes mid-solve — planning next Tuesday's delivery route, or the exam timetable you are handed on Friday.

A dynamic problem keeps moving while the algorithm runs: re-routing a ride-hailing driver as new fare requests come in through the day, or a trading strategy where prices change second by second. Dynamic problems need algorithms that can keep adapting rather than run once and stop, and that is a real strength of CI — a population is already a set of alternatives standing by to be re-scored when the data shifts, where an exact method would have to start over.

Every test scenario so far has been static, so write the assumption explicitly — “I treat this as static: all ship ETAs and container counts are known at 08:00” — and then add the caveat that a late arrival would make it dynamic and force a re-solve. The assumption earns marks; the caveat earns critical-awareness marks.

Careful with the word, though: dynamic also names a kind of penalty in Lesson 7 — a weight that grows as generations pass. Different word, different job.

Why these problems are genuinely hard

Take the scenario type you are most likely to be handed: exam timetabling. A university has a list of exams and a fixed number of day-and-room slots to put them in, and every exam must go somewhere. That is the decision — one slot per exam — and the slider below simply counts how many complete timetables that produces. Drag it and watch the number stop meaning anything.

Try it — how fast search spaces explode

Real numbers on the explosion, the ones worth quoting in an answer:

ProblemSearch space
4-digit PIN10,000 combinations — brute force is fine
Route 10 cities3,628,800 orderings
Route 15 cities≈ 1.3 trillion
Route 20 cities≈ 2.4 quintillion (2.4 × 10¹⁸)
Route 25 citiesmore orderings than stars in the galaxy
Assign 50 tasks to 10 machines10⁵⁰ — bigger still

Five factors make real optimisation hard. Naming them is the standard justification paragraph for “why not brute force / why CI”:

  • Combinatorial explosion — options multiply rather than add. If each of n exams independently takes one of k slots, the number of complete timetables is kn — not n × k. With 40 exams and 20 slots that is 2040 ≈ 1.1 × 10⁵² schedules. Brute force is dead on arrival; this justifies a CI approach in your answer's opening line.

    Problems of this shape are NP-hard — shorthand for a class with no known method that guarantees the best answer in a time that stays reasonable as the problem grows. That is the formal version of “brute force is dead on arrival”, and it is precisely why CI trades the guarantee away: a very good answer you actually receive beats a perfect one you never do.

  • Local optima — “good enough” traps: a schedule that no single small change improves, yet far from the best. Nature-inspired search escapes via randomness (mutation — small random changes to a solution, Lesson 6) and populations exploring in parallel.
  • Interacting constraints — moving one exam to fix a clash creates two new ones. Improvements don't compose, and with enough interlocking rules, finding any valid solution is hard before you start optimising at all.
  • Uncertainty and noise — real data lies: forecasts are wrong, sensors drift, customers change their minds. Exact methods assume clean inputs; CI tolerates mess.
  • Conflicting objectives — the goals fight one another, so improving one makes another worse: schedule cheaply and you schedule unfairly; clear every ship fast and crane costs climb. There is no single best answer, only trade-offs you have to defend. This is the factor students forget, and it is expensive — the walkthrough's own mistake list flags “only one objective: the scenario lists six aims, and an answer with one objective cannot pass Q2 well”.

A sixth reason, and the one that decides which family of algorithm you are even allowed to use: there is usually nothing to differentiate. Classical optimisation methods work by computing the gradient — the slope of the objective at the point you are standing on — and walking downhill. That needs three things a real brief rarely supplies.

It needs the objective in analytical form, an equation you can do calculus on; but “the total delay this timetable produces” is not an equation, it is whatever a decoder reports after laying out the entire day. It needs the derivative to exist, which fails even for some perfectly continuous functions — g(x, y) = (|x| + |y|)·e−x²−y² has its minimum at (0, 0) and no derivative there, because of the absolute values.

And where it does exist it may simply be too expensive to compute. So modern nature-inspired algorithms are almost all gradient-free: they never differentiate anything and only ever ask your fitness function to score a candidate. One sentence of that in Q3 gives you the technical case for a CI method, not just the big-number one.

Notice what that list quietly implies: size alone does not make a problem hard. A list of ten million numbers sorts in under a second, because sorting has structure you can exploit and no rule forbidding any particular arrangement. What hurts is constraint interaction — rules whose satisfaction depends on one another, so that fixing one breaks another and nothing can be settled in isolation.

That is why a 40-exam timetable with room compatibility, student clash rules and travel gaps is brutal while sorting 40,000 cities alphabetically is trivial, even though the second number is bigger. So when you justify a CI approach in the test, open with the big number but argue from the tangle: the rules interact, improvements don't compose, the landscape is full of traps. The big number is the headline; the interaction is the case.

The investigation checklist — eight questions, before you pick an algorithm

The module's own checklist for meeting a new problem, and the best possible use of your first ten minutes on Friday. Answer all eight in note form in the margin and Q1 and Q2 are half-drafted before you write a sentence of prose. (1) What are the decision variables — what shape does one complete solution have? (2) What is the objective: maximising or minimising, one goal or several? (3) What are the constraints, and which are hard and which are soft? (4) How big is the search space — could you just try every option? (5) Is the problem continuous, discrete, or mixed? (6) Is it static, or does it change while you solve it? (7) Is the data clean, or noisy and uncertain? (8) How will you measure success — what counts as a good solution?

Each answer has a home on the paper: 1 to 3 are the three ingredients and become Q1's decision list and Q2's constraint table, 4 is your “why not brute force” number, 5 to 7 are your assumption lines, and 8 is the fitness function itself. The warning the lecturer attaches to it is worth carrying into the hall: the hardest part of a CI project is usually not the algorithm, it is understanding the problem — pick the wrong representation, the wrong objective, or miss a constraint and nothing downstream can rescue you.

Reading a scenario like an examiner

Drill this ritual — it's the first 15 minutes of your test:

  1. Read once for the story. Read again with a pen, sorting every sentence into: entity data (things to schedule), resource data (halls, staff, machines), hard rule (must hold, or the solution is not a solution at all), soft preference (you would rather it held; breaking it only costs you score), or cost. That hard/soft split decides validity versus fitness and carries a lesson of its own — Lesson 7.
  2. List the decisions. Ask: “what does the scenario leave up to me?” — assignment? order? timing? on/off activation?
  3. Name the objectives — what makes one legal answer better than another, and in which direction (maximise or minimise)? Count them: scenarios normally list five or six aims, and an answer carrying only one cannot pass Q2 well.
  4. Put the rules into two columns on the page, hard and soft, and keep them there. Q2 hands out marks for that split alone, and mixing the two columns is the single most expensive slip in the paper.
  5. Size the search space in one line — could you just try every option? The answer is always no, and that single line is your written justification for using CI at all.
  6. Write assumptions for anything the brief doesn't state (time granularity, resource behaviour). “I assume [X] because the brief does not state it.” Assumptions carry explicit marks.

Do all of that in plain English, before you write a single symbol. The sentence you are trying to complete is: “I am choosing [what] for [which things], so as to [goal], without breaking [rules].” For a hospital rota that reads: “I am choosing a shift for each nurse on each day, so as to cover every ward cheaply and fairly, without anyone working two shifts back to back.” Once that one sentence exists on your page, the decision variables are the first blank, the objective is the third, the constraints are the fourth — and the notation that follows is only bookkeeping on top of it. Students who jump straight to symbols invent variables the scenario never asked for and quietly lose the ones it did.

Expect the same brief to admit several defensible models, and stop hunting for the one true answer — there isn't one. In an exam timetable you can frame the decision as “which slot does each exam get” (one variable per exam) or as “which exams go into each slot” (one group per slot).

You can treat hall capacity as a hard rule that may never be broken, or as a cost you pay for exceeding. You can fold money and fairness into a single combined score, or keep them as separate objectives. Every one of those is markable. What is not markable is choosing silently.

The marks live in the sentence immediately after the choice — “I model capacity as a penalty rather than a hard rule because a slightly over-full hall is recoverable, whereas an encoding with no valid solutions is not.” A defensible design plus its justification beats a better design with none.

His marking advice, walking through a scheduling brief that mentioned neither part-time students nor holidays — lightly tidied from the automatic transcript

“The scenario doesn't mention full-time, part-time students or staff. You can, you want to do it, you can, but it just makes it more complicated and therefore more things to go wrong as far as your answer is concerned. So leave it out… Doesn't mention holidays… it's not mentioned, so you can leave it out.” (The ellipses mark where he moves between his two examples.) Complexity you invent is risk you volunteered for.

Lesson 3 · ~20 min

The Genetic Algorithm, From Zero

The GA is the module's core algorithm and the assumed solver in Q1 and Q2. Here is the whole machine and its vocabulary — the words the examiner expects you to use.

Lesson 3 on one slide
  • Chromosome = one complete candidate written as a string · gene = one slot in it · allele = the value in that slot · population = the current set of candidates.
  • The loop: initialise → evaluate → select → crossover → mutate → replace → repeat until a stopping rule fires.
  • Encoding is schedule → string; decoding is string → schedule. Two directions, both named, both marked.
  • Fitness is computed on the decoded object — you score timetables, never strings.
  • The convergence curve: steep early gains, then a plateau — which is why you name a stopping rule (generations, time, or no improvement for k rounds).
Tomorrow this buys you: the exact vocabulary Q1 is marked in — using “gene/allele/decode” correctly is the cheapest credibility on the paper.
Meet the running example — a container port. Every lesson from here reuses it, so here it is in full; you need nothing else to follow along.

A port must unload four ships (SH1–SH4) in one working shift, and they do not all arrive at once. SH1 is there from 08:00 with 150 containers, high priority, perishable cargo; SH2 from 09:30 with 200, normal priority, too long a vessel for section A; SH3 from 10:15 with 100, emergency priority, hazardous; SH4 from 11:00 with 180, normal — 630 containers in total.

That arrival time is the ship's ETA (estimated time of arrival), and those ETAs and priorities are the raw material of every waiting term you will later write into a fitness function. The quay (the dock edge where ships tie up) is divided into 3 sections, A, B and C, written as 1/2/3 inside chromosomes; a ship's parking spot in a section is its berth.

Behind each section is a buffer zone, the yard area where unloaded containers wait for collection, with a limited capacity (A 200, B 250, C 150). The port owns 3 quay cranes (C1–C3), the big dockside machines that lift containers off ships; they differ in speed and fuel, and any crane can be sent to any section — repositioning costs one 15-minute slot — but only one crane may work a given section at a time, so two cranes can never double up on one ship.

What is being decided: where each ship docks, which crane serves it, in what order ships are handled when they share a section, and at what time each job runs. What counts as good: little waiting, urgent ships early, cranes kept busy, energy and berth costs low. The rules that bind you: not every ship fits every section (SH2 is too long for A; SH3 carries hazardous cargo and needs a certified berth, which B is not), only one ship per section at a time, only one crane active in any one section at a time, a 30-minute changeover before the next ship takes that berth, no ship starts before its ETA, a buffer zone must never overflow, and every container must be unloaded before the shift ends at 16:00. Note where that last one sits: completeness is a hard rule, not an aim.

Unloading three ships beautifully and leaving the fourth aboard is not a mediocre schedule, it is an invalid one — and the hard/soft split is worth marks in Q2 on its own. One figure in that list is worth writing down twice rather than assuming, and his own walkthrough deck does exactly that: the 30-minute changeover appears once among the hard constraints and again on the slide headed “The assumptions you must state”, phrased there as “30 minutes between one ship leaving a berth and the next arriving”.

His slide planning your two hours in the hall is blunter still: “Read twice. Write your assumptions down first — especially buffer clearance, berth occupancy and changeover.” So even though the brief hands you the number, put the line “I assume a 30-minute changeover between one ship leaving a berth and the next arriving” in your assumptions. Assumptions carry explicit marks, and that is the cheapest one on the page.

The numbers the cranes run on. The shift is 08:00–16:00 — eight hours. The cranes lift at C1 50 containers/hour (electric), C2 60/hour (diesel) and C3 45/hour (electric): 155/hour combined. Every crane stops 30 minutes after 3 hours of continuous work, and the two electric ones need 1 hour of charging per 4 hours worked.

Those two rules are why the honest capacity is not 155 × 8 = 1,240: C2 gets 7 working hours out of its 8 (420 containers), C1 and C3 only 6.5 each (325 and 292.5), for roughly 1,037 containers liftable in the shift against the 630 that must move — about 40% spare. Keep those figures; Lesson 12 turns that one sum into the move that reframes the whole answer, and you cannot make it without them.

That is everything these lessons use. The Walkthrough page adds the two tables you only need once you are actually scoring schedules — the berth handling cost of docking each ship in each section, and the worked timetable — and solves the whole thing end to end.

The metaphor

Evolution improves species without a designer: individuals that fit their environment survive, breed, and pass on traits; random mutation adds novelty; over generations the population adapts. A GA does exactly this to solutions:

Biology wordIn a GA it meansPort example
IndividualOne complete candidate solutionOne full berth-and-crane schedule
ChromosomeThe encoded form of that solution — a string of values1231 = which section each ship uses
GeneOne slot in the chromosome — one decisionGene 3 = “ship 3 goes to section 3”
Allele / legal valuesAn allele is one particular value a gene holds; the set it may draw from = the gene's legal valuesIn the chromosome above, ship 2's gene holds allele 2 (= section B); its legal values are {2, 3}, never 1, because SH2 is too long for section A
PopulationThe set of individuals alive this generation (e.g. 100)100 different schedules
FitnessThe score saying how good an individual is — decide which direction “good” runs before you write a single component, and never mix the twoWeighted cost of the schedule, so here lower is better (Lesson 6 shows how selection is told which way to face)
GenerationOne full cycle of the loop below—
Genotype vs phenotypeThe encoded string vs the real-world solution it decodes toThe digits vs the actual timetable

The loop (memorise this — it opens many answers)

  1. Initialise a random population of chromosomes.
  2. Evaluate — decode each chromosome and compute its fitness.
  3. Select parents — better fitness ⇒ better chance of breeding (Lesson 6).
  4. Crossover — combine two parents' genes into offspring.
  5. Mutate — randomly tweak a few genes for novelty.
  6. Replace — form the next generation (optionally copying the best few through unchanged first: elitism — Lesson 6).
  7. Repeat until a stopping condition. The lecture names two — a maximum number of generations, or no noticeable improvement over the last few generations. Two more are standard practice: a wall-clock time budget, and reaching a target fitness, which is only usable when you already know what “solved” looks like.

Step 1 is a design decision, not a formality

“Initialise a random population” means: for every individual, fill each gene with a value drawn at random from that gene's own legal set — so if SH2 may only berth in sections 2 or 3, its gene is drawn from {2, 3} and never from {1, 2, 3}. Do it that way and generation 1 is already compatible by construction, which is the alphabet-restriction argument (Lesson 4) paying out before the search has taken a single step.

Two consequences worth a sentence each in an answer. First, where you start matters: a genetic algorithm is stochastic, so results can depend heavily on the initial population, and if the best region of the search space is small and isolated and no starting individual lands near it, the run may never find it.

The two standard defences are to run the algorithm several times from different random starting populations and report the mean and standard deviation rather than one lucky run, and to run long enough that the population “forgets” where it started. Second, the initial population does not have to be uniformly random: you can seed part of it with solutions built by a quick greedy rule — the module's Acme lab builds 20% of its population that way (Lesson 5) — which converges faster but costs you initial diversity. Stating which you chose, and admitting that cost, is exactly the kind of line the “implementation” marks are for.

What that loop looks like from the inside

Generation 1 is noise: a hundred schedules built by random choices, nearly all of them poor, with fitness scores scattered from terrible to merely bad. Scattered is exactly the point — among a hundred random guesses, a few will accidentally get one thing right: two ships that happen not to clash, a crane that happens to stay busy all shift.

Selection notices those, breeding copies them into the next batch, and by generation 10 that lucky feature is present in most of the population while everything else is still churning. By generation 50 the population has usually collapsed into a family of near-identical near-solutions differing in a handful of genes, and the best-fitness curve has gone flat — that flattening is precisely what a “no improvement for k generations” stopping rule is watching for. The characteristic shape is a steep early climb, where easy gains are everywhere, then a long shallow tail grinding out the last few percent.

The curve, with real numbers on it

The module's first lab runs a GA on a 100-gene binary chromosome whose fitness is simply the count of 1s (so a perfect score is 100), with a population of 100, and prints one line per generation. Its log is the shape described above made concrete: generation 0 best 61, average 50.3; gen 10 best 79, average 75.19; gen 20 best 90, average 87.09; gen 30 best 96, average 94.73; gen 68 best 100, average 98.13. Read two things off it.

First the steep-then-flat shape: roughly three quarters of the whole gain (61 → 90) arrives in the first twenty generations, and the last ten points take another forty-eight. Second — and this is the part worth a mark — the run stalls without being finished: best fitness sits at 96 from generation 29 all the way to generation 45 while the average actually drifts downwards (95.95 → 95.87), then breaks out and reaches 100. A “stop after 10 generations with no improvement” rule would have killed this run at 96 and never seen the optimum.

So when you name a termination criterion in an answer, name the patience k as a judgement call and say what it costs you either way.

Which leads to the idea most students miss: the population, not the individual, is the unit of progress. No single chromosome ever improves — a chromosome is a fixed string of values; it learns nothing and changes nothing. What improves is the distribution: good gene values get more copies each generation, bad ones get fewer, and the crowd's average fitness drifts upward.

That reframing also explains why population size is a real design decision rather than a detail. Too small, and the crowd runs out of raw material to recombine and locks onto the first decent idea it stumbles on; too large, and every generation costs a fortune in fitness evaluations to buy variety you were not short of.

Sizing a chromosome when a gene holds a number, not a yes/no. Here is the whole machine on the smallest problem in the module's reading, worked end to end — the first time in this site you see a chromosome sized rather than assumed.

The problem, in full. Minimise z = x² − 2y + 3, where x and y are integers from 0 to 7 inclusive. Nothing else; no constraints.

Step 1 — size each gene. A binary gene holds only 0 or 1, so a variable with V possible values needs enough bits that 2bits ≥ V. Here x has 8 possible values and 2³ = 8, so 3 bits suffice: x = 0 is 000, x = 7 is 111. y is identical. Step 2 — concatenate.

3 bits + 3 bits = a 6-bit chromosome, left half = x, right half = y. The search space is 2⁶ = 64. Step 3 — decode one by hand. 101010 → x = 101 = 5, y = 010 = 2, so z = 25 − 4 + 3 = 24. Step 4 — fitness. z itself, minimised; no penalty is needed because every 6-bit string decodes to a legal (x, y) pair. A few generations find the minimum, z = −11 at x = 0, y = 7 — chromosome 000111.

Carry the rule, not the example: count the values a gene must express, then give it enough bits to express exactly those. Write that sentence in Q1 whenever a decision is a quantity (how many drones, which of eight zones, which 20-minute slot) rather than a choice from a short list — and it is also the antidote to the classic blunder in Lesson 4, spending 32 bits on a value from 1–10.

Schema, seen rather than defined. Run that same 6-bit problem in a room and the good answers come back clustered: z = −11 from 000111, −10 from 001111, −9 from 000110, −8 from 001110. Line the four up and the common pattern is visible without any theory: the first two bits are always 0 and the fourth and fifth are always 1, while bits 3 and 6 vary freely.

Write the shared part with a wildcard for “don't care” and you have the schema 0 0 * 1 1 * — the pattern of values a genetic algorithm is really manipulating, underneath the individual chromosomes it appears to be copying. That is what Lesson 6 means when it says crossover preserves schemas (it copies contiguous stretches wholesale, so the block 00 or 11 travels intact) while mutation disrupts them (it changes one gene at random, and one flipped bit destroys the pattern) — which is the whole reason crossover fires at a high rate and mutation at roughly one gene per chromosome.

Watch a live GA solve a knapsack

The knapsack problem, stated in full (you'll meet it constantly): you have a set of items, each with a weight and a value, and a bag that can carry only so much total weight. You choose which items to take; you want the highest total value; the one rule is that total weight must not exceed the bag's capacity.

Here there are 10 items and a capacity of 400, and selections that bust the capacity are penalised rather than forbidden — the machinery behind that choice is Lesson 7's business. The penalty route is chosen here so you can watch fitness react to a bad pick; Lesson 7 explains why the module's own lab instead handled capacity inside the decoder, skipping any item that would not fit, and why the cheapest tool that works should win.

Each bar = best fitness in the population that generation. This is the module's classic first example running for real, in your browser — expect the steep-then-flat shape described above.

Press Run.

Exploration vs exploitation — the tension behind everything

Before the two words, the picture they describe. Imagine the search space as a landscape: every possible solution is a spot on the ground, and the height of that spot is its fitness. Two spots are neighbours if one small change turns one into the other — move a single exam, swap two cities, send one ship to a different section.

Optimising is climbing this landscape in thick fog: you can feel the slope under your feet but you cannot see the horizon. A simple hill-climber — always step to a better neighbour, never step down — therefore stops dead on the first hilltop it reaches. That hilltop is a local optimum: a solution that no single small change improves, and which may still be far below the true best, the global optimum.

Real problems are multimodal — hills everywhere — so this is not an unlucky edge case, it is the normal situation. A GA survives it two ways at once: it keeps a hundred climbers scattered on different hills, and its random mutation lets a climber occasionally step downhill and discover a better slope on the other side.

Every design choice in a GA balances two forces:

  • Exploitation (textbooks also say intensification) — concentrate on the best solutions found so far (strong selection pressure — how heavily breeding favours the current best — plus elitism). Too much ⇒ premature convergence: the whole population turns near-identical too early and gets stuck in a local optimum.
  • Exploration (textbooks also say diversification) — keep trying new regions (mutation, diverse selection). Too much ⇒ random search that never settles.

Use these two words when justifying operators (operators = the GA's moves: selection, crossover, mutation) in Q1/Q3 — they are the professor's favourite axis, and an entire session of the module is built around them.

The same tension explains why the loop needs both crossover and mutation, and saying so is worth marks. Crossover is recombination: it assumes good solutions are built out of good parts, and mixes parts from two parents in the hope the child inherits both. It moves in large jumps, but only ever within the material the population already holds — if no chromosome anywhere currently carries a 3 in gene 7, crossover can never invent one. Mutation is the opposite: a tiny random change, independent of everyone else, and the only operator able to reintroduce a value the population has lost.

Run crossover alone and the population converges quickly and then dies, every individual a copy of every other, no further progress possible. Run mutation alone and you have an aimless random walk. Together they are the ratchet from Lesson 1 made concrete — mutation supplies the variation, selection supplies the direction, crossover compounds the winnings.

Vocabulary the textbooks add (Yang's Nature-Inspired Optimization Algorithms opens with these — cheap marks for sounding well-read):

  • Who invented this (Holland, 1975) — the genetic algorithm was developed by John Holland and his collaborators at the University of Michigan across the 1960s and 1970s; as early as 1962 he was the first to use crossover and recombination to model an adaptive system, and the book that gathers the work is Adaptation in Natural and Artificial Systems (University of Michigan Press, 1975).

    Six words in your opening line — “I would use a genetic algorithm (Holland, 1975)” — cost you nothing and read as though you have opened a book. It is the same cheap-credibility move as citing Wolpert & Macready for No-Free-Lunch, Kennedy & Eberhart (1995) for PSO, Bonabeau, Dorigo & Theraulaz (1999) for swarm intelligence and Deb et al. (2002) for NSGA-II.

  • No-Free-Lunch theorem (Wolpert & Macready, 1997) — averaged over all possible problems, no algorithm outperforms any other. Consequence: there is no universal best solver; you tailor the algorithm to the problem. A ready-made opening or closing line for Q3.
  • Heuristic vs metaheuristic — a heuristic is a trial-and-error rule of thumb that finds good-enough solutions with no optimality guarantee; a metaheuristic is a higher-level strategy combining randomisation with local search, managing the exploration/exploitation trade-off. GA, PSO and ACO are all metaheuristics.
  • Classification axes — deterministic vs stochastic (Lesson 1); and trajectory-based (one solution walks the space — simulated annealing is the classic) vs population-based (many solutions searched in parallel — GA, PSO, ACO).
  • Unimodal vs multimodal — a fitness landscape with one peak vs many. On unimodal problems exploitation wins; on multimodal ones exploration earns its cost.

  • Parameter tuning vs parameter control — two words that make one sentence of any answer sound like a postgraduate wrote it. Tuning means fixing a parameter's value before the run and leaving it alone: a crossover rate, a population size. Control means varying it during the run according to a rule: inertia decay in PSO is parameter control, so is a cooling schedule in simulated annealing, and so is any mutation rate you raise when diversity collapses.

    Every algorithm on the Q3 menu has parameters, and their setting “can largely influence the behavior and performance of an algorithm” — which is exactly why “name your parameters” is a mark row. The closing line, if you have room: tuning is itself an optimisation problem, since you are optimising the optimiser, which Yang calls a hyperoptimisation problem — and there are “no well-established methods for universal parameter tuning”. That converts a list of Greek letters into critical awareness, which is the more expensive commodity.

Where the GA sits in your test answer

Q1 and Q2 assume a GA. You are not asked to code one — every closed-book paper, this one included, says “explain” or “outline”, and the only papers that ever wanted skeletal code or DEAP snippets were older open-book sittings on a different mark split. You're asked to design its inputs: the chromosome (Lessons 4–5), the fitness function (Lessons 7–8), and to say which genetic operators you would use and how they would be applied to that chromosome — the newest paper makes “how the genetic operators will be applied” an explicit bullet of the 15-mark Q1, so if your chromosome has two segments of different types you name a different operator for each and say that running one across both would produce invalid offspring (Lesson 6).

Q3 asks what changes if you hand the same problem to a different cook — any other computational-intelligence optimisation algorithm. That can be a swarm (PSO, ACO), a single-solution searcher (simulated annealing, tabu search), a grouping GA with local search, or an Artificial Immune System (AIS), which several older papers name outright in the question. All of them are on the menu in Lessons 10–11.

His tailor's-suit analogy — why an off-the-shelf algorithm must be customised to your problem

He used this in class while explaining the coursework, in an exchange about whether his supplied baseline code was “the only solution”. Lightly cleaned from the automatic meeting transcript — the substance is his, the punctuation is not, and the transcript's “I'm a trainer” is plainly “I'm a tailor”:

“Let me give you an analogy. I'm a tailor… I make the clothes for people. You need a suit… you go to a shop, H&M, you buy a suit, but this is a one-size-fits-all suit, that means that doesn't fit you very well. So you bring it to me, and my job is to customise it to fit you specifically… You have a problem, and I bring my suit to you.

This is a general, well-fitting suit. It's a suit, I can wear it, but it doesn't quite fit my proportions… so you need to tweak and tailor that suit to fit me as well.”

What this is and is not. He was talking about adapting a generic GA to a particular problem — its initialisation, its operators, its parameters — not about encoding specifically. Take it as the module's governing attitude and as ready-made Q3 material: a textbook algorithm is the H&M suit, and the marks are in the alterations you make for this scenario. Q3 asks for exactly that tailoring, which is why roughly half its ten marks are for applying the algorithm rather than describing it.

Lesson 4 · ~25 min · core exam material

Encoding I — The Five Encodings

Encoding is the translation from real-world solution to chromosome. It is the single most examined skill in this module — and five encoding types cover essentially everything it will ask you to represent.

Lesson 4 on one slide
  • The five encodings: Binary · Integer · Real · Permutation · Tree (grid is a bonus sixth pattern, not one of the five).
  • Match decision flavour → gene shape: categorical → integer genes · on/off → bits · order → permutation.
  • A permutation breaks under ordinary crossover — it needs OX or PMX plus swap mutation. Saying so is a justification mark.
  • Five properties to judge any encoding: Completeness · Non-redundancy · Connectedness · Feasibility · Simplicity.
  • Restrict the alphabet and an illegal choice becomes unwritable — the constraint vanishes and the search space shrinks.
Tomorrow this buys you: Q1's representation row (4 marks) and the “I chose ___ over ___ because” justification (2 marks).

The translation problem

A GA can only manipulate strings of values. So you must decide: how does a string of values represent a complete solution? That choice determines which operators work, which constraints can even be violated, and how big the search space is. Choose well and half your constraints disappear; choose badly and every offspring is invalid.

Keep the working cycle in view: encode once, when you design the representation (and again only to write the initial population), then for every individual of every generation decode → check feasibility → evaluate fitness. That inner loop runs thousands of times per solve, which is why a cheap, mostly-valid encoding matters so much — you pay its decoding cost on every single evaluation.

Understand why this one decision dominates the entire project, because that understanding is what separates a 60% answer from a 90% one. The chromosome is not a storage format; it is the shape everything else is built on, and every other component inherits it. Your operators inherit it: a fixed-length integer string accepts textbook one-point crossover unchanged, while an ordering does not and needs specialised order-preserving surgery instead.

Your constraints inherit it: a rule you make unwritable in the encoding costs you nothing ever again, whereas the same rule left writable must be caught by a decoder, a repair routine or a penalty on every one of the thousands of evaluations. Your fitness inherits it: each component has to be computable from the decoded chromosome, so a cost your string cannot express is a cost you cannot optimise.

Choose the encoding last and you spend the project patching around it; choose it first and well and most of the remaining design falls out for free. This is why Q1 comes first on the paper, and why a poor encoding cannot be rescued by a brilliant fitness function. One caution before you fall in love with your genes: on his indicative split only about 4 of Q1's 15 marks are for the chromosome itself, the rest going to problem understanding, decoding, data requirements and justification (Lesson 11 sets out the whole split). The encoding decides everything downstream — but drawing it is not where the marks are.

Sanity-check a proposed encoding before you commit to it — four questions, a minute of work. They are the five properties below asked in plain English, so run them here and use the formal names when you write up. Can I write down the answer I'd give by hand? Take one sensible solution and encode it; if you cannot, the encoding is incomplete and some real solutions are unreachable. Can I read a random string back?

Fill the genes with random legal values and decode it out loud; if the decoding is ambiguous, or leans on rules you never stated, your decoder is doing undeclared work that will not survive marking. What fraction of random strings are legal? If the honest answer is “almost none”, the GA will spend its life repairing instead of searching. Does changing one gene change one thing?

If a single flip rearranges the whole solution, crossover and mutation will scramble rather than refine, and the search degenerates towards random guessing. Those four questions are the five properties below in everyday words: question one is completeness, question three is feasibility, question four is connectedness, and question two is really the decoding marks in disguise, since a decoder you cannot state unambiguously is a decoder you cannot write out as a numbered procedure.

Notice what the four do not test — non-redundancy — so add it by hand: can two different strings decode to the same solution? An encoding that survives all five is defensible, and the question it stumbles on is the weakness you name when you compare your design with the alternative you rejected, which is where the justification marks actually live. When you write the answer up, use the five formal names, because those are the words the marker is scanning for.

The five types (plus a bonus pattern)

1 · Binary — yes/no decisions

One bit per decision. The classic: Knapsack — items with weight and value, a capacity; gene i = 1 means “take item i”. 01101

Also perfect for on/off activation decisions. A real one from a past paper: a university pays a fee every time it opens a building for an exam session, so “is building B open in session S?” is itself a decision worth one bit — leave a building shut and you save the fee, but every exam it would have hosted must fit somewhere else. Same shape in machine learning as feature selection: gene i = 1 means “feed feature i to the model.”

Search-space size: a binary chromosome of length L spans 2L possibilities — and L is simply the number of decisions. Write both facts in Q1; they cost one line each.

Decode one by hand (an exam-day warm-up): items A–E weigh 3/5/2/6/4 kg, are worth RM40/70/30/90/50, capacity 10 kg. 10101 = take A, C, E → 3+2+4 = 9 kg, value RM120, valid. Chromosome 11101 = A, B, C, E → 3+5+2+4 = 14 kg — over capacity, invalid. That two-line check is decoding.

Then size it, in the same breath. That knapsack has five items, so it has five decisions, so the chromosome is five genes long and the search space is 25 = 32 chromosomes — small enough to write out on one sheet of paper, which is precisely why it is a teaching example and not a real problem.

Add five more items and you are at 210 = 1,024; the ten-item knapsack in the demo below is exactly that. At fifty items it is 250 ≈ 1.1 quadrillion, and brute force is finished. Doing this arithmetic out loud on your encoding is a standing instruction for Friday, not an optional flourish: it converts “I chose binary” into “I chose binary; my chromosome has L genes because the scenario leaves L yes/no decisions open; that is a space of 2L candidates, which is why a population search rather than enumeration”. One line of counting, and you have justified the whole method before describing a single gene.

Try it — knapsack encoding, live fitness

Click items to toggle their gene. Capacity 400. Watch validity and fitness respond. Overweight picks are penalised here rather than blocked, so the score reacts where you can see it; the module's own lab skipped the offending items in the decoder instead, and Lesson 7 is where you learn to argue that choice either way.

2 · Integer — picking from a list

Each gene holds an index into a list of options. The workhorse of scheduling: one gene per exam holding its hall number; one gene per ship holding its section number; one gene per guard per day holding the shift that guard works — the module's own guard scenario runs three shifts a day, so the legal values are 0 = off, 1 = morning, 2 = afternoon, 3 = night (Lesson 5 works that rota in full; its lab codes the same rota the other way round, as one bit per guard-shift slot — either is defensible provided you state your alphabet). SH11SH22SH33SH41 reads “SH1 to section 1, SH2 to 2, SH3 to 3, SH4 to 1”.

A second integer chromosome, shaped differently on purpose. Integer genes need not all index the same list. Assign five students to three supervisors and every gene draws from the same set {1, 2, 3}: the chromosome 21312 reads student 1 → supervisor 2, student 2 → supervisor 1, student 3 → supervisor 3, student 4 → supervisor 1, student 5 → supervisor 2. Now build a set meal instead.

The chromosome 4271 means starter #4, main course #2, drink #7, dessert #1 — four genes indexing four different menus, one item chosen from each by position. Same encoding type, two quite different shapes, and the second is the one that fits a scenario where each decision picks from its own catalogue: a surgery's theatre from the theatre list, its block from the block list, its anaesthetist from the pool.

The exam consequence is one sentence: say which list each position indexes and what its allowed range is. A marker cannot check a decode against a list you never named, and “gene 3 holds a 7” means nothing until you have said 7 of what.

Killer move (worth marks): restrict each gene's legal values to what that entity is actually allowed. Take the port from Lesson 3 — four ships, three sections. Unrestricted, that is 3⁴ = 81 possible assignments. But SH2 is too long for section A and SH3 needs a certified berth that B does not have, so each of those two ships has only two legal sections: 3 · 2 · 2 · 3 = 36. Two constraints just became unwritable — no chromosome in the entire search space can violate them — and the space shrank by more than half at zero running cost. Compare that with checking the same rule inside a fitness function on every evaluation, forever.

3 · Real-valued — continuous numbers

Genes are floats, each with a defined range (e.g. 0.0–1.0, or −10 to 10). Used for tuning continuous parameters — antenna angles, a chemical reactor's speed, temperature and pressure, the continuous settings of a machine-learning model being tuned by a GA (learning rate, dropout rate, weights) — and crucially for random keys, the trick that lets PSO handle discrete problems (Lesson 10). Real-valued encoding is also used heavily in PSO itself, whose particles fly through continuous space natively.

Write one out — an abstract range is not a worked example. Suppose you are aiming an antenna that has three adjustable angles. The chromosome is three floats, one per angle, read in degrees: 47.2−12.891.5 means set angle 1 to 47.2°, angle 2 to −12.8°, angle 3 to 91.5°. Decoding is a single sentence — point the antenna at those three settings and measure the signal; that measurement is the score.

Notice what makes it legal rather than merely numeric: each gene carries its own declared range, and the ranges need not match (an azimuth might live in 0–360 while a tilt lives in −90 to 90). State the range beside every real gene, exactly as you state the legal value set beside every integer gene — it is the same mark, claimed the same way, and without it “a float” is not a representation.

The same discipline transfers straight to Q3: a PSO particle is precisely this, a vector of real numbers with a declared range per dimension, which is why real-valued encoding is the one PSO speaks natively.

4 · Permutation — when ORDER matters

The chromosome is an ordering; every ID appears exactly once. The classic: Travelling Salesperson (TSP) — visit every city exactly once and return home (a closed loop); in problem-type language: discrete, single-objective, constrained, static. 3142 = visit city 3, then 1, then 4, then 2. Decoding is one rule: sum the pairwise distances along the tour — that total is the score.

State whether the hop home counts, because it is a convention and not a law — and his own labs split on it. The ACO notebook's cost function adds only the n−1 forward edges (for i in range(len(path) - 1), and nothing after the loop); the bee-colony notebook runs the same loop and then adds map[path[-1]][path[0]], so it charges for the return leg; the TSP tutorial hands you def distance(self, route) with the body left blank for you to complete.

Take the closed loop as your default — a salesperson who never goes home has not finished the tour, and it is the loop that makes the (n−1)! count below the right one — then write your choice down in one clause. What happens when nobody writes it down is visible in his bee notebook itself: its cost function charges for the return leg while its pheromone update deposits on the forward edges only, so the two halves of one file are scoring different tours. Declaring the convention costs you six words and is exactly the kind of stated assumption Q1 pays for.

Now write a bad one, because that is the half everyone skips. Take the module's own five-city version: cities A–E, the salesperson starts and finishes at A, so the chromosome permutes only the other four. BCDE decodes to the tour A → B → C → D → E → A. CEBD decodes to A → C → E → B → D → A. But DABC is invalid: A appears twice — once as the fixed home city and once in the body of the tour — and E never appears at all, so this string is not a tour of five cities and there is nothing for the decoder to measure.

That is the permutation rule broken in both directions at once: every ID exactly once, none repeated, none absent.
