The same failure is exactly what one-point crossover hands you when you cut two parents mid-permutation, which is why order-preserving operators are not a refinement but a requirement. Reproducing this pair — one legal string, one broken one with the broken rule named underneath — is the cheapest way to prove you understand your own validity rules.

Search-space size: n cities ⇒ n! orderings. 5 cities → 120; 10 → 3,628,800; 20 → ≈ 2.4 quintillion. Checking 20-city routes at a million per second would take ~77,000 years — the factorial explosion is your standard one-liner for “why CI.”

Two conventions for counting tours — know both, never mix them. You will meet both n! and (n−1)! quoted for TSP, sometimes in the same table, so be ready to say in half a sentence which one you used. n! counts every ordering of n items in a row, and that is the number to quote for a pure sequencing problem: the order jobs run on a machine, the order ships are served at a berth.

A TSP tour is different because it is a loop that starts and ends at a fixed home city, so rotations of the same loop are the same tour — nail the home city down and only the other n−1 are free to permute, giving (n−1)! genuinely distinct tours: 5 cities → 24, 10 → 362,880. Same problem, two conventions, and both are correct for what they count. Say in half a sentence which one you used and why, and your number is defensible either way.

Also: the order jobs are served in, or a priority order fed to a greedy placer (a decoder that walks the list top to bottom and drops each item into the first legal spot it finds). Warning you must write in the exam: standard crossover breaks permutations (you'd get a city twice). Permutations need order-preserving operators — OX / PMX crossover, swap or inversion mutation (Lesson 6).

5 · Tree — evolving formulas and programs

The chromosome is a tree: internal nodes are operators or functions (+, ×, if…), leaves are values or inputs. This is the encoding behind genetic programming (the GA sibling from Lesson 1's family tree) — instead of tuning a fixed-length string, you evolve the structure of a formula or small program itself. It resurfaces later in the module; for the test, knowing it completes the official list of five.

One chromosome, several types — the mix is allowed

Nothing forces every gene to be the same kind of thing. Take a worked case from outside scheduling: you are tuning a machine-learning model that has three settings — a learning rate (how big a step the model takes when it corrects itself), a dropout rate (the fraction of the network switched off during training to stop it memorising), and a number of layers.

The first two are real-valued, allowed ranges 0.0001 to 0.1 and 0.0 to 0.5; the third is an integer from 1 to 10. So the chromosome has length 3 and mixes real and integer values: 0.0120.304. Decoding is not arithmetic at all — build a model with those settings, train it, and measure its accuracy. The accuracy IS the score, and the GA maximises it.

Two things to carry into Friday. First, a count is never a real-valued gene: if a quantity counts things — layers, staff, trucks, sessions — it takes an integer gene even when every gene beside it is a float, because you cannot build 4.3 layers. Second, mutation and crossover must then be chosen per gene type — a small random nudge on the two floats, a legal-value reset on the integer — never one operator for the whole string.

That is the same idea as the heterogeneous segments of Lesson 5, with the types differing one gene at a time rather than one segment at a time.

Bonus pattern · Grid / matrix (2-D)

Not on the official list of five, but a pattern you'll want for timetable scenarios. Rows = resources, columns = time slots, cell = what's happening there. A timetable drawn literally. Exclusivity is automatic (one entry per cell) — but offspring from crossover are almost never valid, so it's repair-heavy (constraint tools: Lesson 7). Usually the design you mention and reject, which itself earns justification marks.

Properties of a good encoding — the five terms to name

  • Completeness — every real solution can be represented.
  • Non-redundancy — one solution ↔ ideally one chromosome; redundant encodings waste search.
  • Connectedness (textbooks outside this module say locality; write connectedness) — small gene change ⇒ small solution change; operators then improve rather than scramble.
  • Feasibility — ideally every chromosome decodes to a legal solution, or invalidity is rare and cheap to repair. His own gloss is the one to quote: “if 99% of chromosomes break a constraint, the algorithm wastes 99% of its time.”
  • Simplicity — easy to code, easy to manipulate; standard crossover/mutation produce sensible children without exotic machinery.

Exam habit: Q1's last 2 marks are labelled justification, and his walkthrough deck says exactly what buys them — “you compare your design with one alternative and name the trade-off you accepted”. So do not simply tick your own encoding off against the five properties: compare. Name one rival design you considered and rejected, then use these five terms as the vocabulary of the comparison — “I rejected the 2-D grid because standard crossover almost never returns a legal timetable, a feasibility failure I would have paid for on every one of thousands of evaluations, and I accepted a slightly longer chromosome in exchange.” One rival, one named property, one trade-off you took deliberately.

That sentence is the 2 marks; a properties checklist with nothing to compare it against is not. Keep the proportions in view too: only about 4 of Q1's 15 marks are for the chromosome itself, so do not spend all your time drawing genes.

Three classic encoding mistakes — the ones the module singles out; recognise them so you never make them:
  • Binary for TSP — a bag of bits cannot guarantee every city appears exactly once: a completeness fail.
  • Random integers for TSP — gene = “next city” with repeats allowed: almost every chromosome is an illegal tour, a feasibility fail.

  • 32 bits to store a value from 1–10 — 232 ≈ 4.3 billion different strings standing in for ten real choices, so over 99% of the search space is dead weight (the module's own word for it is “wasteful”). Label it a non-redundancy fail: crowds of different chromosomes decode to the same value, and the GA pays to rediscover that value under every one of its names.

    If instead your decoder rules the surplus codes illegal rather than letting them alias onto the ten, the same mistake becomes a feasibility fail — say which reading you are using and either label scores. It is not a simplicity fail: a 32-bit field is perfectly easy to code and to cross over, which is all simplicity asks. The cure is to size the gene to the decision — 4 bits, or better, one integer gene with legal values 1–10.

The lecturer's debugging heuristic: when a CI project won't work, look at the encoding first.

Hard vs soft, in one breath

“No lecturer should be taking two classes at the same time. Then we have soft constraints. It would be nice if you didn't have one class at 8:30 and another class at 5:00 with nothing in between… That would be a nicer solution.”

A favourite trip-up: state your direction (penalties: Lesson 7)

“Because our fitness function adds penalties, we want to minimize those penalties. If my fitness function provided rewards, then we want to maximize.”

Lesson 5 · ~30 min · core exam material

Encoding II — Real Scenarios & the Four Patterns

Test scenarios need several decisions encoded at once: assignment AND order AND time. This lesson gives you the four reusable chromosome architectures from the professor's walkthrough — one of them will fit whatever scenario Friday brings.

Lesson 5 on one slide
  • Four architectures: ① vector + permutation (the default) · ② blocks with separators · ③ direct heterogeneous · ④ grid — and the walkthrough rejects ③ and ④ for the port.
  • The port chromosome: 17 genes = 4 integer section genes (alphabet restricted per ship) + a 13-job permutation.
  • Decode in phases, and let each phase kill a named rule — sequential placement kills double-booking; max(ETA, prev + 30) kills two rules in one expression.
  • Position in the permutation = priority, not clock time — the decoder assigns actual times.
  • The decoder's lookups ARE your data requirements — every number it consults goes in the Q1 data bullet list.
Tomorrow this buys you: a chromosome for any multi-decision scenario, plus Q1's decoding row (4 marks) written as numbered phases.

Which way does the arrow point? Encoding is the backwards arrow: you start from the real timetable you want and work back to a string of genes the GA can breed. Think of a bus card — the card is a compact code (the chromosome); the journey it buys is the real thing (the schedule). Every pattern below is a different answer to one question: what should the string say, and what should the decoder work out?

Heterogeneous vs homogeneous — the professor's own vocabulary

Heterogeneous

The chromosome has segments of different gene types — e.g. segment A: integer section per ship; segment B: permutation of jobs. Each segment gets its own mutation/crossover.

1231‖2413

Simple genes, more of them; light decoder.

Homogeneous + decoder

One uniform gene type and a smarter decoder that works out the rest as it reads. His worked case on the board was a university class timetable: one week of teaching, and a set of sessions — a session is listed there as id + module + intake + type (lab or lecture) — to be placed into days, teaching slots and classrooms.

The chromosome was nothing but a series of session IDs, and the note under it hands everything else to the decoder — day, slot and classroom for each session. His own words in that session, tidied from the automatic transcript: “you have a decoder which is responsible for assigning… assign a room, assign a slot, assign a day… so now it's a homogeneous design, but a simple homogeneous design, all the complexity is part of the decoder.”

Simpler chromosome ⇄ heavier decoder. Naming this trade-off = marks.

The four patterns (from the walkthrough deck — learn all, deploy one)

Pattern 1 · Assignment vector + permutation — the workhorse

Segment A: one integer gene per entity = its resource/group. Segment B: a permutation = service order. The decoder derives all timing.

Strengths: short; standard operators per segment (uniform crossover on A, Order Crossover — OX — on B, the crossover that keeps a permutation legal; both worked in Lesson 6); compatibility enforced in the alphabet (= the gene's set of legal values) so offspring are always legal. Weakness: the segments interact — a good order for one assignment can be bad after crossover swaps the assignment.

Read segment B as priority order, not clock order — a position says when the decoder considers an entity, never when it starts (the full version, and the sentence to write in Q1, is the callout further down this lesson).

Default choice. If unsure on Friday, use this.

Pattern 2 · Block / grouping chromosome — the elegant one

One sequence of entity IDs cut by separator genes. Which block an entity sits in IS its assignment; its position in the block IS its order.

SH1SH4‖SH2‖SH3 → “Section A serves SH1 then SH4; B serves SH2; C serves SH3.”

Strengths: shortest possible; assignment and order can never contradict; workload visible per block; maps to the recognised grouping GA family (name it — it reads as expertise). Weakness: standard crossover shreds it — needs a block-aware crossover or a repair step (operators: Lesson 6; repair: Lesson 7). Admit this cost explicitly. Two more weaknesses, one clause each: it works at entity level, so an entity is served by one resource throughout — if you need two cranes to share a ship you must drop back to job-level genes; and different chromosomes encode the same partition, so the search keeps rediscovering solutions it has already seen (that is non-redundancy failing, in the vocabulary of Lesson 4). Empty blocks, the fixed-length variant and Falkenauer's Grouping GA by name are worked in full on the Port Walkthrough.

Pattern 3 · Direct heterogeneous segments, no decoder — the cautionary tale

One gene per entity per decision (assignment, resource, start slot); the chromosome IS the schedule, read directly.

Strengths: no decoder to explain — and it can deliberately idle a resource: a direct start-slot gene can park a crane for an hour to save energy, a choice no greedy decoder will ever make. It is not alone in this, so do not write “only”. His own comparison table asks “Can it leave a crane idle on purpose?” and answers No for the permutation-plus-decoder design but Yes for both this pattern and the time-slot grid (Pattern 4), because a grid cell can simply be written as idle.

Claim the property for the two direct-control patterns, not for this one alone. That freedom is exactly what costs it feasibility. Weakness: offspring almost never valid — two things collide constantly, so you drown in penalties/repair. In the walkthrough its verdict is “it goes wrong a lot.” Use it as your rejected alternative for the justification marks.

Pattern 4 · Resource × time grid

Rows = one resource each, columns = fixed time slots, each cell holds the entity (and any secondary resource) occupying it — cell (A, 09:00) = “SH1, worked by C2”. Size = rows × slots: three sections against the 08:00–16:00 shift cut into 16 half-hour slots is 48 cells. Exclusivity is structural — one cell holds one entry, so a collision cannot even be written.

Three costs to state. (1) What it hides: anything not indexed by a row has nowhere to live — in a grid indexed by section, a crane's break counter and charging counter are invisible, so what indexes your grid decides what your encoding can and cannot say (worked in full on the Port Walkthrough). (2) Fixed slots cannot express a job that finishes at 12:40, so you round and quietly lie about it. (3) Crossover of two grids almost never yields a valid child; if you use one, swap whole columns — entire time slots — rather than cell by cell, and repair afterwards (operators: Lesson 6; repair: Lesson 7).

Verdict: the clearest picture and the worst chromosome — use it to explain your answer, not to run your GA. Mention it when the scenario is literally a timetable; usually rejected.

The four side by side — this table is your justification answer

Q1 gives two marks for comparing your design against an alternative. His own comparison slide sets the four patterns out field by field on the port scenario; reproduce four rows of it, argue one column, and those marks are banked.

1 · Vector + permutation2 · Block / grouping3 · Direct heterogeneous4 · Section × time grid
Length17 genes6 genes39 genes48 cells
Section stored asan explicit gene valuewhich block you are inan explicit gene valuewhich row you are in
Compatibility handled byrestricted alphabetrepair after crossoverpenaltyrepair

The row that settles the argument is are offspring valid?, because it converts straight into wasted compute: a design whose children are almost never legal spends most of its evaluation budget measuring how illegal things are rather than how good they are. Quote the length and that row, name the trade-off you accepted, and stop — his note against the slide is that both routes reach full marks, and that the distinction band is about explaining the cost of the design you chose.

A fifth architecture — Acme Manufacturing, the variable-length nested chromosome (a module lab)

The scenario first. A factory (“Acme Manufacturing”) has 5 machines making 9 different components, A–I. A machine works in fixed 20-minute production sessions; each day it has a 1,440-minute budget, and after 100 minutes of continuous running it must take a 10-minute cooldown. Every component must be produced at least 25 times — the brief says “a minimum number (ie 25) of each component”, and the lab counts that as 25 production sessions of that component across the whole factory, not 25 finished units.

Here is the twist that shapes everything: when a machine switches from one component to another it must be recalibrated, the recalibration time depends on the (from, to) pair, and some transitions are forbidden entirely. Goal: minimise total recalibration time.

Why none of the four patterns fits. Nobody knows in advance how many sessions each machine will run, so no fixed length is natural: you could pad every machine out to its worst case with “idle” filler genes — the same 0-padding trick the fixed-length block variant uses — but you would then be paying for search space you never use, and every idle gene is one more thing crossover can shuffle for no gain.

The lab takes the other road. The lab's answer is a list of 5 machine schedules, each itself a variable-length list of sessions (each session = which component to make). Nested, and different lengths per individual.

  • The cooldown rule becomes one modulo test — the same “legislation into a counting function” move the guard rota is praised for. “A 10-minute cool-down after 100 minutes of continuous use” never appears in his code as a clock. A production session is 20 minutes, so 100 minutes is exactly 5 sessions, and the rule collapses into a position test on the chromosome: if (index + 1) % 5 == 0 and index != len(machine) - 1: machine_cooldown_time += self.cooldown_time.

    Two things there are worth copying on Friday. The % 5 is the conversion — divide the stated limit by the session length and a sentence of factory rules becomes arithmetic on gene positions, exactly as “8 hours between shifts” became “no two adjacent 1s” in the guard rota (Lesson 7). And the second clause, index != len(machine) - 1, suppresses the cooldown after a machine's final session, because there is nothing left to cool down for; boundary cases like that are worth a clause of their own, since a cooldown charged at the end of the day is time nobody pays for. The cooldown minutes are then added to production time and recalibration time, and it is that total that gets tested against the 1,440-minute day.

  • Fitness = total recalibration time + penalties: a forbidden transition costs 10,000; every minute of overtime, every session short of a machine's minimum and every unit of under-production cost ×1,000 (constraint tools: Lesson 7).

  • That “machine's minimum” is the most interesting penalty in the whole lab set, because the brief never asks for it. His code sets MIN_SESSIONS = 30 and charges 1,000 for every session a machine falls short of it. Read the scenario document and there is nothing there — it gives the 1,440-minute day, the 20-minute session, the 10-minute cooldown and the minimum of 25 per component, and no per-machine floor at all.

    So it is not enforcing a stated rule; it is closing a loophole his own objective opened. If the objective is “minimise total recalibration time”, then the cheapest schedule imaginable is an empty one: no sessions, no switches, no cost — and the GA will happily shrink every machine toward nothing unless something stops it.

    The same instinct shows up a second time in his operators, which build each machine with a random 40–60 sessions and refuse to delete below 10. Carry the distinction into Q2, because it is precisely what the critical-awareness band pays for: some penalties enforce a rule the scenario states, and some exist only to stop the search exploiting the fitness function you wrote — name which of yours is which.

  • The two coefficients are not the same, and that is the design rather than an accident. Both are hard-rule penalties, but the physically impossible thing is priced ten times as heavily as a unit of shortfall. The reasoning generalises to any scenario: Pk is per-constraint, not global, and its size should track how badly the world breaks when rule k is broken.

    A plan that finishes twenty units short is still a plan somebody can run on Monday; a plan containing a transition the machinery physically cannot perform is not a plan at all, so it must never be reachable by trading away a little output. Carry that into Q2: rather than setting every Pk to one shared BIG_WEIGHT, split the hard rules into two or three tiers — physically impossible, legally forbidden, operationally undesirable — say which rules sit in which tier and give the one-line reason. Differentiating the coefficients is exactly what “constraint handling is reasoned” is asking you to show.

  • Custom operators, forced by the encoding: standard crossover would splice unrelated machines together, so crossover runs per machine (a two-point crossover applied machine-by-machine); mutation is 4-way, applied to one randomly chosen machine: replace a session's component (40% of the time), swap two sessions (30%), insert a new session (15%) or delete one (15%) — and the delete only fires if that machine still holds more than 10 sessions, so mutation can never shrink a schedule to nothing. That guard is the point: a bespoke operator has to protect the structure it is mutating.

  • Greedy seeding: 20% of the initial population is built by a greedy heuristic (chain sessions to keep recalibrations cheap) rather than at random — the only lab in the module whose code actually seeds part of its population with a heuristic instead of random values.

    What the builder actually does, because “greedy” on its own is not an answer: for each of the 5 machines it picks a random starting component, sets a target length of random.randint(40, 60) sessions, then repeatedly appends the cheapest legal successor of the component the machine is currently making — nearest-neighbour on the recalibration matrix — with a random.choice fallback for a component that has no legal successor at all.

    Now the honest observation, which is ours and not his: that fallback can never fire, and the heuristic is weaker than it looks, both for the same reason — the diagonal of his matrix is 0 (A→A costs nothing), so the cheapest successor of any component is always itself.

    The builder therefore hands the GA five machines each producing one single component for forty to sixty sessions with no recalibration whatsoever: zero on the objective it was pointed at, and buried under under-production penalties, because at most five of the nine components get made at all and every one of the others is 25 short at 1,000 a unit.

    That is the classic greedy failure and it is a gift of an exam sentence — a heuristic seed optimises the one thing you aimed it at and is blind to every constraint you did not build into it, so seeded individuals are a head start the GA must then repair, not a shortcut past it.

    Call the technique heuristic seeding of the initial population; the NSGA-II deck raises the identical idea under the name priority-aware initialisation, its example being to seed the population with solutions that schedule the highest-priority jobs first. Name it when asked how to speed up convergence; the risk to admit is reduced initial diversity.

Moral: when the natural chromosome is exotic, the operators must be redesigned to match it — encoding choice drives operator choice.

Why the representation decides everything downstream

It is tempting to treat the chromosome as packaging — a container you pour the problem into before the interesting work starts. It is the opposite. The chromosome is the entire vocabulary the search has. Anything the string cannot express, the algorithm cannot consider, no matter how many generations you give it: if your genes only say which section a ship goes to, then “delay SH3 by twenty minutes to free a crane” is not a bad idea the GA rejected, it is a sentence the GA cannot form.

Equally, anything the string says twice is effort you pay for twice. When two different chromosomes decode to the same timetable — swap the order of two ships that were never going to compete for a berth, and nothing changes — the search space is strictly larger than the space of real solutions, and the GA spends part of its budget rediscovering the same schedule under different names. Completeness and non-redundancy are not tick-box properties; they are the two ways an encoding wastes your generations.

The representation also silently fixes what “a small change” means. Every operator is a definition of neighbourhood: a bit-flip means reverse one yes/no decision; a swap on a permutation means two entities trade priority; a one-point cut through a grouping chromosome means hand half of one parent's block structure to a child that has never heard of it.

That is why Pattern 2 needs a bespoke crossover and Pattern 1 does not — the operator is only as sensible as the thing it is cutting. The property to reach for is the one his slide calls connectedness (the wider literature calls it locality — use his word on the paper): a small change in the chromosome should cause a small change in the solution. When connectedness breaks, crossover stops being recombination and becomes a random restart wearing a costume, and the run degenerates into an expensive coin-flip.

Finally, the representation decides where the rules get enforced and therefore how expensive every single evaluation is. Push the work forward — restrict the alphabet so an illegal assignment cannot be written, let the decoder insert changeovers and rest periods as it lays the schedule out — and offspring are born legal, so every fitness evaluation measures quality.

Push it backwards into penalties instead and a large share of each generation is illegal, so most of your evaluations are spent measuring how illegal things are rather than how good they are. That is the real reason the design order is fixed: list the decisions, choose the representation, write the decoder, then pick constraint tools (Lesson 7), then build fitness (Lesson 8).

Answers fall apart when the chromosome is chosen last, because by then the fitness function has been promised information the genes were never designed to carry.

The decoder — always describe it in numbered phases

The decoder turns genotype into phenotype. For scheduling scenarios it is nearly always two-phase, and saying why the order is forced is worth marks:

  1. Phase 1 — build the allocation plan. Read assignment genes → group entities per resource → order each group (by permutation segment, or by ETA/priority rule) → lay out time windows respecting release times (release time = the earliest moment an entity is available and work on it may legally start — a ship's ETA, an exam's window opening, a machine coming free) and changeover buffers.

  2. Phase 1b — check the shared capacity before you commit. Before fixing a start time, work out what this entity does to the shared buffer / yard / hall it feeds — occupancy at every moment, never a cumulative total — and if it would breach capacity at any instant, push the start later until it fits.

    His step-by-step decoder slide does exactly this: “work out how full the section's buffer would become. If it would go over capacity, push the start time later until it fits.” The alternative is to let the overflow through and charge it to a graded penalty (Lesson 7). Both are defensible: say which you chose.

  3. Phase 2 — layer the secondary schedule. Assign cranes / invigilators / rooms greedily: for each placed entity take the fastest/cheapest legal resource, inserting breaks, charging, rest periods as the rules demand.

The sentence that earns the mark: “The decoder must build the berth plan before the crane schedule, because crane availability cannot be evaluated until ship positions and times are known.” — Adapt to any scenario.

Then annotate the steps — one clause per phase naming the rule that phase kills

A decoder written as numbered phases earns Q1's four decoding marks. The same decoder with enforcement clauses earns those marks and a share of Q2's three constraint-handling marks, because you have shown the marker that your two answers are one design rather than two essays. His own speaker note against the step-by-step decoder slide is an instruction, not a suggestion: certain steps are where every hard constraint is enforced — point that out explicitly.

Done to the phases above, on the port scenario (four ships to unload, three quay sections, three quay cranes):

  • Phase 1group ships by section and lay them out one after another (this is where berth occupancy is enforced: sequential placement makes two ships in one section unwritable); set start = max(ETA, previous departure + 30 minutes) (this single expression enforces both the no-start-before-ETA rule and the 30-minute changeover).
  • Phase 1bzone capacity.
  • Phase 2give each job the fastest crane that is free, legal for that section and not due a rest (section exclusivity and crane eligibility); insert a 30-minute break at three hours of continuous running and a one-hour charge at four hours for an electric crane (both working-time rules).

Five clauses, six constraints, no extra paragraph — and your Q2 constraint-to-tool table now has something concrete to point back at.

The single most misunderstood idea in permutation encodings

A position in a permutation is a priority, not a time. If your chromosome reads [SH3, SH1, SH4, SH2], that does not say SH3 starts first on the clock. It says SH3 is considered first — the decoder picks it up before the others and places it at the earliest moment the rules actually allow, which for SH3 is never earlier than its ETA of 10:15, and later still if the section is occupied or its crane is on a break. SH1, considered second but available from 08:00, may well end up starting earlier than SH3 in the finished timetable.

Keep the two ideas apart and a lot of confusion disappears: the chromosome carries the order of decisions; the decoder produces the order of events. This is exactly why a permutation is such a cheap encoding for scheduling — you never write a single time into a gene, so you can never write an impossible one. Times are computed, not stored. Say this in Q1 and you have shown you understand what your own encoding means.

Worked micro-example — the guard rota

The scenario in full, as he set it on the board

It is not a generic security firm — he dressed it in exactly the style the exam uses, and the recognition cue is worth keeping. His board's opening line, verbatim: “Asia Pacific University requires you to help optimise the scheduling of its security guards for its Cyber Security Talent Zone, so as to abide by new legislation requiring sufficient rest and days off for security staff.

APU current employs 16 guards working 8 hour shifts (there are 3 shifts a day).” So: Asia Pacific University, its Cyber Security Talent Zone, new government legislation, 16 guards, and each day divided into 3 shifts of 8 hours — morning, afternoon, night — which tile the 24-hour day exactly.

The rota is planned one week at a time (the one-week horizon is the lab's; his board does not state it). The only decision is: which guard works which shift on which day. Four rules apply. The new legislation demands a minimum 8 hours between any two shifts a guard works, and a maximum of 5 shifts per week per guard, and it sets a staffing band for each shift: 3–4 guards on mornings, 3–4 on afternoons, 1–2 on nights — his board lists all three of those bullets under the heading “New Government legislation states that:”, so treat the band as law rather than as an operational preference.

Finally, guards submit shift preferences — nice to honour, not obligatory. The first three are hard; preferences are soft. Lesson 7 turns each of these into a counting function; here we only need the chromosome.

  • Binary flattened 3-D: gene (g, d, s) = 1 if guard g works shift s on day d. Length 16×7×3 = 336 bits. The flattened reading order must be stated (“the first 21 genes are guard A's week…”). (The module's lab codes the same problem with 8 guards, giving 8×7×3 = 168 bits, and it relaxes the staffing band to match — his code sets shiftMin = [2, 2, 1] and shiftMax = [3, 4, 2], i.e. morning 2–3, afternoon 2–4, night 1–2 unchanged. Quote the board's 16 guards and 3–4 / 3–4 / 1–2 as the scenario; scaling a scenario down to a runnable instance, and saying out loud that you have done so, is exactly what he did. The arithmetic, not the number, is what you reproduce.)

  • Homogeneous alternative — the shape on his whiteboard: one gene per staffing position, each gene holding a guard ID. The position says WHEN (his board groups the cells shift by shift, then day by day), the value says WHO. Size it at full staffing — 4 morning + 4 afternoon + 2 night = 10 positions a day, so 7 × 10 = 70 genes, each an integer 1–16 (that arithmetic is ours; the board draws the shape, not the number), with 0 as a sensible convention for “this post is left unfilled”.

    Comparing the two is the justification: the 336-bit version can express any rota at all, including illegal ones, so every rule has to be checked afterwards; the 70-gene version makes the upper end of each staffing band structural — you cannot write five guards into a night shift that only has two slots — while the lower end, the 8-hour rest rule and the 5-shift cap can all still be broken, so a decoder, a repair pass or a penalty must still enforce them. Say which rules your encoding makes unwritable and which it merely makes checkable; that sentence is the trade-off the justification marks are for.

Data requirements — the grouped list (2 easy marks, every year)

GroupWhat goes in itPort example
Entity dataThe things being scheduled: ID, size/duration, priority, special needs, time windowShip: ID, ETA, containers, priority, hazmat (dangerous-goods cargo) / reefer (refrigerated container needing shore power) flag
Resource dataID, capacity, capabilities, availability, cost ratesSection: berth length, certification, buffer capacity; Crane: speed, fuel type, break rules
Relationship dataCompatibility matrices, cost matrices, overlap sets, travel timesShip×section compatibility; berth handling cost per pair
Policy dataWeights, penalty rates, buffers, staffing ratiosPriority weights 5/3/1 (emergency/high/normal); 30-min berth changeover; overtime penalty rate past 16:00; assumed buffer clearance of 30 containers/hr/zone
Calendar / horizon dataThe clock the decoder counts in: planning window start and end, time granularity (how long one slot is), number of days in the horizonPort: shift 08:00–16:00 = 480 minutes; his own list names a 30-minute granularity, which gives 16 slots — go to a 15-minute grid if you want a 10:15 ETA to land exactly on a slot boundary

Close the list with one line on provenance and volatility

His slide asks for it in as many words — say where each group comes from and how often it changes: entity data arrives fresh each shift, resource specifications are fixed, live buffer occupancy has to be read from the yard system. Hardly anybody writes it, and it turns a list into an analysis for the price of a sentence.

Include, too, the data your own assumptions create: an assumed clearance rate or an assumed cost per crane-hour is a number your decoder needs and nobody handed you.

Lesson 6 · ~25 min

The GA Engine — Selection, Crossover, Mutation

A 48-slide lecture on deconstructing a genetic algorithm lives in this module just for these operators. In the test they appear inside Q1 justifications and Q3 comparisons.

Lesson 6 on one slide
  • Selection: roulette (fitness-proportional, dominated by freaks) · rank (fixed gaps) · tournament k = 3, the module's default · SUS; fitness scaling tames a runaway leader.
  • Crossover: 1-point, 2-point, uniform for vectors; OX/PMX for permutations; block encodings cut only at block boundaries.
  • Mutation has two rates: per-individual (0.1) and per-gene (indpb ≈ 1/length) — quote both and say which is which.
  • Elitism / Hall of Fame: the champion can never be lost — one sentence, one mark, in any operator discussion.
  • Everything above is one dial: exploration vs exploitation — name the trade-off when you justify any setting.
Tomorrow this buys you: the operator sentence in Q1 (“crossover cuts at block boundaries, so no exam's genes are split”) and Q3's implementation-differences row.

Selection — who gets to breed

MethodHow it worksCharacter
Roulette wheel — a.k.a. fitness-proportionate selection (FPS)Each individual gets a wheel slice proportional to fitness; spin once per parentSimple; the same individual can be picked several times; breaks down when one fitness dominates or fitnesses are negative
Stochastic Universal Sampling (SUS)One spin of the same wheel with N evenly spaced pointers — that single spin picks all N parents simultaneouslyRoulette with less luck variance; stops one high-fitness individual saturating the parent pool, so weaker individuals keep a fair chance
Rank-basedSlice by rank position, not raw fitnessKeeps pressure steady even with extreme fitness gaps
Tournament (k)Pick k at random, best of them winsThe practical default — his own words are “in the code that we use, we always use tournament”, and he runs k = 3 live; across the labs it is mostly k = 3, with the zoo lab on k = 2. (DEAP = Distributed Evolutionary Algorithms in Python, the lab library.) Pressure tunable via k
Fitness scalingRescale raw fitness before rouletteFixes early-domination and late-stagnation

One fact worth a mark on its own: selection never opens the chromosome — it reads only the fitness number. So every method above works unchanged for any representation: binary, integer, real, permutation, even nested lists. Crossover and mutation are the parts you redesign per encoding.

Try it — spin a roulette wheel

Four schedules with fitness 40 / 30 / 20 / 10 → slice sizes 40% / 30% / 20% / 10%. Spin repeatedly: good solutions are favoured, not guaranteed. That's selection pressure with exploration preserved.

Winners so far: —

Which direction is “fit”? Reconcile this now. In this module the fitness you design is usually a cost to minimise — so selection must favour LOW fitness. Rank and tournament handle that trivially (sort the other way; the smaller number wins the tournament); roulette needs the fitness inverted first, because a slice proportional to value assumes bigger is better. Say the distinction in one sentence and you have pre-empted the obvious follow-up question: selection is representation-agnostic but not direction-agnostic.

Every method here works unchanged whether your chromosome is a bit string, an integer vector or a permutation, because selection only ever looks at the fitness number and never at the genes — that is why swapping your encoding never forces you to swap your selection operator. What it is sensitive to is which way “better” points: rank and tournament only compare, so they flip for free, while roulette does arithmetic on the value itself and therefore breaks silently on a minimisation problem. The demo above uses higher-is-better purely for visual clarity.

Worth one line whenever you have to justify a selection operator: the module made exactly this swap live on its own guard-rota code — tournament out, roulette in, nothing else changed — and the run regressed sharply. Tidied from the recording: “changing this from tournament to [roulette], in this particular case, adversely affects… we have a hell of a lot of violations here.” DEAP's roulette and SUS both assume bigger-is-better, so on a cost fitness they must be inverted first or they will faithfully breed your worst schedules.

The completed notebook he distributed still carries the swap — tools.selRoulette registered, with selTournament, tournsize = 3 commented out on the line directly above it — so if you open his guard file and find roulette sitting on a minimisation problem, that is the exercise preserved, not a bug. One thing to take into the hall: if you name roulette in Q1 or Q3, add the clause “having inverted the cost first, since roulette assumes higher-is-better” — 1/f, or (max − f), or switch to rank or tournament, which only ever sort and so do not care which way is good.

In code the direction is not left to convention — it is declared. DEAP attaches a weights tuple to every fitness, one entry per objective, and the sign of each entry sets the direction: +1.0 means maximise that objective, −1.0 means minimise it. Mixed signs in one tuple, e.g. weights=(+1.0, −1.0), are legal and normal — “maximise value, minimise weight” in a knapsack.

Worth knowing because past papers have asked DEAP specifics directly, and because it makes the point concrete: the sign carries the direction, the magnitude does not rescale anything. DEAP stores weight × value and then compares those tuples element by element, in order, so weights=(−10.0, −1.0) — which the module's guard lab actually writes — ranks individuals in exactly the same sequence as (−1.0, −1.0) would: the 10 buys nothing.

The rule that carries into Q2: if you want one objective to outweigh another, do the weighting inside your fitness function, where you can defend the number — not in the weights tuple, where it does not act.

Worked numbers — roulette vs rank vs scaling (from the 48-slide deck)

Roulette / FPS. Six individuals with fitness 8 / 12 / 27 / 4 / 45 / 17 get wheel shares 7 / 11 / 24 / 3 / 40 / 15%. The failure mode is visible: the 45 hogs 40% of the wheel, and since each spin is independent it can win again and again.

Rank-based. Replace raw fitness with rank position, then slice by rank: the same six become 9 / 14 / 24 / 5 / 29 / 19% — the leader's dominance is capped. The converse is the half everyone forgets, and the deck states it as a condition rather than a stage: when all individuals have similar fitness values, rank spreads them apart, giving a clearer advantage to the better ones even when the raw differences are small — which in practice is exactly where you are late in a run. Rank protects the start of a run and rescues the end of it.

Where those rank numbers come from, because the shares are unusable without it. Sort the population by raw fitness, then hand out ranks by position: with a population of six the best individual gets rank 6, the next 5, and so on down to rank 1 for the worst.

On the fitnesses above that is E = 6 (fitness 45), C = 5 (27), F = 4 (17), B = 3 (12), A = 2 (8), D = 1 (4). Now slice the wheel by rank rather than by fitness: the ranks total 6+5+4+3+2+1 = 21, so E takes 6/21, C 5/21, F 4/21, B 3/21, A 2/21 and D 1/21 — the 29 / 24 / 19 / 14 / 9 / 5 % quoted above.

Notice what has happened to the leader: 45 was 40% of the raw wheel and is 29% of the rank wheel, while the worst rose from 3% to 5%. The gaps are now fixed by the population size alone and no longer by how freakish one fitness happens to be, which is the whole point of the method and the sentence to write when you justify choosing it.

Fitness scaling. Linear transform scaled = a·raw + b. Worked: map the raw range [4, 45] onto [50, 100] by solving 50 = 4a + b and 100 = 45a + b → a = 1.22, b = 45.12. Now actually apply it to the same six, because the punchline is only worth a mark if you can show it:

IndividualRaw fitnessRaw wheel shareScaled = 1.22·raw + 45.12Scaled wheel share
A87%54.913%
B1211%59.815%
C2724%78.119%
D43%50.012%
E4540%100.025%
F1715%65.916%
Total113100%408.6100%

Read the two share columns against each other and the method explains itself. E falls from 40% of the wheel to 25%; D rises from 3% to 12%. In raw terms the best was 45 ÷ 4 = 11.25× more likely to be chosen than the worst; after scaling it is 100 ÷ 50 = exactly 2×.

Selection pressure is kept — E is still the most likely parent and D the least, so the ordering never changes — but E can no longer flood the next generation with copies of itself and collapse your diversity in three generations. That is the sentence to write when you justify scaling: it preserves the ranking while compressing the ratio.

Tournament, one round, same six. The number of individuals dragged into each round has a name — the tournament size, three in the lecture's example. Draw three at random: A (fitness 8), B (12) and F (17). F wins, because 17 is the largest of the three, and F becomes one parent.

All six then go back in the pot and you draw again for the next parent, so a strong individual can win repeatedly but is never guaranteed a place. Now look at what the arithmetic never touched: no percentages, no wheel, no population total. Tournament selection only ever compares, which is why it works unchanged on negative fitnesses, on wildly skewed fitnesses, and on a minimising fitness function like yours (the smallest number wins the round) — none of which plain roulette survives without repair.

The larger the tournament size, the more often genuinely good individuals appear in a round and the less often a weak one sneaks through, so the size is the selection-pressure dial.

Selection pressure — what it actually feels like

Selection pressure is just this: how much more often a better-than-average individual gets to breed than an average one. It sounds like a dial you set once, but the thing to picture is a run over time. Turn it up hard — tournament size 7, or plain roulette with one runaway individual — and within a handful of generations the population is essentially copies of one lucky early winner.

That is premature convergence, and its real damage is not that the answer is mediocre; it is that the population has lost its raw material. Crossover between two identical parents produces identical children, so the only operator still doing anything is mutation, and you are now paying for a population of a hundred to run a very slow random walk from a single point.

Turn pressure too far down — tournament of 2 with a huge population, or scaling so aggressive that everyone's odds are nearly equal — and the opposite happens: good genes never spread fast enough to combine with each other, average fitness barely lifts off the initial random population, and you have bought an expensive random search.

The dials, in the order you should reach for them: tournament size k is the honest one (k = 2 is gentle, k = 3 is the common default and what the module's labs and his live demo actually run, k ≥ 5 is harsh — asked in class for a recommended size he refused to name one, so justify your k by the trade-off he gave instead: a large pool is more likely to contain the fittest, a small one more likely to pass on something different), then elite count, then population size — a bigger population holds diversity longer and so tolerates more pressure.

What catches people out is that the same setting feels different at different points in the run. Early on, the random population contains a few individuals that are far better than the rest, so any method has plenty of pressure — the risk is having too much. Late on, when everything surviving is nearly equally good, raw-fitness methods lose their grip entirely: differences of 0.3% produce wheel slices you cannot tell apart, and the search stalls with nothing to prefer.

That is the whole argument for rank-based selection and for fitness scaling — they are not decoration, they are what keeps pressure roughly constant across a run whose fitness distribution changes shape underneath you.

You can diagnose which failure you have with two lines on one graph: best fitness and average fitness per generation. If average races up to meet best and both then flatline early, pressure is too high and you have converged onto one solution — cut k, add mutation, raise the population, or name niching and sharing, the lecture's own diversity mechanism (its own card below).

If best stays stubbornly far above average and neither improves much, pressure is too low and good genes are not propagating. Two more habits belong here, because a GA is stochastic — the same parameters on the same problem give a different answer every run. Never quote the result of a single run: run it several times and report mean ± standard deviation, which is the standard way of reporting any stochastic algorithm.

Five or ten runs is the least you could defend; his own stated figure, given in class for the coursework, is at least 30 runs. His reason is the honest one and the one to quote — tidied from the automatic transcript: “you can't just run your code, get a solution, and that's it… you need to run it at a minimum of 30 times.

These are stochastic algorithms… random is a key aspect of it,” and with 30 runs “you have a better set of averages, the standard deviation… a more accurate, stable mean.” So 30 buys you a mean and a spread you can actually defend, not a significance test — do not claim a particular statistical test requires 30, because none of the module's material says so.

Quote 30 rather than “a few” and it reads as research literacy in a written answer. And when you are asked why use a GA at all, three properties are the citable ones: it is gradient-free (it needs only a fitness score, never a derivative, so it copes with fitness functions that are lumpy, discontinuous or produced by a simulation), highly explorative (a whole population searches many regions at once rather than following one path downhill), and intrinsically parallel (every individual's fitness can be evaluated independently, so the expensive part scales across cores or machines).

Crossover — recombining parents

  • One-point: cut both parents at one position, swap tails. 10|11
  • Two-point / n-point: swap the middle segment(s).
  • Uniform: each gene tosses a coin for which parent it comes from — highest mixing, so the greatest diversity potential of the three. The second offspring is normally the complement of the first: wherever child 1 took parent A's gene, child 2 takes parent B's, so one coin-toss sequence produces both children and nothing is thrown away.

  • For permutations — Order Crossover (OX): copy a slice from parent 1, fill remaining positions in parent 2's order, skipping duplicates. PMX — Partially Mapped Crossover is the named alternative, and his own walkthrough offers it as an equal choice (“Order Crossover (OX) or PMX — these keep the permutation legal”). How PMX runs: copy parent 1's slice into the child as before, then fill the rest from parent 2, and wherever a value would duplicate one already sitting in the slice, follow the slice's own position-by-position mapping between the two parents until you land on a value not yet used, and place that instead.

    The contrast worth writing in Q1: OX preserves the relative order of the remaining entities, PMX preserves their absolute positions — so “OX if the sequence of jobs is what matters, PMX if a job sitting in a particular position is what matters”, and you have justified the choice rather than just named it.

    These preserve the every-ID-exactly-once property that standard crossover destroys. The fill detail people get wrong: the scan through parent 2 does not start at position 1 — it starts just after the second cut point and wraps around to the beginning, and each ID is either skipped (already present in the copied slice) or dropped into the next empty position. Say “starting after the second cut and wrapping” in Q1 and the marker knows you have actually run one.

What happens the rest of the time

Crossover fires with probability pc (typically 0.7–0.9), which means 10–30% of pairings do not cross. Those pairs are not discarded and not re-drawn: both parents are simply cloned — copied unchanged into the next generation, where they may still be mutated. This is the quiet reason a good individual can persist without elitism, and it is a one-line answer to “what happens when crossover is not applied?”

Try it — Order Crossover (OX), step by step

Two parent tours of 6 cities. Press Step.

OX traced by hand, gene by gene

The lecture demonstrates OX on chromosomes of length six and narrates the fill like this: going over the genes in their original order, starting after the second cut point, “we find a 6, but this is already present in the offspring, so we continue (with wrapping around) to 1; this is already present too.

The next in order is the 2. Since 2 is not yet present in the offspring, we add it there.” The trace below is that narration written out in full so you can run it on paper — the fill sequence 6, then 1, then 2 is his; the surrounding gene values are chosen to produce it.

Parent 1 = [4, 5, 6, 1, 3, 2], parent 2 = [2, 5, 3, 4, 6, 1], and the two random cut points fall so that the copied window is positions 3–4.

  • Step one. Copy that window from parent 1 into the child with its positions intact — child = [·, ·, 6, 1, ·, ·].
  • Step two. Walk parent 2 starting just after the second cut: position 5 first, then 6, then wrapping to 1, 2, 3, 4 — which reads off the values 6, 1, 2, 5, 3, 4 in that order.
  • Step three. Take them one at a time. 6 is already in the child, skip. 1 is already in the child, skip. 2 is not, so it drops into the first empty slot after the window, position 5. Then 5 into position 6, and wrapping again, 3 into position 1 and 4 into position 2.

Child = [3, 4, 6, 1, 2, 5] — every city exactly once, parent 1's middle preserved in place, parent 2's relative order preserved everywhere else. Run that once on paper before Friday and “starting after the second cut and wrapping” stops being a sentence you memorised.

Real-coded crossover — BLX and SBX

When a gene is a continuous number (a panel angle, a learning rate, a start time in minutes), cutting-and-swapping is pointless: swapping tails just hands whole genes across intact, and the child can never hold a value neither parent had. Real-coded crossover instead computes a new number from the two parent numbers. Two named operators cover it, and both are worth naming if your Q1 encoding is real-valued.

BLX-α (blend crossover). Draw the child's gene uniformly at random from the interval [p₁ − α(p₂−p₁), p₂ + α(p₂−p₁)], where α ∈ [0,1] controls how far outside the parents you are allowed to look. Write the smaller of the two parent values as p₁ — feed them in the other way round and the two ends come out swapped, which is the one way to get this wrong by hand.

In words, so you can rebuild it under pressure: take the interval between the parents and stretch it by α times its own width at each end. Parents 1.33 and 5.72: with α = 0 the interval is exactly [1.33, 5.72] — children only ever land between the parents. With α = 0.5 it opens to [−0.865, 7.915], roughly twice as wide as the parents' own gap, so the operator can explore beyond them; α = 1.0 widens it to about [−3.06, 10.11]. α is therefore a direct exploration dial, which is exactly the language to use when justifying it.

SBX (simulated binary crossover). Why it is called that, which is also why it exists: SBX is built to imitate the properties of the single-point crossover normally used on binary chromosomes, so that a real-coded GA behaves like the binary one people had already tuned their intuitions on. The property it copies is the one quoted below — the average of the two children equals the average of the two parents, exactly as swapping the tails of two bit-strings leaves the pair's combined material untouched.

Two children by formula, using a spread factor β — a random number drawn afresh for each crossover, not a value you set: O₁ = ½[(1+β)p₁ + (1−β)p₂] and O₂ = ½[(1−β)p₁ + (1+β)p₂]. Same parents with β = 0.8 give 1.769 and 5.281. The property to quote: the offspring average always equals the parent average — (1.33+5.72)/2 = 3.525 and (1.769+5.281)/2 = 3.525. SBX only moves the pair apart or together, never shifting their centre.

The deck lists four states together and they are worth memorising as a block: β = 1 duplicates the parents, β < 1 pulls the children closer together than the parents were, β > 1 pushes them farther apart, and the parent average is preserved regardless of β. What you control is the distribution β is drawn from; the worked values below simply show what each region of that distribution does.

The other direction, worked. Take β = 1.2 on the same parents: O₁ = ½[(1+1.2)(1.33) + (1−1.2)(5.72)] = ½[2.926 − 1.144] = 0.891 and O₂ = ½[(1−1.2)(1.33) + (1+1.2)(5.72)] = ½[−0.266 + 12.584] = 6.159. Both children now sit outside the interval [1.33, 5.72] — that is the exploration β > 1 buys — and the centre has not moved a millimetre: (0.891+6.159)/2 = 3.525, the parents' average again.

Quote one pair each way (0.8 inward, 1.2 outward) with that invariant and you have shown the operator does exactly one thing: it sets the spread, never the centre.

Applied one dimension at a time. A real chromosome is not crossed as a block. Parents [1.23, 7.213, −25.39] and [−30.10, 100.2, 42.42] are handled gene by gene: run BLX or SBX on the first pair, then independently on the second, then the third. Real-valued mutation works the same way — each dimension is nudged on its own.

Hold that against the selection rule above: selection is representation-agnostic, crossover and mutation are the two parts you redesign per encoding — and per dimension, once the genes are real.

Mutation — the novelty tap

EncodingMutation
BinaryBit-flip with small probability per gene
IntegerRandom-reset within that gene's legal values. Swap and inversion (row below) work on binary and integer chromosomes too — the deck introduces both of them that way — they are simply compulsory for permutations, because there they are the only operators that keep every ID exactly once
RealGaussian nudge — add a number drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and a chosen standard deviation σ. Mean 0 means the nudge is as likely up as down; σ sets how far the gene can wander, so a small σ keeps the child in the parent's vicinity
PermutationThe three that preserve validity: swap two positions; inversion — reverse a slice; scramble — pick a random run of consecutive genes and shuffle their order. All three preserve the every-ID-exactly-once property; scramble is the most disruptive of the three, inversion the most structured

Low mutation ⇒ stagnation in local optima; high ⇒ random search. Typical rates: crossover probability ~0.7–0.9. Mutation carries two numbers and naming both is what makes an answer precise. The per-individual rate is the chance that a given child is handed to the mutation operator at all (DEAP calls it mutpb; the module's labs set 0.1–0.2).

The per-gene rate applies once it has been handed over (DEAP calls it indpb), and its common default is about one expected mutation per chromosome, i.e. pm ≈ 1 ÷ chromosome length. Say it that way rather than quoting a bare number, because the number is a consequence of the length: the 336-bit guard rota from Lesson 5 gives 1/336 ≈ 0.003, while a 10-gene chromosome gives 0.1. The 0.01–0.1 band you see quoted in textbooks is that same rule evaluated on short chromosomes (10–100 genes) — it is not a contradiction, and if your Q1 encoding is long you should quote 1/length and let the decimal fall where it falls.

Some GAs make the mutation rate adaptive. The weak version raises the mutation probability as the generations advance, so that a population which has gone quiet gets shaken rather than left to stagnate. The sharp version, and the one he volunteered in class, triggers on a plateau instead of on the generation counter: watch best fitness and, if it has not improved for N generations — his spoken example was 20 — change a parameter to buy diversity back.

He was demonstrating it on tournament size (shrink k), and the same logic lifts the mutation rate. Say “plateau-triggered” rather than “increasing over time” and you have shaken a quiet population for a reason instead of on a timer. Name it as a tuning option and you are answering “how would you stop premature convergence?” before it is asked.

Why those two numbers are so lopsided — this is the reason, and it is citable. A schema is a pattern of genes shared by good solutions: not a whole chromosome, but the partial recipe inside it that keeps showing up in the winners (“ships 2 and 3 in the same section, whichever order”).

Crossover, because it copies contiguous stretches wholesale, tends to preserve such patterns and pass them intact to the next generation; mutation, because it changes genes at random, tends to disrupt them. So you run the preserving operator often (0.7–0.9) and the disrupting one rarely (~1/length): the GA's real business is assembling good schemas from different parents, and mutation is only there to reintroduce values the population has lost entirely.

Niching — the named answer to “how would you keep several different good designs?”

The lecture deck this lesson is built from closes on a concept the rest of the module leaves alone, and it is the one thing to reach for if a scenario wants options rather than an answer. In nature an environment divides into niches — a forest is treetops, shrubs, forest floor, tree roots — each supporting species specialised to the resources there; when several species crowd into one niche they compete over the same resources, and the pressure pushes some of them to go and find an unpopulated niche instead.

Carried into a genetic algorithm, niching is any mechanism that makes crowding costly: individuals sitting close together in the search space have their fitness reduced (the classic implementation is called fitness sharing), so a peak that is already crowded stops being worth colonising and the population spreads itself across several peaks.

Two payoffs, and both are exam sentences: it maintains the diversity of the population, which is a direct answer to premature convergence, and it lets the run find several optimal solutions at once, each one a niche — the port manager gets three genuinely different berth plans rather than three near-copies.

Be honest about its status when you name it: the deck flags niching as an advanced topic to be covered in a separate session, so you are naming a mechanism the module points at rather than one it teaches in detail. Even so, one clause of it in a Q2 or Q3 critical-awareness line puts you a step past everyone who wrote “increase the mutation rate”.

Elitism & parameters

Elitism copies the best n individuals unchanged into the next generation — n being a small predefined number, 1–5 in practice (the module's zoo lab keeps 5; 2 is a safe value to quote in Q1) — and it exists because every selection method above is deliberately permissive: they favour good solutions rather than guaranteeing them, so on any given generation the best individual in the population can simply fail to be picked, or be picked and then wrecked by crossover.

That is “bad-luck loss”. Plot best-fitness per generation without elitism and the line is visibly noisy — it goes down as often as a run gets unlucky. NSGA-II (Lesson 9) builds the same idea in.

Two pieces of nuance that turn a one-line definition into a paragraph worth marks. First, the loss is usually only temporary — a population that found a good solution once will normally find it again within a few generations, because the genes that made it are still spread around. What elitism buys is not permanence but time: you stop paying for the re-discovery.

Second, elites are not put in a museum — they are copied into the next generation and remain fully eligible to be selected as parents, so they keep contributing genes rather than just occupying slots. And conceptually, elitism is the counterweight in the explore/exploit balance: selection was made permissive on purpose so the search keeps exploring, and elitism re-introduces exploitation so that exploration never costs you the best thing you have found.

How it is actually implemented — the Hall of Fame

Rather than special-casing the best individual, the usual implementation keeps a Hall of Fame holding the n best individuals seen so far. Each generation you then select only (population size − n) individuals to breed the next generation, and drop the Hall of Fame members into the remaining n slots. Population size stays constant; the elite count is simply subtracted from the number you fill by selection. Say it that way and “elitism of 2” stops sounding like a slogan and starts sounding like something you have coded.

The word for the other outcome, and it is worth having

Every generation ends with a survival decision, and the module's Week 1 introductory reading names both halves of it in one sentence: after each generation, individuals may undergo culling — discarded, so they play no part in the next generation — or they may survive to the next generation, which is what elitism means.

Say it in Q1 as a policy rather than as a fact, because the paper asks how the operators will be applied: “I copy the best 2 chromosomes forward unchanged (elitism), so a champion can never be destroyed by an unlucky crossover, and cull the rest, replacing them with offspring.” Then add the cost in the same breath — elitism guarantees the best-so-far fitness never drops, but too much of it is pure exploitation and drives premature convergence, so keep it to a small handful out of a population of a hundred.

Parameters you can name when asked what you'd tune: population size, max generations, the second stopping condition — stop early if the best fitness has not improved over the last few generations, the item the lecture's own hyperparameter list ends on and the one candidates forget — crossover rate, both mutation rates (per individual and per gene), tournament size, elite count.

And his labs' own settings, if you want numbers that came off his keyboard rather than out of a textbook. Three of his notebooks — the guard rota, the moth example and Acme — run the identical block: pop_size = 100, p_cx = 0.9, p_mut = 0.1, with tools.HallOfFame(3) driven by algorithms.eaSimple; the generation count is the only thing that moves, 100 for moth and Acme and 500 for the guard rota.

The zoo feature-selection lab is the deliberate outlier — population 50, 50 generations, mutation 0.2, hall of fame 5, tournament k = 2 — a smaller, shorter run because every single fitness evaluation there trains and cross-validates a classifier, so evaluations are expensive rather than free. Two habits ride along and both are worth a clause of their own in an answer: he seeds every run (random.seed(42)) so a result can be reproduced, and he registers tools.Statistics and plots best-against-average per generation at the end — the two-line diagnostic graph described above is literally what his labs draw.

Two words that make a parameter sentence sound like it came from someone who has run the thing: tuning versus control. Parameter tuning is choosing a value before the run and holding it fixed throughout — population 100, tournament k = 3, crossover rate 0.8. Because you are optimising the settings of an optimiser, the textbook calls tuning a hyper-optimisation problem: “parameter tuning is the process of optimizing the optimization algorithm”, and it adds that there are no well-established methods for universal parameter tuning — which is exactly why “I would tune these by experiment” is an honest and markable sentence rather than a dodge. Parameter control is deliberately varying a value during the run, so the algorithm can explore early and exploit late.

You have already met three examples without the label: the cooling schedule in simulated annealing (Lesson 11), which the same textbook names as a basic form of parameter control, inertia decay in PSO (Lesson 10), and the dynamic penalty that grows with the generation counter (Lesson 7). Use the pair in Q3 and the implementation-differences mark is banked: not “the parameters are T₀ and the cooling schedule”, but “T₀ is tuned before the run; the cooling schedule is parameter control — a value designed to change while the algorithm runs, which is how SA shifts itself from exploration to exploitation with no extra machinery.”

Exam link: after choosing an encoding in Q1, one sentence on operators: “Uniform crossover and legal-value reset mutation on the assignment segment; OX and swap mutation on the permutation segment; tournament selection (k=3) with elitism of 2.” Precision like this reads as mastery and costs you 20 seconds.

Lesson 7 · ~20 min · core exam material

Hard & Soft Constraints — and the Five Tools

Q2 opens with validity. The skill: sort every rule in the scenario into hard vs soft, then pick the cheapest tool to enforce each. This exact framework is in the walkthrough's “sort the rules” and “pick the cheapest tool” slides.

Lesson 7 on one slide
  • Hard = defines validity (break it and you have a non-solution) · soft = costs quality. Sort every stated rule into those two columns before anything else.
  • Four tools, cheapest first: alphabet restriction (unwritable) → decoder enforcement (unbuildable) → repair → penalty. One rule, one tool, one reason.
  • The penalty for a “≤” rule is just max(0, overflow) — zero while legal, the excess when not; static → dynamic → adaptive if asked to be fancy.
  • Every tool has a price: repair biases the search · penalties need the weight guessed right · rejection wastes evaluations. Naming one is what “reasoned” means.
  • Buffer/capacity rules are peak levels over time, not totals — simulate the level, don't add the deliveries.
Tomorrow this buys you: Q2's hard/soft marks and the constraint-to-tool table — plus the trap-avoidance on any buffer constraint in the scenario.

Hard vs soft

One vocabulary note before the tools

This site says valid and invalid, and the exam paper says validity, but the optimisation literature says feasible and infeasible for exactly the same property: a feasible solution is one that satisfies every hard constraint, and the feasible region is the part of the search space made up of them.

Use whichever pair you prefer, but pick one, stay in it, and define it in a clause the first time it appears, because a marker cannot award “validity enumerated” marks for a word you never pinned down. The textbook's extreme case is a useful check on what it means: a problem with no objective at all and nothing but constraints is called a feasibility problem, “because any feasible solution is an optimal solution”.

That is the tight end of the spectrum your scenarios sit near, and it is why “can my encoding even produce a legal schedule?” is a real design question rather than a formality.

Hard constraints — validity

Physically or legally impossible to break. A solution violating one is invalid, not just bad.

  • Capacity exceeded
  • Two uses of one resource at once (exclusivity)
  • Start before release time / ETA
  • Mandatory gaps: changeover, cleaning buffer, 48-h chain gap
  • Compatibility / certification (GPU lab, hazmat berth)
  • Staffing minimums, pairing rules (junior + senior)
  • Working-time limits

Soft constraints — quality

Preferences and costs. Violating them makes a solution worse, not illegal — they become fitness components (Lesson 8).

  • Waiting time, delays
  • Money / energy cost
  • Fairness / workload balance
  • Serving priorities early
  • Congestion, student comfort
  • Preferences (guard shift wishes)

Two shapes of hard constraint, and the shape decides the tool

Written formally, constraints come in two kinds. An inequality constraint has the form g(x) ≤ 0 — “yard section A must not exceed 200 containers”, “no guard works more than five shifts a week”. An equality constraint has the form h(x) = 0 — “every ship is assigned exactly one section”, “each flight must have exactly one purser”.

Algebraically the two are interchangeable, since h(x) = 0 is the same as h(x) ≤ 0 and h(x) ≥ 0 together, but computationally they behave nothing alike, and saying so is a cheap mark in Q2's constraint-handling row. The textbook's warning is that the volume of solutions satisfying an equality is essentially zero in the search space, so random sampling practically never lands on one exactly, and “some tolerance or allowance is used in practice”.

The exam-usable consequence: never leave an equality to a penalty and hope the GA finds it. Build it in instead — one gene per ship makes “exactly one section” structurally true, and a decoder that appoints the purser first guarantees exactly one — or, for a numeric quantity, relax it into a tolerance band, which is what a staffing requirement of “3 to 4 guards on mornings” already is: one equality rewritten as two inequalities, handing the search a slope to walk down instead of a point to hit. Save penalties for inequalities, where the degree of violation is a real number.

Write validity as numbered checkable tests, each with a concrete example from your own Q1 timetable: “Check 3 — changeover: ≥30 min between one ship leaving a berth and the next arriving. In my worked example: out 10:30, in 11:00 ✓.” Enumerating them explicitly is 3 marks.

Where the line falls is partly your decision — and the walkthrough deliberately puts two port rules on both sides of it. (1) Buffer capacity. His own hard column reads “a buffer zone must never go above its capacity”, and his soft column, on the same slide, reads “stay well below buffer capacity, not just under it”.

Read hard, it is a validity test — zone A's occupancy may never top 200 at any instant — enforced by a penalty on the overflow so the search still has a slope. Read soft, it is an objective measured in container-hours. His fitness slide says so outright: if you enforce the buffer as a hard rule, this becomes a penalty term instead — say which you chose. (2) The 16:00 shift end.

Hard, and any unloading still running at 16:00 makes the schedule invalid; soft, and it is an overtime cost in minutes past 16:00 that a good plan may deliberately buy. His note: the paper says a penalty applies past 16:00, you may treat it as a soft cost or as a hard rule, and both are defensible.

What is not defensible is failing to say which you took. One clause each does it — “I treat the buffer as hard, because a yard that overflows stops the port; 16:00 as soft, because overtime is paid, not forbidden.” That sentence is what “constraint handling is reasoned” is asking for.

Validity comes before fitness — the ordering the walkthrough hammers

The example

Recall the running scenario: four ships (SH1–SH4) to unload; three sections A–C, each a stretch of quay where one ship at a time ties up, with its own yard buffer zone behind it (capacities A 200, B 250, C 150) into which the containers are stacked; and three quay cranes doing the lifting.

Keep the two halves of a section apart when you write Q2: one ship, and one working crane, per section is an exclusivity rule about the berth, while occupancy ≤ that zone's capacity is a separate rule about the zone behind it — two checks, two objects, and marks for testing them separately.

Now imagine a candidate schedule that parks all three cranes on one section and consequently clears every ship by 11:00 — hours earlier than anything sensible. Score it and the fitness function is delighted: minimal waiting, tiny makespan (the moment the last job finishes — how soon the quay is finally clear; Lesson 8 turns it into a fitness component in its own right), superb crane utilisation.

It is also worthless, because a section physically cannot host three cranes at once. The schedule is not a good solution that breaks a rule; it is not a solution.

The principle. A GA must never be in a position to prefer a fast illegal solution to a slower legal one — and it will, every time, unless you stop it, because illegal solutions are usually the fastest ones (that is exactly what the rules were preventing). So the evaluation order is fixed: ask validity first, always, then score quality.

Every tool below is a different mechanism for enforcing that ordering — the alphabet stops the illegal solution being written, the decoder stops it being built, repair converts it, the penalty makes it lose. Write the ordering sentence into Q2 explicitly; it frames every tool choice that follows.

The five tools, cheapest first

#ToolHowBest for
1Encoding (alphabet restriction)Restrict legal gene values so the violation cannot be writtenCompatibility / eligibility rules. Bonus: shrinks the search space
2Decoder (construction)The decoder lays solutions out so the rule never arises — sequential placement means no overlaps; buffers auto-insertedExclusivity, changeover, release times
3RepairDetect the violation in an offspring and fix it (swap to nearest legal option)When crossover breaks structure (blocks, permutations)
4Penaltyfitness += weight × amount of violationWhatever remains; when degree of violation matters
5RejectionDiscard invalid offspring, generate againLast resort — wastes evaluations when valid solutions are rare. But his own table gives it two virtues: it is the easiest of all to implement and it guarantees a clean population, so name it, then say why you didn't pick it

Present this as a mini-table in your Q2 answer — one row per constraint: constraint → tool → one-line how. The table format itself matches how the marks are awarded (3 for “constraint handling is reasoned”).

The whole thing done for the port — compatibility → ENCODING, berth occupancy → DECODER, changeover → DECODER, crane breaks and charging → DECODER, buffer capacity → PENALTY, block structure → REPAIR — sits on the Practice page's walkthrough. Copy its shape, not its rows, and drive it with his one-line rule of thumb: enforce a constraint in the encoding if you can, in the decoder if you cannot, and by penalty only as a last resort — every constraint you move leftwards is search effort you stop wasting.

Note also which design you chose in Q1, because it decides the mix: a permutation-plus-decoder chromosome leans on the decoder and repair, while a direct encoding forces you onto penalties. Saying which, and why, is worth a mark on its own.

Tool 5 in close-up — the death penalty (and what the knapsack labs actually did)

Rejection's textbook name is the death penalty, and it comes in two forms. The strict form is the one in the table — throw the invalid offspring away and generate another. The practical form keeps the individual but returns the worst possible fitness the moment any hard constraint is broken: 0 for a maximise problem, a huge number (or ∞) for a minimise one.

The individual stays in the population but can essentially never be selected, so it dies out on its own. The module's multi-objective knapsack lab does exactly this — an overweight rucksack is scored (0, 0) on both objectives regardless of what is inside it.

Why it is a blunt instrument. Every illegal solution scores identically, so the fitness function tells the GA nothing about how illegal a solution was. One gram over capacity and forty kilos over are the same score, which means there is no slope leading back into the legal region — the GA cannot walk out of trouble, it can only get lucky. Use it when illegality is genuinely binary and rare; reach for a graded penalty when the degree matters.

The clarification worth having, because it contradicts the obvious answer. The classic knapsack — a set of items each with a weight and a value, and a rucksack with a fixed capacity; gene i = 1 means “take item i” — is usually taught as “overflow is invalid, so penalise it”.

But the module's single-objective knapsack lab does neither: its decode function walks the items in order and simply skips any item that would push the bag over capacity. The overflow never reaches the fitness function at all. That is a decoder/repair solution — tool 2 or 3, not tool 4 — and it is a live example of the whole doctrine: use the cheapest tool that works.
