If you are asked how a knapsack GA handles overflow, the complete answer is “several ways: skip during decoding, repair by dropping the worst item, penalise the excess, or return the worst fitness — and here is which I chose and why.” For the record his instance is 22 items against a capacity of 400 — the same figure he wrote on the board, KnapsackWeight<=400 — while the site's live demo uses a cut-down 10-item version so the bars fit on screen; and the notebook ships with only the Knapsack class, its second cell reading ## ADD THE DEAP CODE, because writing the GA around a decoder you were handed was the exercise.

The trade-offs nobody mentions, which is why mentioning them scores

These tools are not free and they are not interchangeable.

  • Repair biases the searcha routine that always fixes a clash by moving to “the nearest legal option” pushes every offspring toward the same style of solution, so the population narrows for reasons that have nothing to do with fitness — you get feasible answers that all look alike.
  • Penalties have a number you must guess righttoo small and the GA discovers that breaking the rule buys more than it costs, so it cheats and your best solution is illegal; too big and the landscape becomes a cliff — everything illegal is equally terrible, the GA cannot tell one minute over from four hours over, and it gets stuck unable to find its way back.
  • Rejection wastes evaluationsin a tightly constrained problem most offspring are invalid, so you spend the entire budget generating and binning.

Naming one such cost against your chosen tool is what turns a list into “reasoned”.

Every tool has a virtue as well as a price, and his own comparison slide lists both columns

Carry both halves, because the three marks are awarded for weighing one against the other rather than for reciting costs. Repair keeps every individual useful — an offspring that crossover would otherwise have wasted still contributes an evaluation — and there is no coefficient anywhere that you have to defend. Penalty is simple to code and, in the phrase from his Good column, lets the GA travel through illegal ground to reach a good legal answer — which is exactly why he assigns buffer capacity to a penalty rather than to repair: it is “hard to repair without wrecking the schedule”. Rejection buys a population in which every survivor is genuinely a solution, and it is the least code of the five, which is why the multi-objective knapsack lab simply scores an overweight rucksack (0, 0).

The rule that decides between the first two: repair when the correction is unambiguous, penalise when the violation is a matter of degree. Name all three, then justify the one you chose against the specific rule — that trade, written down, is the mark.

Penalty design — the lab formula

The module's guard-rota problem — 16 guards, 3 shifts a day, a 7-day roster, from Lesson 5, and coded up in Python with DEAP in the labs — uses the canonical shape. (His own file runs the same problem at 8 guards with the bands relaxed to 2–3 / 2–4 / 1–2, so 168 bits rather than 336. Quote the scenario's numbers; it is the arithmetic that transfers, not the count.) Memorise it:

fitness = (hardViolation₁ + hardViolation₂ + hardViolation₃) × BIG_WEIGHT + softPreferenceViolations

In the lab BIG_WEIGHT = 10. The problem object is constructed as Guard(10), the cost line returns 10 × (hard violations) + (soft violations), and in class he says it plainly — “one violation here is equal to 10.” So one hard break costs the same as ten unhonoured preferences. Quote the number: it is far easier to reproduce under pressure than a symbol, and it turns the hard-beats-soft claim from an assertion into something checkable.

Then quote his caveat, because that is the actual principle: “the values here don't really matter; the difference matters.” Ten, a hundred or a thousand all work, provided the weight exceeds the largest soft gain a solution could buy by breaking one hard rule.

  • Hard violations share one large weight so any hard break outweighs every soft gain — the GA is steered to feasibility first, quality second.
  • Count the degree of violation (how many, how far over), not just yes/no — gives the GA a gradient to climb down.

  • The converse, which is the same rule stated as a warning: a GA cannot converge on a fitness function that only reports right or wrong. If every illegal solution scores 1 and every legal one scores 0, the landscape is a flat plain with a hole in it — there is nothing to climb, so selection has no preference to act on and the search degenerates into random guessing.

    This is why puzzles like Sudoku defeat a naive GA and why “count how many rules are broken, and by how much” is not a refinement but the thing that makes the algorithm work at all.

  • Reward or penalty — his framing, from the guard-rota session. Tidied from the automatic transcript: “when we have a set of constraints, set of conditions, either we apply a reward if we meet some particular criteria, or penalty if we violate that… if it's this way, the higher the better; if it's this way, no — as long as we really understand and don't mix up.” The two are the same information turned upside down: penalties count what is broken and you minimise; rewards count what is satisfied and you maximise.

    Pick one direction, say which, and stay in it for every component — mixing them inside one sum is the mistake he is warning against in that last clause.

The guard rota, rule by rule — legislation turned into counting functions

This is the most transferable worked example in the module, because it shows the step everyone skips: turning a sentence of employment law into a number a computer can add up. The setup, restated so it stands alone: 16 guards, 3 shifts a day (morning / afternoon / night), a 7-day week; the chromosome is one bit per (guard, day, shift) saying whether that guard works it. Four rules:

Rule as writtenHard/softImplemented as
Minimum 8 hours between shiftsHardBecause the three daily shifts run back to back, “8 hours off” simply means a guard may never work two adjacent shifts. Read each guard's week as one strip of bits and count every occurrence of two consecutive 1s. Elegant: a legal clause becomes a pattern-match on the chromosome
Maximum 5 shifts per weekHardSum each guard's bits; add max(0, total − 5). Note the max(0, …) — you count how far over, not just that they are over
Staffing bands: morning 3–4, afternoon 3–4, night 1–2HardFor each of the 21 shifts, sum the guards assigned and add the distance outside the band — below the minimum or above the maximum, both count
Guards' shift preferencesSoftCount the requests not honoured. No weight multiplier

Combined exactly as the canonical shape predicts:

fitness = (consecutiveShiftViolations + max5Violations + staffingBandViolations) × BIG_WEIGHT + preferenceViolations

Use his own function names — he wrote them out on the board. The Lab 2 whiteboard carries the same line with the identifiers spelled in full: “FitnessFunction: (consecGuardShiftsViolation() + Max5ShiftsViolation() + minMaxGuardShiftViolation()) * weight + GuardPreferenceViolation()”. The naming policy is the transferable part, and it costs nothing to copy on Friday: one function per rule, each named after the rule it polices, each returning a count — then a single line that combines them.

Write your four names that way for whatever scenario you are given and the marker can see the mapping from legislation to arithmetic without reading a word of prose. Directly beneath that line he wrote one more call, Decode/Print(), and it belongs in your Q1 decoder answer: decoding does not finish at an internal data structure, it finishes by emitting a human-readable rota somebody can be handed. If a paper asks you to decode into a full timetable, say that the last step of your decoder prints one.

Three separate hard counts, one shared big weight, soft count added raw. Once you have seen it done here, you can do it for any scenario Friday brings: read the rule, decide hard or soft, write the function that counts how badly it is broken, then wire it into that one line.

The DEAP variant worth knowing — and the trap inside it. In the shipped lab the priority is enforced the plain way, inside the cost function: the object is built as Guard(10) and the evaluation returns a single number, return guard.getCost(individual),. The lab's declaration line nevertheless reads weights=(−10.0, −1.0) — two minimised objectives, negative meaning minimise (Lesson 6) — and in class he builds the version that would use it, splitting the one cost function into two, a hard count and a soft count, and returning them as a two-element tuple.

Say that carefully, though, because the magnitudes are not a 10:1 exchange rate: DEAP stores weight × value and compares fitness tuples position by position, so once hard violations sit in the first slot, any hard break outranks every soft gain outright, and 10 versus 1 rescales nothing. That happens to be the behaviour you wanted, but it is lexicographic ordering doing it, not the number.

In the lab as shipped the second weight is never exercised at all, because only one value is returned. So if a question asks how the priority is enforced in code, point at the multiplier inside the cost function, and add his gloss on the number — “the values here don't really matter; the difference matters.”

The evidence that the multiplier works — one line, and it is quotable. Run that lab to completion and it prints a rota with consecutive-shift violations 0, shifts-per-week violations 0, guards-per-shift violations 0 — and 10 shift-preference violations still outstanding. Read the result twice, because it says two useful things at once.

First, a multiplier of just ten did the job: you do not need an enormous number, you need one above the threshold where breaking a hard rule stops paying, which is the sizing rule below confirmed by an actual run rather than asserted. Second, and this is the part worth writing into Q2: it drove the hard violations to zero and then stopped.

Ten soft misses survive in the final answer, and that is the correct end state rather than a failure. A weighted penalty buys you legality; quality is then whatever the soft terms can win inside the legal region. If your answer promises a schedule that is both perfectly legal and perfectly preferred, you have promised something the mechanism does not deliver.

Penalty engineering — sizing the number, and the three named kinds

The general form generalises the lab line to any number of rules:

Fitness = weighted objectives + Σₖ Pₖ · vₖ

where vk is the measured amount by which constraint k is violated (minutes over, containers over capacity, shifts too many — never a yes/no) and Pk is that constraint's penalty coefficient.

Writing vk properly is the step most answers skip, so here is his own weak-versus-strong table, done for the port's rules. Most of these are cheaper to handle in the decoder; this is how you measure any of them that ends up on the penalty route.

Rule brokenWeak (yes/no)Strong — the quantity you actually add up
Buffer overflowcount it as 1 violationΣ over zones and slots of max(0, occupancy − that zone's capacity) — container-hours
Start before ETAcount it as 1 violationΣ over jobs of max(0, ETA − start) — minutes
Crane collision (two cranes sharing a section)count it as 1 violationthe number of slot-minutes in which two cranes share a section
Over-long continuous workcount it as 1 violationminutes worked beyond the 3-hour continuous limit

His justification line, to write underneath: a schedule 5 containers over capacity is much closer to a good answer than one 300 over, and only the strong version can tell them apart — degree of violation gives the GA a slope to walk down. Notice the shape all four strong versions share: a sum of max(0, actual − allowed), expressed in the rule's own natural unit, over every unit the rule applies to — every job, every slot, every zone.

State the summation set out loud; “per zone per slot” is doing as much work as the arithmetic. Learn that pattern once and you can convert whatever rule Friday's scenario sets into a countable vk in a single line — even one that looks binary, because an overlap becomes graded the moment you measure how long it lasts. A bare formula earns very little; formula + unit + why the port cares earns the mark.

Two rules govern Pk, and both are quotable:

  • The sizing rule. Pk must be large enough that the worst legal solution still scores better than the best illegal one. That single sentence is how you justify a number you otherwise cannot defend — you are not claiming 1,000 is correct, you are claiming it is above the threshold where cheating stops paying. If you can estimate the biggest possible objective gain from breaking rule k, then Pk just has to exceed it per unit of violation.
  • The dynamic-penalty trick. Instead of one fixed number, raise Pk as the generations advance. Early on the penalty is gentle, so the GA is free to wander through illegal territory and discover promising structures; later it tightens, squeezing the population back into the legal region. You get exploration first and feasibility at the end, which is exactly the shape you want.

Which gives the three names the professor flags as distinction-level detail: a static penalty is a fixed coefficient set once; a dynamic penalty changes on a fixed schedule, typically growing with the generation counter; an adaptive penalty changes in response to what the population is actually doing — pushed up when too many individuals are illegal, relaxed when almost all are legal. Naming all three and saying which you chose costs one sentence and reads as reading beyond the slides.

The worked example that proves why the penalty is there

Set-up. Two candidate port schedules, X and Y, scored on the same fitness function. On the crane-utilisation component alone — lower is better — Y scores 0.400 and X scores 0.493. On that objective Y is genuinely, measurably the better schedule. Intuition would take Y.

Roll the components up before you touch the penalty

That 0.400 is one component, not the objective total — waiting, cost, energy and the rest still have to be normalised, weighted and added in. Do that and the weighted-objective subtotals come out at Y 0.262 and X 0.114 (this is his first scoring sheet — six components, weights 0.20 / 0.25 / 0.15 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.15. There is a second, revised sheet in Lesson 8 which scores a different pair of schedules on eight components and lands on X 0.207 and Y 0.173. Two sheets, not one: quote one or the other, never both sets of figures in a single answer.): the other components have already eaten Y's crane advantage, though nothing so far says Y is illegal.

What the rules say

Y breaks three hard constraints; X breaks none. Charge each break at a coefficient of 1.0 and the arithmetic closes in one line: Y = 0.262 + 3 × 1.0 = 3.262 against X = 0.114 + 0 = 0.114. The gap widens from about 0.15 to over three. Be precise about what the penalty did: X was already ahead on the objective subtotal (0.114 against 0.262, lower better) before any penalty was charged — the paragraph above concedes it — so the penalty did not reverse a ranking, it made an existing one unassailable.

Note where the penalty is added: to the objective total, never to a single component — add it to the 0.400 and you get a tidy-looking 3.400 that is simply the wrong number.

The two lessons. First, an illegal solution can genuinely beat a legal one on an individual objective — that is not a bug in your fitness components, it is the normal state of affairs, because illegality is usually what makes a schedule efficient. Second, therefore, the penalty is the only thing standing between the GA and being fooled by exactly this. Quote the numbers if you have space; quote the conclusion if you do not.

Try it — penalty fitness, live

A guard rota with sliders for violations. Watch feasibility dominate.

Why this is a design decision, not a formality

The five tools look like a menu of equivalent options with different price tags. They are not. Every constraint gets enforced somewhere — the only genuine question is which stage of your pipeline pays for it, and each stage pays in a different currency. Enforce it in the alphabet and you pay in expressiveness: the illegal solution becomes unwritable, but so does anything that would have needed those gene values for a reason you did not anticipate.

Enforce it in the decoder and you pay in freedom: a decoder that always places the next job as early as legally possible produces valid schedules every time, and can never produce the schedule that deliberately leaves a crane idle for twenty minutes to save energy — waiting for a cheaper electric crane to come free rather than starting now on the thirstier diesel one, because the fuel saved is worth more than the twenty minutes lost — and that solution is not rejected, it is unreachable (which is precisely the honest strength Pattern 3 buys, and why it pays for it in feasibility).

Enforce it in repair and you pay in bias. Enforce it in the fitness function and you pay in evaluations, because now a large share of every generation is illegal and most of your compute measures how illegal things are rather than how good.

There is also a hard limit on which tool can express which rule, and it is worth stating because it makes the choice look inevitable rather than arbitrary. Alphabet restriction is the cleanest tool available, but it can only encode constraints about one gene at a time — “SH2 may only berth in sections 2 or 3” fits perfectly, since it is a statement about SH2's own gene.

Anything relational — no two ships in the same berth at once, at least 30 minutes between a departure and the next arrival, at least 8 hours between one guard's shifts — involves two or more genes simultaneously, and no restriction on a single gene's legal values can express it. Those constraints must be handled further down: by a decoder that lays things out sequentially so overlap cannot arise, by a repair pass, or by a penalty.

Sorting your rules by this test — is this about one decision, or about a relationship between decisions? — hands you the tool assignment almost automatically, and it is a far better justification than “penalty because it is flexible”.

Underneath all of it sits one tension that never fully resolves. Harder enforcement gives you a smaller, safer search space where every individual is a real solution and no evaluation is wasted — but a smaller space might no longer contain the best answer, and you will never find out, because the GA cannot report on solutions it was structurally prevented from writing.

Looser enforcement keeps the whole space reachable, including the good solutions hiding just past a rule boundary, at the cost of spending your budget in territory that will be thrown away. The professional position — and the one to write down — is that you chose deliberately: “I enforced compatibility in the alphabet and exclusivity in the decoder because those rules are absolute and cheap to build in; I left working-time limits to a graded penalty because near-misses are informative and I want the GA to be able to approach that boundary from the wrong side.” That sentence is the difference between listing tools and reasoning about them, and it is where the marks for “constraint handling is reasoned” actually live.

Lesson 8 · ~25 min · core exam material

Designing the Fitness Function

The heart of Q2: turn every soft goal into a component with a formula, a unit, and a purpose — then combine them honestly.

Lesson 8 on one slide
  • Every soft goal becomes a component: formula + unit + purpose — count the brief's aims; one objective cannot score Q2 well.
  • Unify directions (utilisation is a maximise → add 1 − U) and normalise units to [0,1] by worst case before any addition.
  • Write an actual weight vector — “the weights sum to 1” is not a weighting; each weight cites something the brief says.
  • Validity is not fitness: legality is settled first; a schedule failing a hard check is a non-solution, not a low scorer.
  • Work one number end to end — computed beats asserted everywhere on this paper.
  • Stochastic algorithm ⇒ report mean ± std over ≥30 runs, never a single run.
Tomorrow this buys you: the biggest block on the paper — Q2's components, aggregation and weights rows (~10 of its 15 marks).

The component recipe

For each thing the scenario says it cares about, write one component: fᵢ = formula (unit) — purpose. The standard library, adaptable to any scenario:

ComponentFormula shapeUnit
f₁ waiting / delayΣ over entities (service start − release time)minutes
f₂ priority-weighted delayΣ wₑ × delayₑ, with w = 5 emergency / 3 high / 1 normalweighted min
f₃ resource utilisation1 − (hours worked ÷ hours available)fraction
f₄ overload / congestionΣ over resources & slots max(0, occupancy − capacity)unit-hours
f₅ money / energy costΣ usage-hrs × rate + activation feesRM (Malaysian ringgit)
f₆ overtime / limit breachesΣ hours beyond allowedhours
f₇ allocation costΣ cost(entity, its assigned resource) from the cost matrixRM
f₈ balance / fairnessstandard deviation of load across resources or staffmixed
f₉ makespanfinish time of the last jobminutes

How the components mark is actually awarded

His mark-hints slide is unambiguous: “A formula on its own earns very little. A formula plus its unit plus why it matters earns the mark.” So never write f₅ = Σ running hours × rate and stop. Write: f₅ measures the total energy the cranes consume, in ringgit, and the port cares because crane running time is its largest controllable cost.

Three clauses, one mark, repeated for every component — that is the whole of the four-mark band, and it is why nine bare formulae score worse than five explained ones.

Evaluate the two awkward components once, on real numbers — almost nobody does

The port's berth handling cost is read straight off the ship × section matrix (SH1: A 40, B 70, C 90 · SH2: B 50, C 80 · SH3: A 60, C 90 · SH4: A 70, B 55, C 45, all in ringgit; the blanks are the berths that ship may not use).

For the plan that berths SH1 in A, SH2 in B, SH3 in C and SH4 back in A, f₇ = 40 + 50 + 90 + 70 = RM 250. The rival plan totals RM 195, and that RM 55 is the entire argument between the two schedules on this term — small enough that any decent waiting or makespan weight will overrule it, which is exactly the point you then make out loud.

For balance, take each zone's peak occupancy across the day — 150 in A, 65 in B, 33 in C — mean 82.7, so f₈ = σ ≈ 49: a large spread, meaning one zone carries the whole yard while two sit half empty. A balanced plan drives the same figure toward zero. Two lines of arithmetic turn two copied phrases into two measurements you own.

Include the components the scenario's special features create — building activation fees, time-window traffic penalties, seating buffers. Those bespoke components are where the 4 “components explained” marks concentrate.

The f₄ trap, and it catches almost everyone

That “capacity” in the overload formula is not one shared number. Each resource has its own capacity, and the sum must use each one's: in the port, yard sections A, B and C hold 200, 250 and 150 containers respectively, so f₄ = Σ over sections and slots of max(0, occupancys − capacitys) — with the subscript on the capacity, not a single constant lifted out of the summation.

Write one shared capacity and you have silently declared a different problem, one in which the tightest zone is invisible. The same applies to any per-resource limit: room seats, machine throughput, staff maximums.

And fitness does not have to be a formula at all

Everything in the table above is arithmetic because scheduling components happen to be arithmetic, but the only thing a GA requires of a fitness function is that it returns a comparable number. It can equally be an algorithm (run a simulation of the day and report the total delay), an external service call (send the design to an engineering solver and read back the stress figure), or the result of a game (play the evolved strategy against a fixed opponent a hundred times and return the win rate).

The module's own feature-selection lab does exactly this: the fitness of a chromosome is the accuracy of a machine-learning model trained using the features that chromosome selects. This is the point behind calling a GA gradient-free — it never differentiates the objective, so the objective is allowed to be a black box.

The one practical consequence to name: when the fitness is an expensive algorithm rather than a formula, evaluation count becomes your real budget, and that is what population size × generations is spending.

That lab's actual formula, since Friday's scenario may not be a port

The dataset has 16 candidate features and gene i = 1 means “feed feature i to the classifier” — a 16-bit binary chromosome, so 2¹⁶ = 65,536 possible feature subsets, and a decision tree cross-validated over five folds scoring every one of them. The fitness is accuracy − 0.001 × (number of features used), and the tiny 0.001 is doing precise work: it is a tiebreaker, not a real cost.

Two chromosomes that both score 96% accuracy are indistinguishable without it; with it, the one using six features beats the one using nine, so the search is nudged toward the smaller model at no risk of trading away real accuracy. The lab also gives the degenerate case a defined answer — select no features at all and the function returns 0.0 rather than handing an empty matrix to the model.

Best run: fitness 0.985, from accuracy 0.99 on 5 features — check the arithmetic yourself, 0.99 − 0.001 × 5 = 0.985 — against 0.91 when all sixteen are used. Half the features, better accuracy: that is the sentence the lab exists to produce. Two honest footnotes. The 0.91 baseline comes from a companion notebook whose cross-validation folds are not shuffled while the GA's are, so it is an indication rather than a controlled comparison.

And the improvement over the run itself is real but modest — generation 0's best already scored 0.972, and fifty generations lifted it to 0.985. Two things to carry into Q2: a mild preference can be a very small subtracted term rather than a full weighted objective, and every fitness function needs a defined answer for the empty or degenerate chromosome. Say what yours returns.

Normalise before you combine

This is the exact place marks go missing, and they go missing quietly

His speaker note on the normalisation slide is blunt: this is where most students lose marks silently — they write a weighted sum with no scaling and never notice the units clash. Silently is the word that matters. Nothing in such an answer looks wrong: the formula is there, the components are there, the weights add to 1 — and the band is simply not awarded, because adding an energy bill in the hundreds to a fraction between 0 and 1 means energy alone decides every ranking and crane utilisation is ignored completely.

The cure is one sentence written explicitly on the page, and the deck says that sentence is worth a mark on its own: “You cannot add minutes to ringgit to container-hours.” Write it, then the scaling formula, then the table of ranges — three lines, and the aggregation band is claimed before you have combined a single number.

So: you cannot add minutes to ringgit to fractions. Scale every component to [0,1] first:

f′ᵢ = (fᵢ − fᵢ,min) ÷ (fᵢ,max − fᵢ,min)

Justify every range, because every minimum and maximum is an assumption you are making — say so, and give the one-clause reason it came from. His own reference table for the port, which you can lift wholesale and relabel:

ComponentUnitMinMaxWhere the range comes from
f₁ ship waitingminutes0600worst case: every ship waits the whole shift
f₂ priority-weighted waitingweighted min02,000f₁'s maximum × the highest priority weight
f₃ 1 − utilisationfraction01already a fraction — no scaling needed
f₄ buffer pressurecontainer-hrs0500worst inflow pattern into the smallest zone
f₅ energy costRM5002,000an all-electric shift against an all-diesel one
f₆ overtimeminutes0240capped at 4 hours past the shift end
f₇ berth handling costRM0400cheapest legal berths against dearest legal berths
f₈ yard balancecontainers0100perfectly even against everything in one zone

Eight rows, one clause each — that little table is the scaling mark. Two cautions, and the first is the one that decides whether your f₁ row survives inspection. His printed ceiling of 600 does not follow from his own formula. f₁ is defined one screen earlier as a sum over ships; the shift is 08:00–16:00 = 480 minutes; and four ships each waiting the entire shift is 4 × 480 = 1,920 minutes.

600 is neither 480 nor 1,920, and nothing in the scenario produces it. So derive the ceiling from the summation your own formula actually performs, and write the multiplication down where the marker can see it: “max waiting = all four ships wait the entire 480-minute shift = 4 × 480 = 1,920 min.” Then keep every component on that same basis.

His rule for f₂ is “f₁'s maximum × the highest priority weight”, and f₂ sums over ships too — the four ships carry Emergency 5, High 3, Normal 1, Normal 1 — so the matching per-quay ceiling is 480 × (5+3+1+1) = 4,800 weighted-minutes. Normalise one component per ship and the other per quay and you have silently re-weighted your own function.

If you prefer the per-ship basis, that is fine: write 480 and put the words per ship beside it. What you must never do is write 600 above a formula that sums over four ships. (His deck prints 600 and 2,000 for these two rows and does not follow its own rule either — 600 × 5 is 3,000, not 2,000. A student who shows the derivation is safe whichever figure the model answer carries.) The second caution is his own and it is reassuring: an examiner will accept any sensible range you have justified, so never leave a min/max blank because you could not derive it exactly.

Then a weighted sum, weights summing to 1, lower = better: F = Σ wᵢ·f′ᵢ. If the scenario says “X is twice as important as Y” — set wₓ = 2wᵧ and cite the line.

And when the scenario says nothing about importance — the commoner case, and the one that panics people in the hall — you still have to commit to numbers. He answered this directly in the mock debrief; tidied from the automatic transcript: “you must have weights. Either you can have just equal hard constraints, soft constraints — all the hard are the same, all the soft are the same… Or you may interpret in terms of: this is very important, this is important, this is less important… the least important.” Two legal routes, and he named both.

Route one — flat within a tier: every component in a tier carries the same weight, and you state which tier each component sits in.

Route two — your own importance bands: sort the components into three or four bands (very important / important / less important / least important, in his words), give each band a descending weight, and attach one clause of scenario justification to the top band and to the bottom one.

Either route earns the “weights stated” marks. What loses them is neither of these — it is a weighted sum with the weights left as letters.

Write an actual weight vector — “the weights sum to 1” is not a weighting

A marker cannot award the aggregation marks for a promise — that is what “you must have weights” above is telling you. His six-component set for the port: w₁ waiting 0.20 · w₂ priority-weighted waiting 0.25 · w₃ utilisation 0.15 · w₄ buffer pressure 0.15 · w₅ energy cost 0.10 · w₆ overtime 0.15 — 1.00 exactly.

Notice which is largest and why: priority carries 0.25 because port policy puts emergency and high-priority vessels first, so the weight cites the scenario rather than your taste. The eight-component version spreads the same total as 0.15 / 0.18 / 0.12 / 0.12 / 0.10 / 0.13 / 0.12 / 0.08, again 1.00. Memorise one set, relabel it for whatever Friday brings, total it out loud, and attach one clause of scenario justification to the largest and to the smallest.

Then write the honest sentence underneath, which is worth a critical-awareness mark on its own: these are policy, not fact about the port, and a different port manager would defend a different set.

One component, all the way through, because a bare formula with no worked value reads as copied. His scoring sheet takes two port schedules — X, the legal timetable, and Y, which looks faster but breaks three hard rules — and pushes every component through the same steps. Take waiting, f₁: X waits 15 minutes in total, Y waits 180. Normalise on his 0–600 range — keep 600 here if you are reproducing his sheet, but see the caution above on deriving it: 15 ÷ 600 = 0.025, 180 ÷ 600 = 0.300. Multiply by w₁ = 0.20: 0.005 and 0.060. Repeat for the other five components and the weighted subtotals land at X 0.114 and Y 0.262.

Only then does the penalty go on, and it goes on the total, never on a component: Y = 0.262 + 3 × 1.0 = 3.262 against X = 0.114 + 0 = 0.114. Raw → scaled → weighted → summed → penalised. Walking one component through all five steps with real numbers is what the aggregation-and-scaling marks are actually for.

Or refuse to choose

The Q2 mark scheme reads “you scale before combining, and state weights or use a Pareto approach”, so the weighted sum is not the only road to those two marks. Keep the objectives separate instead and hand them to a multi-objective algorithm — NSGA-II (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II) or MOEA/D — and the output is no longer one schedule but a non-dominated set: a group in which no plan beats another on everything, so each is the best available at something.

For the port that reads as a menu: Plan X clears the quay at 14:00 for RM 250 of berth handling cost; Plan Y at 15:30 for RM 195; Plan Z at 14:45 for RM 215, the best balance of the three. Nothing there dominates anything else, and in his words that set is the honest answer to the question — the port manager picks on the day, using judgement the algorithm does not have.

Either route earns full marks; naming both and saying why you took one, and what you gave up, is what lifts the answer. Lesson 9 has the machinery.

What to do when one component points the wrong way

A weighted sum needs every term pulling in the same direction, and scenarios rarely oblige — “minimise waiting, minimise cost, maximise crane utilisation” mixes both. The fix is a one-line identity worth memorising: maximising X is exactly the same problem as minimising −X. Nothing is lost, because optimisation only ever compares solutions, and negating a quantity reverses every comparison at once — the solution with the highest utilisation is, without exception, the solution with the lowest negative utilisation.

So flip the sign and drop it straight into the minimising sum. In practice you usually flip it into something even tidier: if utilisation is already a fraction in [0,1], use 1 − utilisation (“idle fraction”) so the term stays positive and normalised — which is precisely why f₃ in the table above is written as 1 − (hours worked ÷ hours available) rather than as utilisation itself. State the identity once in Q2 and every mixed-direction scenario stops being a problem.

The makespan story — the professor's most important slide

“The most important slide” (walkthrough, verbatim structure)

What X and Y actually are, before the moral

They are two timetables for the same four ships, the same three quay sections and the same three cranes, differing only in how the ships are spread across the sections. The crucial property: both are fully valid — neither breaks a single hard rule, so nothing here is settled by a penalty. (Careful: this is a different pair from the X and Y in the penalty walk-through above and in Lesson 7, where Y was the illegal one. Same letters, different schedules, opposite lesson.) The visible difference is the finish: X clears the quay at 14:00, Y at 15:30 — X is done ninety minutes earlier.

Intuition takes X. The weighted sum takes Y. Why? Nothing in f₁…f₈ measured when the quay is clear. Taken together the eight components score Y lower, and not one of them can see those ninety minutes, because waiting time only measures the start of service — once a ship has begun unloading, f₁ has stopped counting. The fix: add makespan as f₉, re-spread the weights so they still sum to 1 — and the ranking flips to X.

His own sentence to copy, verbatim from the “What to write in your answer” panel on that slide: “I include a makespan term because the six aims listed in the brief do not measure quay turnaround, and a port is paid for turnaround. Without it the model prefers a cheaper, slower plan.” And the generalised version for a scenario that is not a port — ours, not his: if the ranking disagrees with intuition, ask what the intuition is measuring that no component captures, then add that component.

The flip in numbers — asserted it is an anecdote, computed it is an argument

Score both schedules on f₁–f₈ (waiting, priority-weighted waiting, idle-crane fraction, buffer pressure, energy, overtime, berth handling cost, yard balance) with weights summing to 1, and the totals come out X 0.207, Y 0.173 (his revised sheet — eight components on weights 0.15 / 0.18 / 0.12 / 0.12 / 0.10 / 0.13 / 0.12 / 0.08. Lesson 7's 0.114 / 0.262 pair is the earlier sheet, six components on a different weight set: two sheets, not one. And the letters moved between them — the plan he labels Y here is the plan he labelled X on the earlier sheet, which you can check from the raw rows, waiting 15 min, 1 − utilisation 0.493, energy RM 890, identical on both. Never carry a letter across from one sheet to the other.).

Lower is better, so the function picks Y — ninety minutes of extra quay time and all. Now add f₉ = makespan, the minutes from 08:00 until the last container lands, normalised over a 240–600 minute range: X 360 → 0.333, Y 450 → 0.583. Give it weight 0.19 and re-spread the rest so they still sum to 1 — f₁–f₆ take 0.65 between them, f₇ berth cost 0.10, f₈ yard balance 0.06. New totals: X 0.231, Y 0.252 — X wins.

Be honest about why: berth cost and yard balance still favour Y; X simply buys enough on makespan to outweigh them. Two pairs of totals, 0.207/0.173 then 0.231/0.252, is the entire proof and it fits on one line of your script. Note the discipline too — the weights were re-spread, never patched, so the total is still exactly 1.00.

And the discipline that goes with the diagnosis. When your score and your judgement disagree, the tempting move is to nudge a weight until the ranking comes out the way you wanted. His instruction is the opposite: do not fix this by fiddling with the weights — work out WHY first. Notice the mismatch and trust it (your intuition says X, your function says Y, one of them is wrong, and it is usually the function); list what you believe makes X better and check it against every component you have written; if none captures it, add the missing term and re-spread.

Weight-fiddling would have produced a number that ranked X above Y while the function stayed blind to quay clearance: right answer, broken model, and the next scenario breaks it again. The sentence to carry into the hall, because it is the distinction-level observation on this entire topic: weights decide how much you care about the things you measure; they cannot help you at all with the things you forgot to measure.

Choosing what goes into the objective function is the harder and more important design decision, and saying so out loud earns more than any amount of tuning.

Try it — watch the ranking flip

Schedules X and Y from the walkthrough. Drag the makespan weight from 0 upward (other weights re-scale proportionally) and watch the winner change.

The job fitness actually does — ranking two mediocre solutions

Almost everyone designs a fitness function by imagining the perfect schedule and checking that it would score well. That is the one case the function will never be asked about. The GA does not see the optimum until it has already climbed to it, and it climbs by making millions of comparisons between ordinary, half-broken candidates — a schedule with two ships waiting versus a schedule with one ship waiting and a mild overtime breach.

So the real test of every component you write is not “does the best solution score best?” but: given two mediocre solutions, does this number separate them, and in the direction I would want? If two visibly different timetables score identically, you have not built a hill for the GA to climb — you have built a plateau, a flat region it wanders across at random because selection has nothing to prefer. Getting the optimum's score exactly right is worth nothing; getting the ordering of the rubbish right is worth everything.

Once you see it that way, the advice that keeps reappearing stops being three separate rules and becomes one. “Count the degree of violation” is this rule applied to constraints: is it overloaded? has two values and is a plateau, whereas by how many container-hours? is a slope the GA can walk down.

“Measure in minutes, not in counts” is the same rule applied to objectives: the number of ships that waited takes five possible values in a four-ship problem, whereas total waiting in minutes takes thousands, so every ten-minute improvement anywhere in the schedule becomes visible to selection. The working heuristic: prefer a component that changes when you shift one job by ten minutes over a component that only changes when a rule flips.

A fitness function full of coarse counters is a staircase; a fitness function of continuous measures is a ramp, and a GA is very much better at ramps.

This is also the deeper reason the makespan story matters. Adding f₉ was not decoration and it was not about scoring the winner correctly — it was about giving the GA a new reason to prefer one mediocre schedule over another, along an axis where previously the two were indistinguishable. Every component you add carves another dimension into the landscape and creates gradient where there was flat ground.

Which brings the honest limit: a component you cannot compute from the decoded schedule cannot be in the fitness function, however loudly the scenario says it cares. If you want to charge for reefer power, the data list must carry each ship's reefer flag and the decoder must produce the hours each ship spent plugged in.

That is why the data-requirements list (Lesson 5) and the fitness function are designed together rather than in sequence — and it is a genuinely good sentence to put in Q2: “I included ship priority in the data requirements specifically because f₂ cannot be computed without it.”

Critical awareness — the 3 free marks

Why “free”: his mark-hints slide is direct about this band — these are “the ones most students never reach. They are also the easiest to write, because they need no calculation at all.” Objectives conflict; the weights are policy and not fact about the port; the aims the brief lists miss quay turnaround. Three sentences, three marks, no arithmetic — and you can write them even if every number in your answer is wrong.

  • Objectives conflict: cheap berths attract every ship ⇒ congestion; low cost fights low waiting. Name one concrete conflict from the scenario.
  • Weights are policy, not fact: “the ranking depends entirely on which components I chose and how I weighted them — neither is a fact about the port.”
  • Time-dependent terms (a 12:00–14:00 traffic penalty) must be computed per assigned slot, not as a constant.

Declare the modelling choices where you had a free hand

Several things in a scenario can honestly be modelled two ways, and the mark is for choosing openly, not for choosing correctly. Buffer pressure can be a soft objective — f₄, charging container-hours of overflow — or a hard rule the decoder never breaks; his slide says in as many words to say which you chose. Overtime past 16:00 can be a soft cost in minutes or a hard prohibition; his note is that both are defensible and the brief does not settle it. f₁ and f₂ overlap, because priority-weighted waiting re-measures the waiting f₁ has already counted; overlap is allowed, but unacknowledged overlap reads to a marker as double-counting, so write “f₁ and f₂ overlap by design; f₂ carries information f₁ cannot — whose waiting it is”.

And every normalisation minimum and maximum is an estimate you invented rather than a figure you were given. One sentence each, four sentences total: an examiner cannot tell a deliberate modelling decision from an oversight unless you label it, and the labelling costs a clause.

Five named mistakes — run your Q2 draft against these before you turn the page

They are his own list, and four of the five are repaired by adding a single sentence.

  • Only one objectivethe brief lists six aims, and an answer with one objective cannot score Q2 well, so count your components before you stop.
  • Mixing maximise and minimiseadding crane utilisation (maximise) to waiting time (minimise) produces a meaningless sum; flip it with 1 − U and say that you did.
  • Adding minutes to ringgitnormalise first, always, and write the sentence that says why.
  • Confusing validity with fitnessa schedule is never “slightly invalid”; validity is settled before any score is computed, and a solution that fails it is not a poor solution but a non-solution.
  • Treating the aims listed in the brief as completethey are not, which is the entire makespan story: the scenario tells you what the port says it wants, not everything the port is paid for.

Lesson 9 · ~25 min

Multi-Objective Optimisation & Pareto

The alternative to weighted sums: refuse to choose. Two full lectures cover this (Multi-Objective Foundations, NSGA-II) — in the test it's your strongest Q2 aggregation argument and a legitimate Q3 pick.

Lesson 9 on one slide
  • When objectives genuinely conflict, refuse to weight them: A dominates B if A is no worse on every objective and better on at least one.
  • The Pareto front = the non-dominated set — the answer becomes a menu of trade-offs, not one number.
  • NSGA-II = non-dominated sorting into fronts + crowding distance (spread keeper) + elitism.
  • Argue it in Q2 when no weight vector is defensible — “rather than commit to weights the brief doesn't justify, I would return the front.”
  • Its cost, stated honestly: someone still has to choose from the front — you've moved the decision, not removed it.
Tomorrow this buys you: Q2's critical-awareness marks (the aggregation alternative) and a full Q3 answer if the paper allows NSGA-II.

Dominance — the core idea

With two goals (say minimise cost, minimise waiting), when is schedule A simply better than B? When A is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on at least one. Then A dominates B. If each wins on a different objective, neither dominates — they're both defensible, just different trade-offs.

Underneath that vocabulary sits one structural change, and everything else in this lesson follows from it. With a single fitness number any two solutions can always be ranked — 4.2 beats 5.1, end of argument — so a population can be lined up first to last. Keep two or more objectives separate and that complete ordering is gone: some pairs still compare (A dominates B) and some genuinely do not (A is cheaper, B is faster).

“Best” stops being a point and becomes a set. Every strange-looking feature of NSGA-II below is a repair for that single fact — ranking by front instead of by score, because you can no longer sort; crowding distance instead of a tie-break on fitness, because inside one front there is nothing left to sort by; and returning a whole population as the answer, because no single member is the answer.

Try it — click the Pareto front

Each dot is a schedule (lower-left is better on both axes). Click every dot you think is non-dominated, then check.

The set of all non-dominated solutions is the Pareto-optimal set; plotted, it forms the Pareto front — the menu of best-available trade-offs. Strictly, that is the true front, defined over every feasible solution that exists — and no algorithm ever sees them all, so what NSGA-II actually hands you is the rank-1 front of the population it happened to sample: in his slide's exact words, “the estimated Pareto front”.

Write “estimated” in the test and you have shown the marker you know the difference; it also hands you the reason a bigger population gives a better front, further down this page — more of the space sampled, so a closer and wider estimate. The decision-maker — the port manager who owns the quay, the university registrar who owns the exam timetable, the hospital board below — picks from the menu using judgement the algorithm doesn't have.

Why bother, when Lesson 8's weighted sum already gives one number? Because the weighted sum forces the value judgement before the search: the moment you write w₁·cost + w₂·waiting you have decided how many minutes of waiting one ringgit is worth — and the search will only ever show you schedules that flatter that exchange rate.

Pareto postpones the judgement until after the search, when you can see what the trade-offs actually cost. There is also a geometric catch worth one distinction-level sentence: a weighted sum finds the point where a tilted straight line first touches the front, so solutions sitting in a concave dent of the front can never win under any weights at all — Pareto is the only way those perfectly reasonable compromises even make the menu.

What a front actually means to the person holding it

Give the abstraction a decision-maker. St. Meridian Hospital runs four operating theatres across a five-day week, each day split into morning, afternoon and evening blocks — 60 blocks a week in all, and only 40 of them daytime. The waiting list holds 96 elective cases plus a handful of emergencies that must go early, so the daytime blocks cannot clear it in a week however they are arranged: whatever is not operated on rolls into next week's queue, and that queue is what the patients are waiting in.

Two things the board cares about pull in opposite directions: how long elective patients wait (shorter is better) and out-of-hours staffing cost (every evening block a theatre is opened carries an RM3,000 fee). Open more evening blocks and the queue clears sooner and the bill grows; refuse them and the bill is small and patients wait.

A weighted sum hands the board one schedule with the exchange rate buried inside w₁ and w₂. A Pareto front hands them a menu instead: this schedule averages 11 days' wait and opens no evening blocks; this one averages 7 days and opens four; this one averages 6.5 days and opens nine.

Reading down that list the board can see that the last five evening blocks bought half a day — and whether half a day is worth RM15,000 is a judgement about patients and money, not about algorithms. That is the whole case for Pareto: the front does not make the decision, it prices it.

The same picture explains why NSGA-II works so hard to keep the front spread out. If the surviving schedules all cluster in one corner — six of them waiting about seven days with three or four evening blocks each — the board has a menu with one real item and five near-duplicates.

The trade-off is technically present and practically useless, because nothing on offer represents a different policy. Spread is not decoration; it is what makes a front a decision tool rather than a scatter plot. Hold on to that when the crowding-distance arithmetic further down starts to look fussy: every line of it exists to stop the menu collapsing into one dish.

NSGA-II in one paragraph (his “in one sentence” slide, expanded)

NSGA-II = Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II — a GA whose selection is driven by Pareto rank instead of one score. Before the loop: build an initial population P of N random but valid chromosomes and evaluate every one — each fitness is a vector (f₁, f₂, …), never collapsed into a single number. Each generation: create offspring Q from parents P by crossover and mutation (mating parents are drawn by a tournament on the rule the algorithm lives by — better rank wins, and on equal rank the lonelier solution wins) and evaluate them; combine R = P ∪ Q (this is elitism — parents compete with children), sort R into fronts (rank 1 = non-dominated; remove them, rank 2 = non-dominated among the rest, …), fill the next population front by front.

When a front only half-fits, break the tie by crowding distance — prefer solutions in sparse regions of the front, so the menu stays spread out instead of clustering (the hospital board above: a clustered front gives them no real choice). Stop on the same conditions as any GA — a generation budget (his baseline is a population of 100 run for 100 generations, with diminishing returns past about 150–200), a time limit, or the hypervolume curve going flat — and return the whole rank-1 front, never one member of it.

One sentence about that loop is worth writing down, because it tells the marker you know what is new and what is borrowed: creating P, breeding Q and pooling them into R is an ordinary genetic algorithm; the sorting, the front-by-front fill and the crowding tie-break are NSGA-II's entire innovation — survival decided by Pareto rank plus a diversity tie-break rather than by one fitness number.

And answer the obvious objection before the marker thinks of it: why build R at all — why not just evaluate Q and keep its best? Because a parent in P may be better than anything Q contains, and pooling before sorting is precisely what stops it being thrown away.

The bookkeeping in numbers (a favourite short-answer): parents N → offspring N → combined pool R = P ∪ Q = 2N → the best N survive. Rank 1 is carried over intact whenever it fits; the crowding cut happens only within the one “critical” front that half-fits — crowding is never compared across ranks.

And because parents compete with children, the best front can never be lost between generations: progress is monotonic. The algorithm is Deb et al., 2002 (IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation) — one citation, instant credibility.

Why elitism deserves a sentence and not just the word

Run the counterfactual on the hospital front above — four theatres, five days, minimising average elective waiting days against out-of-hours evening-block cost. Say generation 12 produces schedule X: 6.5 days' average wait with only two evening blocks opened, the best thing the run has found. In an old-style multi-objective GA the next generation is the offspring Q and nothing else.

If X simply happens not to be picked as a parent, or is picked and then broken by crossover, X is gone — permanently, and the algorithm must rediscover it from scratch, spending generations re-climbing a hill it already stood on. That unreliability is exactly why multi-objective GAs were distrusted before NSGA-II.

NSGA-II removes the possibility by construction rather than by luck: because R = P ∪ Q, X is still sitting in the pool, non-dominated sorting puts it in Rank 1, and Rank 1 is admitted before anything else. That is what monotonic progress means. In an answer, write the failure you can describe — “NSGA-II is elitist” on its own is a word, not an explanation.

Non-dominated sorting, worked by hand

The dominance check is three questions asked of a pair (A, B), both objectives minimised: (1) is A at least as good as B on goal 1? (2) at least as good on goal 2? (3) strictly better on at least one? Three yeses → A dominates B; anything else → no dominance. Run it on six schedules:

ScheduleCostWaitingDominated by…Rank
A2090nobody1
B4060nobody1
C7030nobody1
D4565B (40 ≤ 45, 60 ≤ 65, strictly better on both)2
E7540C (70 ≤ 75, 30 ≤ 40)2
F8070B, D and E, among others3

The sorting itself is a strip-and-repeat loop: find every solution nobody dominates → label them Rank 1 → remove them from the pool → find the non-dominated among what's left → Rank 2 → repeat until the pool is empty. (Once A, B, C are stripped out, D and E are dominated by nothing still in the pool — that is why they're Rank 2, not “second best overall.”)

Two misconceptions the marker is primed for: (1) “A beats B on 2 of 3 goals, so A dominates” — no. Dominance needs at-least-as-good on all objectives plus strictly-better on at least one; two wins and one loss is “neither dominates.” (2) Rank direction: Rank 1 is the BEST front — lower rank number = better.

Crowding distance — the tie-break, actually computed

When the critical front half-fits, NSGA-II keeps its spread-out members. The computation (a lab exercise, and a classic short-answer): sort the front by each objective in turn. The two extremes on each objective get ∞ — they are the irreplaceable anchors of the front and are always kept. Every interior solution gets, per objective, (right neighbour − left neighbour) ÷ that objective's range across the front, and you sum those terms across all objectives.

Read “right” and “left” in that objective's own sorted order — you re-sort the front for every objective, so the neighbour above minus the neighbour below is always the larger minus the smaller and every term comes out positive. Write it as |f(i+1) − f(i−1)| ÷ (fmax − fmin) if you want to be safe: a negative crowding distance means you subtracted in the order of the previous objective's sort, which is the one mistake this calculation invites.

Higher = lonelier = kept; the lowest crowding distance is trimmed first (a CD of 0.03 goes before a CD of 0.85 — always within the same rank, never across ranks).

Solutionf₁f₂f₁ termf₂ termCrowding distance
P1109.0extreme on both objectives∞
P2207.5(35−10)/45 = 0.56(9.0−5.5)/8.5 = 0.410.97
P3355.5(50−20)/45 = 0.67(7.5−3.0)/8.5 = 0.531.20
P4503.0(55−35)/45 = 0.44(5.5−0.5)/8.5 = 0.591.03
P5550.5extreme on both objectives∞

The divisors are the front's objective ranges: f₁ spans 55 − 10 = 45, f₂ spans 9.0 − 0.5 = 8.5. If this front had to shed one member, P2 (0.97) goes first; P1 and P5 can never go.

The survival arithmetic, run once end to end

Take N = 8: eight parents, eight offspring, so R = P ∪ Q holds 16 solutions and exactly 8 seats must be filled. Suppose the sort returns Rank 1 with 5 members, Rank 2 with 5 and Rank 3 with 6. Rank 1 fits — 5 ≤ 8 — so all five are admitted whole and three slots remain. Rank 2 offers five candidates for three slots, so Rank 2 is the critical front: the one place in the whole algorithm where crowding distance is consulted.

Compute it across those five and nobody else — if they are the five in the table above, the two ∞ anchors take the first two slots (infinity beats every finite value), the third goes to the highest remaining, 1.20, and the 1.03 and 0.97 solutions are dropped. Rank 3 is never examined at all; the population is already full, so its six members simply die.

Two examinable rules fall straight out of that: crowding distance is computed within one front and never compared across ranks, and a wildly isolated Rank-3 solution still loses to the most crowded Rank-2 solution, because rank is checked first and distance only breaks ties.

Population size drives front quality. The module's lab ran one two-objective patient-scheduling problem three times over — population 10, then 50, then 200 — and plotted the three fronts side by side. The lab leaves the conclusion to you; the lecture states it outright — “Smaller populations find less diverse Pareto fronts”, with pop_size = 100 named as the baseline and the instruction to go bigger rather than smaller if you can afford it.

Expect the pop-10 run to give a handful of scattered points and the pop-200 run a far wider, denser spread. Smaller population → less diverse front is the one-line takeaway, and the warning behind it is worth a sentence in an answer: shrinking the population because a run is taking too long does not just cost you a little accuracy, it costs you coverage — whole regions of trade-off simply never get sampled, and the decision-maker never learns they existed.

Talking about front quality (distinction-level vocabulary)

  • Report the WHOLE front, never one point — in multi-objective optimisation (MOO) the front is the answer.
  • Hypervolume (HV): the area (with two objectives) or volume (with three) of objective space your front dominates, measured against a fixed reference point — one deliberately bad point, normally set at or just beyond the worst value seen on every objective, so that everything you found beats it and every solution contributes some area. Bigger is better, and watching hypervolume across generations is how you show the run is actually converging.
  • IGD+: the average distance from a reference front — the best front known for the problem: the true one where it is known, otherwise the best points pooled from all your runs — to the nearest point of yours. Smaller is better, and because it starts at the reference and looks for you it punishes both sitting far away (poor convergence) and leaving a stretch of the reference uncovered (poor spread): closeness and coverage in one number.
  • Ideal point: the (usually unattainable) corner where every objective sits at its individual best — the front bends toward it; worth one orientation sentence.
  • MOEA/D, breadth one-liner: it decomposes the multi-objective problem into many single-objective sub-problems solved in parallel — versus NSGA-II's compare-everyone-against-everyone sorting.
  • In DEAP (the module's lab library) the incantations exist ready-made — weights=(-1.0,-1.0,-1.0) to minimise all three objectives, tools.selNSGA2, eaMuPlusLambda, a tools.ParetoFront() hall of fame; one line to know they exist, details on the practice page.

When to argue which (Q2's aggregation marks)

Weighted sum

One number, one answer, quick. Use when: the organisation has a stated policy you can cite; one schedule is needed now; limited writing time. Danger (say it): the ranking is an artefact of your weights.

Pareto / NSGA-II

Keep objectives separate; return a front of non-dominated schedules; the manager picks. Use when objectives genuinely conflict and no defensible weights exist. Cost: more complex, needs a human decision at the end.

Exam move: if the clock is against you, propose the weighted sum as your main answer — it is faster to write, and his mark scheme accepts either route in the same breath (“you scale before combining, and state weights or use a Pareto approach”). Then add 3 sentences: “Alternatively, keeping objectives separate and using NSGA-II would return a Pareto front of trade-off schedules… I would prefer this when no defensible weighting exists.” That paragraph covers aggregation + critical awareness at once. But know which way his thumb points.

The walkthrough says “either answer scores full marks” and that mentioning that both exist, and why you picked one, “is what separates a good answer from an average one” — and of the Pareto route it adds that it “matches the module content directly” and is “the stronger answer if you have time to explain dominance”.

So if dominance is fresh in your head and Q1 left you the minutes, run it the other way round: lead with the front, explain dominance properly, and demote the weighted sum to the three sentences. Either order banks the marks. Writing only one of them is the only way to lose them.

NSGA-II as a Q3 answer, ready to adapt

Same three-heading shape as the PSO and ACO paragraphs (Lessons 10–11) — NSGA-II is the alternative that lets you drop the weights entirely. One caveat before you commit to it. Q3 asks how your answer would differ under “another CI optimisation algorithm”, and the three his walkthrough puts on the table are PSO, ACO and a grouping GA with local search; NSGA-II appears in his decks under Q2, not Q3, and it is still a genetic algorithm.

His note is on your side — “any sensible algorithm is acceptable” — but make the argument rather than assume it. Earn the 2 marks for “a sensible algorithm is named” in your very first sentence by stating what genuinely changes: “NSGA-II differs from my Q1 GA in its selection and in its output — survival is decided by Pareto rank and crowding distance over a combined 2N pool rather than by one aggregated fitness, and it returns a front of schedules rather than a single schedule, so no weights need defending.” Say that and the choice is safe.

If you would rather not argue the point at all under exam pressure, take PSO, ACO or simulated annealing from the next two lessons instead:

Encoding/decoding: the NSGA-II loop itself is fixed — you never redesign it. The three swap hooks are crossover, mutation and the initialiser: I keep my chromosome, decoder and fitness components unchanged, plug in a permutation-safe crossover (PMX or OX) with swap mutation, and seed the population with a priority-aware initialiser. Evaluation: the fitness components carry over — but they stay separate as a vector instead of being weighted into one number; selection is replaced by Pareto rank + crowding distance, so no weights need defending. Implementation: parameters are population ~100, number of generations, crossover probability ~0.9, mutation probability; the output is a Pareto front, so a decision-maker must pick the final schedule. Judgement: I would prefer NSGA-II when the objectives genuinely conflict and no stakeholder can defend a weighting — the front makes the trade-off explicit instead of burying it in the weights.

Designing the three hooks — this is the applied half of Q3. Naming PMX or OX and stopping is the general half; the applied marks come from operators that know something about your scenario. His own slide lists exactly three rows as “design opportunities” — crossover, mutation and the initialiser — and gives an example of each. Take the hospital again, with a chromosome whose permutation segment fixes the order surgeries are fed to the decoder, so earlier in the list means placed sooner:

  • Crossover. Rather than plain order crossover, copy the slice from parent 1 as usual but bias the reconstruction so that high-priority surgeries land in the first half of the child permutation. The child inherits real structure from its parents and inherits urgency.
  • Mutation. Rather than a uniform random swap, choose the swap so that it moves one emergency surgery to an earlier position. Every mutation then nudges the solution in the direction the objectives already reward, instead of nudging it at random.
  • Initialiser. Rather than random permutations, seed part of generation 0 with lists that schedule all emergency cases first, so the run starts from defensible schedules instead of climbing out of noise.

Close with one line that shows you have thought past the idea: each of the three must still return a valid permutation — every surgery exactly once, because a tailored operator that quietly breaks validity costs far more than the head start it buys.

Lesson 10 · ~25 min · Q3 material

Particle Swarm Optimisation

The cheapest Q3 answer to write: the smallest possible swap away from a GA. From the swarm lecture: “a third of your marks in your test, approximately, is dedicated to this” — explained in words, applied to a scenario; no code. (Nominally Q3 is 10 of 40 — his “third” is generous, which tells you he cares about it.)

Lesson 10 on one slide
  • The sentence he dictated: in a GA an individual is a solution; in PSO an individual is a particle — an agent whose position is a solution.
  • Search-space dimensions = your Q1 chromosome length — 17 port genes ⇒ a 17-dimensional space.
  • The whole algorithm is one line: v ← ωv + c₁r₁(pbest − x) + c₂r₂(gbest − x), then x ← x + v.
  • Parameters to name with numbers: ω (inertia, exploration) · c₁ (own memory) · c₂ (swarm's memory) · swarm size.
  • No crossover, no mutation — movement replaces breeding; your decoder and fitness function carry over unchanged (random keys handle orderings).
Tomorrow this buys you: Q3's general half in six sentences, and the applied half by answering one question — “what is a particle in this scenario?”

What “swarm intelligence” means — the sentence to open a swarm answer with

Define the swarm before you define the intelligence, because the module's own opening slide does and an answer that starts there reads like someone who was in the room. A swarm is an aggregation of similar animals, generally cruising in the same direction, and — the clause that matters for optimisation — swarms generally have a common goal or purpose: termites swarm to build colonies, birds swarm to find food, bees swarm to reproduce.

Ask why the behaviour exists at all and the same lecture gives three reasons: animals swarm to forage better, to migrate, and as a defence against predators, because a swarm can achieve things an individual cannot. Thirty seconds of that at the top of a Q3 answer buys the first thing the marker is checking — that you can define the phenomenon before you start quoting update equations for it.

Swarm intelligence (SI) has a textbook definition worth carrying into the hall verbatim, because it is the cleanest possible first line of any Q3 answer proposing PSO, ACO or bees: swarm intelligence is “any attempt to design algorithms or distributed problem-solving devices inspired by the collective behaviour of social insect colonies and other animal societies” — Bonabeau, Dorigo & Theraulaz, 1999 (Swarm Intelligence: From Natural to Artificial Systems, Oxford University Press).

Unpack it in your own words in the very next sentence and the framing marks are already banked: no individual in the swarm is clever, no individual is in charge, and the useful behaviour is a side-effect of many simple agents reacting to each other and to their shared environment. PSO itself is Kennedy & Eberhart, 1995 — one citation, the same cheap credibility trick as Deb et al. for NSGA-II.

The word for that side-effect is emergence: behaviour that belongs to the group and to no member of it, arising with no leader, no plan and no central coordinator. Carry one of the module's own cases into the hall, because a concrete example beats a definition every time. Termites build nest structures of a complexity far beyond the comprehension and ability of a single termite; tasks are dynamically allocated inside an ant colony without any central manager or task coordinator; and a fish sets its swimming direction and speed from a small number of neighbouring individuals, not from a view of the whole school.

Underline that last clause, because it is the design principle the algorithms copy: local information only, and the global result falls out. For PSO the same lecture puts it in one sentence — the collective behaviour that emerges from this simple behaviour is that of discovering optimal regions of a high-dimensional search space.

One more sentence turns the biology into a purpose statement, and it is the cleanest bridge from metaphor to algorithm available: the objective of computational swarm intelligence is to model the simple behaviour of individuals, and their local interactions with the environment and with neighbouring individuals, in order to obtain more complex behaviours that can be used to solve complex problems — mostly optimisation problems.

It says out loud that the modelling is deliberately simple at the individual level, which pre-empts the objection that no particle is doing anything clever; and it names optimisation as the target, which keeps the answer pointed at the ships or the surgeries in front of you rather than drifting into robotics and film crowds.

One structural line to add underneath it: PSO combines local and global search inside a single update rule. The pull toward a particle's own best-ever position (local — its private experience) and the pull toward the swarm's best-ever position (global — the shared find) are computed in the same equation, on every step, for every particle.

That is why PSO needs no separate local-search phase bolted on the side the way a GA sometimes does: the balance is built into the arithmetic, and you tune it with two constants rather than with extra machinery.

The metaphor

A bird flock finds food none of them has seen: each bird follows a blend of its own best experience and the flock's best find. Three rules are enough to produce that behaviour, and the swarm lecture names them one to a slide: collision avoidance (avoid colliding with neighbouring individuals), directional matching (match the direction of your neighbours — which may or may not include matching their speed) and flock centring (stay near your neighbours rather than drifting off alone).

Then make the link his own slide makes, because it is the cheapest outline mark on this page: PSO is built to follow all three — carrying momentum along the current heading is directional matching, the pull toward the swarm's best find is flock centring, and collision avoidance is the neighbour-awareness he opened the lecture with (his words at the foot of this page), each individual moving with regard to where the others are rather than blindly.

The mechanics (know these names)

The one-line analogy that unlocks your similarities column

The module frames PSO explicitly against the algorithm you already know: in analogy with evolutionary computation, a swarm is similar to a population, and a particle is similar to an individual. Say that sentence and the whole comparison against your GA becomes mechanical — swarm is population, particle is individual, the particle's position is the chromosome, the fitness function is the fitness function, and the termination criteria are word for word yours.

What has no GA counterpart is the pair of things a particle carries that a chromosome does not: a velocity, which the slides describe as a memory of the previous flight direction, and a pbest, memory of the best place it has ever been. A GA individual has no memory at all — it is scored, bred from and replaced.

  • Each particle is a position x in the search space — a vector of real numbers — plus a velocity v.
  • It remembers its personal best position pbest; the swarm shares the global best gbest.
  • Every step: v ← ω·v + c₁r₁(pbest − x) + c₂r₂(gbest − x), then x ← x + v.
  • ω = inertia (exploration), c₁ = cognitive pull (own memory), c₂ = social pull (swarm's find), r₁ r₂ = random numbers. That equation in words: “keep some momentum, drift toward what worked for me, drift toward what worked for anyone.” In the lecture he calls those three terms the three velocities — “the cognitive velocity, the inertia velocity… and the social velocity” — and says you plug in weights “to determine the influence”: a high cognitive weight pulls the particle back toward its own best, a high social weight toward where everyone else is, a high inertia weight straight on along its current heading. Use his vocabulary and he will recognise it on your script.

Two footnotes on that equation, each worth a mark if the question asks you to explain it. First, the symbols split into two kinds: r₁ and r₂ are fresh uniform random numbers drawn on [0,1] — redrawn for every particle, in every dimension, on every step, and, in the slide's own words, what “introduce a stochastic element to the algorithm”: they stop two particles that happen to share a position from tracing identical paths, and keep the swarm spread out instead of collapsing onto one trajectory — whereas c₁ and c₂ are positive acceleration constants, fixed by you before the run, which scale how hard each pull tugs.

Randomness and policy, side by side in one line. Second, the equation printed on the swarm slide is written without ω, as v ← v + c₁r₁(pbest − x) + c₂r₂(gbest − x). That is not a different algorithm — it is the same equation with ω = 1, momentum kept in full.

Do not read the omission as inertia being optional: in the lecture itself he teaches it as one of the three velocities, each with its own weight, so write the ω form and you are writing what he taught. The inertia weight ω is the standard modern refinement, added so the swarm can start exploratory (large ω, long strides across the space) and finish exploitative (small ω, careful steps near the best find). Quote either version, but say which one you are quoting and what ω buys.

If the paper asks for the formal form

The vector shorthand is fine for an outline, but the version on the module's own slide carries subscripts, and reproducing it costs one line and reads as fluency: vij(t+1) = vij(t) + c₁r₁j(t)[yij(t) − xij(t)] + c₂r₂j(t)[ŷj(t) − xij(t)], with the position update written xi(t+1) = xi(t) + vi(t+1).

Decode the indices once and you never think about them again. i is which particle; j is which dimension of the search space (j = 1, …, nx, and in a random-key design nx is simply the number of keys); t is the time step, which the slide is explicit is discrete. yij is that particle's own best-ever value in that dimension — pbest — and ŷj is the swarm's best-ever value in that dimension — gbest. The subscripts prove the update runs per particle, per dimension.

Put a number on every parameter you name

“I would tune ω, c₁ and c₂” is half an answer and takes the same ten seconds to write as the whole one, and the mark row is parameters named and defended. The acceleration constants c₁ (cognitive) and c₂ (social) are conventionally set equal and at about 2 — the module textbook's own wording is that they “can typically be taken as, say, α ≈ β ≈ 2”, α and β being its names for c₁ and c₂.

Equal values say you trust a particle's own experience exactly as much as the swarm's; that is the neutral default, and the one to quote unless something in the scenario argues otherwise. The inertia weight ω has no value in the lecture's version of the equation at all, because that version omits it — which is the same as fixing ω = 1 and keeping momentum in full.

If you add ω, do not quote a single number, quote a schedule: high at the start, low at the end, because decaying is the entire point of the parameter. For swarm size, quote the same order of magnitude as the population you defended in Q1 and say why — a swarm is a population under a different name, and a fitness evaluation costs the same whichever algorithm asked for it.

The loop, numbered (hold it against the GA loop)

  1. Initialise every particle's position x and velocity v at random.
  2. Evaluate — decode each position into a real solution and compute its fitness.
  3. Update the memories — if a particle's current position beats its own record, that becomes its pbest; if it beats every record in the swarm, it becomes the shared gbest.
  4. Update velocity using the equation above.
  5. Update position: x ← x + v.
  6. Repeat from step 2 until a termination condition fires — iteration limit, time limit, no improvement for k iterations, or a target fitness reached.

Set that beside the GA loop from Lesson 3 and the difference is stark: no selection, no crossover, no mutation, and nobody dies. The same particles exist from the first iteration to the last; all that changes is where they are. That single fact is why PSO is the cheapest Q3 swap available to you — there are no operators to design, so there is nothing in your Q1 encoding that an operator could break.
