Then the deeper contrast he draws in class, which reads as understanding rather than recall: in a GA an individual IS a solution, and progress comes from taking two of them and chopping them together; in a swarm the particle is an agent that goes and finds a solution, and progress comes from where it chooses to move next. That is why a particle keeps a pbest at all — a chromosome has no memory of where it has been.

One nuance on “no operators”, and it is worth a mark

The walkthrough deck's line is that PSO has no crossover and no mutation, and that is the right thing to write, because it is the practical claim: there is nothing for you to design and nothing that can break the encoding you justified in Q1. Do not stretch it to “no selection”, though, because the module textbook's analysis of the same algorithm reads it the other way — PSO consists mainly of mutation and selection, and there is no crossover.

The position update — take where you are and step somewhere near it — behaves like a mutation; and selection happens implicitly, through the decision to keep the current global best and each particle's own best, which is exactly what selection is. Write the sharper version: “PSO has no crossover and no explicit operators to design; selection survives, but implicitly, in the pbest and gbest updates.” It is also an entry your similarities column would otherwise miss — the GA and PSO both select, they just do it in different places.

The comparison line that works in any Q3, in either direction: most swarm algorithms have no crossover at all. A GA makes progress by recombining two parents, which searches hard inside the region its population already occupies; PSO, ACO and the bee algorithms have no such operator and move individuals instead by attraction and reinforcement.

The consequence is a genuine trade-off you can state with confidence. Dropping crossover buys high mobility and strong exploration but weak exploitation — these methods are poor at grinding out the last few per cent inside a region they have already found. The module textbook puts it most sharply for ACO and the bee algorithms: they explore well, but “their exploitation ability is comparatively low”, so “the number of function evaluations can be very high”.

PSO sits differently, and you must say so or you will contradict yourself in the next breath: the pull toward gbest speeds convergence up, which is why PSO's characteristic failure is premature convergence rather than slowness. What is safe to say across the whole family is that losing crossover costs you exploitation, and that where exploitation is weak the fitness function gets called far more often.

When your fitness is expensive (a decoder that lays out an entire timetable, or a machine-learning model that must be trained before it can be scored) that cost stops being academic, and naming it is exactly the kind of critical awareness the mark scheme rewards.

gbest is a double-edged sword — say so, and you have your PSO weakness sentence. Sharing one global best is what makes the method converge so quickly: every particle is pulled toward the best thing anyone has found, immediately, with no waiting for good genes to spread through a population. But the swarm found that point by sampling a small and biased slice of the search space, and the moment everyone is pulled toward it the sampling narrows further.

If the point happens to sit on a local optimum — a peak that beats everything near it but is not the best peak on the map — the entire swarm can lock onto it and stop looking anywhere else. That is premature convergence wearing PSO's clothes. The named remedy is to change who a particle listens to: the gbest topology (the star) lets every particle see the single best of the whole swarm, while the lbest topology (the ring) lets each particle see only the best within its own small neighbourhood, so several promising regions are worked in parallel and good news spreads gradually instead of instantly. Slower convergence, better coverage — the exploration/exploitation dial again, in a different costume.

Randomness that switches itself off

Here is a genuinely comparative line almost nobody writes. Every stochastic search needs its randomness turned down as it converges, or the wandering that saved it early stops it settling late. Simulated annealing (Lesson 11) does this with an explicit cooling schedule — a temperature curve you personally have to design and defend.

PSO gets it for nothing: the textbook's own observation is that randomness is automatically reduced as the particles swarm together, because the distance between each particle and the current global best gets smaller and smaller. The mechanism is visible in the update equation — r₁ and r₂ multiply the gaps (pbest − x) and (gbest − x), so as the swarm closes on a point those gaps shrink and the random contribution shrinks with them.

One fewer parameter than SA, and a clean sentence for a judgement paragraph. State the cost in the same breath: the mechanism cannot tell good convergence from premature convergence, so it damps the search just as obligingly around a local optimum as around the true one.

The improvement to name if you are pushed on how you would strengthen PSO

The textbook's verdict is that PSO may lack mixing and crossover, and therefore hybridisation may be useful to enhance its performance. “Mixing” is precisely the job crossover does that nothing in PSO does: taking two good solutions apart and recombining their pieces, so a child can inherit one parent's berth assignments and the other's service order.

A swarm never does that — it only ever moves whole solutions toward other whole solutions. So beyond inertia decay, velocity clamping and the ring neighbourhood, the fourth mitigation has a name: hybridise. Run PSO to locate a promising region and hand its gbest to a GA or a short local search, or splice a recombination step into the swarm loop.

Offer it as a proposal rather than as standard PSO, and pair it with the honest cost — a hybrid inherits both algorithms' parameters to tune, giving back the “no operators to design” advantage that made PSO the cheap answer in the first place.

Watch a swarm converge

Particles seek the greenest point of a hidden fitness landscape — fitness plotted over the search space like terrain, where peaks are good solutions and valleys are bad ones. Watch exploration collapse into exploitation around gbest.

The exam problem — PSO is continuous, your scenario is discrete

A particle's position is a vector of real numbers, and it moves by adding a velocity to it. Ships, surgeries and exam halls are not real numbers, and “ship 3 plus 0.4” means nothing. The bridge — and the device the walkthrough uses for its own PSO answer — is random keys: let the particle fly in real-valued space, and let a decoder translate whatever it lands on into a legal schedule.

Worked on the running port scenario (four ships SH1–SH4 arriving in one shift to be unloaded, three quay sections A–C — the berths a ship docks at, each with its own yard buffer behind it, so choosing the section chooses both the berth and the buffer that fills — three quay cranes doing the lifting, and a compatibility table saying which ships may berth where, because A is too short for SH2 and B is not hazmat-certified for SH3):

  • Assignment key: one real number in [0,1] per entity; split [0,1] into bands over that entity's legal resources only. If ship 3 may berth only in sections {A, C}: 0–0.5 → A, 0.5–1 → C. There is no band for B, so no particle anywhere in the space can produce the illegal assignment. Compatibility survives the move to PSO — say this explicitly, because it is the same alphabet-restriction argument you made in Q1, transplanted.
  • Order key: one more real number per entity; within a group, sort ascending — the smallest key is served first. The name for that decoding rule is Smallest Position Value (SPV); using it costs you a second and reads as expertise.

So a particle = 2 real numbers per entity, and your existing decoder and fitness function run unchanged on the decoded result. “That is the point worth making” — the walkthrough's own words.

What changes about the questions you have to answer

A GA answer carries obligations that follow from having a chromosome: what each gene means, which values are legal, why crossover will not shred the structure, what mutation does to a permutation. A swarm answer has none of them — a particle is a point in space, and points do not have genes.

But dropping those obligations creates one new one, and this is where the marks in Q3 actually sit: with no chromosome to restrict, you must say where feasibility now lives. In the random-keys design the answer is clean — it lives entirely in the decoder, because the bands are cut over legal options only, so an illegal assignment is not merely penalised but unrepresentable.

Answer that question out loud and the marker can see you understand what you swapped and what you kept; skip it and the same paragraph reads as a memorised second algorithm parked next to the first.

Q3 paragraph, ready to adapt

Algorithm: Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO), Kennedy & Eberhart 1995 — a population of particles, each one a position x in the search space carrying a velocity v. Every particle remembers its own best position (pbest) and the swarm shares the best position anyone has found (gbest); each iteration sets the new velocity to a blend of momentum, the pull toward pbest and the pull toward gbest, moves the particle by it, re-evaluates, and repeats until a termination condition fires.

No selection to write, no crossover, no mutation, and nobody dies. I choose it here because the section decision is a small set of legal choices per ship, and random keys turn exactly that kind of choice into the real numbers a particle flies through. Encoding/decoding: instead of a discrete chromosome, each particle is a vector of random keys — one banded assignment key per entity (bands restricted to legal resources, preserving compatibility) and one order key (sorted ascending within each group).

My two-phase decoder is reused unchanged. Evaluation: the fitness function carries over completely unchanged. Implementation: no crossover or mutation operators to design; parameters are inertia ω, cognitive c₁, social c₂, and swarm size; less code than the GA. Risks: many key vectors decode to the same schedule (redundancy) and premature convergence around a shared gbest — mitigated by inertia decay (shrink ω over the course of the run, so the swarm starts bold and ends careful) or velocity clamping (cap the maximum step size so no particle can hurl itself across the space in one move), and by using a ring (lbest) neighbourhood instead of one global best. Judgement: I would prefer PSO when implementation effort is the constraint and my decoder already guarantees feasibility.

How he opened the PSO lecture

“If you've got a bunch of birds flying across, have you ever seen two birds collide?… They don't. So generally, there are certain rules. One of those rules are that individuals do not collide. So if we want to mirror that, then we have to ensure that each individual has an awareness of its neighbors.”

Lesson 11 · ~30 min · Q3 material

Ant Colony Optimisation (and the Bees)

The Q3 answer that scores when constraints are dense: ACO all but never creates an invalid solution, because it only offers legal moves while building (and the rare ant that paints itself into a corner is simply discarded and restarted). This lesson also closes out the rest of the Q3 menu — bees, AIS, grouping GA with local search, and simulated annealing — and ends with how to choose between them in under a minute.

Lesson 11 on one slide
  • An ant is not a solution — it's an agent that builds one, move by move, over nodes taken from the scenario; the pheromone matrix τ is the colony's shared memory.
  • Choice rule: P(option) ∝ τ^α · η^β — pheromone (learned) × heuristic (greedy), then evaporation forgets and the best ants deposit.
  • The exam argument: only legal options are offered during construction — constraints are filtered out as the ant walks, not repaired after.
  • Numbers you can quote from the module's own runs: α 1.5 · β 3 · 40 ants · 200 iterations (or α 4 · β 5 · decay 0.5 · elitist top-10).
  • Rest of the menu in one line each: bees = scouts recruit to the best patches · AIS = clone the best detectors, mutate inversely to affinity · SA/tabu = one solution, accepts worse to escape, cheapest to implement.
  • His 12-Aug board: Part A differences, Part B application — nodes → options → filtering.
Tomorrow this buys you: the strongest Q3 answer for a constraint-dense scenario — and ACO is the one algorithm every past-paper menu contains.

The metaphor

Ants find shortest paths with no map: each ant lays pheromone on its route; shorter routes get re-walked sooner, accumulating pheromone faster; ants probabilistically prefer stronger trails; evaporation fades unused ones. Indirect coordination through the environment — stigmergy.

The lecturer's own bridge from Lesson 10. He presents ACO not as a new family but as a refinement of the same swarm idea, and the parts map one-to-one: a particle is an ant; the swarm is the colony; a particle's velocity — the thing that carries it toward good regions — becomes the ant's path; and gbest, the one shared memory of what has worked, becomes pheromone strength, a shared memory that lives in the environment rather than in a variable.

Our gloss now, not his — two things get better in the translation. Pheromone is spread across every individual decision instead of being concentrated in a single best point, so the colony's memory is far richer than “here is the best solution anyone found”. And pheromone fades, so the colony can change its mind — something a swarm all sprinting toward one gbest finds very hard indeed.

The mechanics

  • Set up first: the problem as a graph of decisions, plus a matching pheromone matrix τ, every entry seeded to the same small default — the slide says any decimal will do; the module's lab uses 0.5. Never zero: the choice rule below multiplies by τ, and zero can never grow.
  • No chromosome, no crossover. Each ant constructs a complete solution one decision at a time.

  • At each step the ant scores every currently legal option as score = τᵅ · ηᵝ — pheromone τ (learned desirability, what has worked before) to the power α, times heuristic η (a greedy hint available now, e.g. 1/distance or 1/cost) to the power β — then turns those scores into real probabilities exactly as the module's slide does, by dividing each option's score by the total of all the candidate scores, and picks one at random on those odds.

    (Where this site writes “P ∝ τᵅ·ηᵝ”, ∝ means “proportional to”; that division is what turns a proportionality into an actual probability. α and β are the dial between learned experience and greedy instinct. Mind those two letters, because they do three unrelated jobs across this module and nothing warns you: here they are ACO's exponents on pheromone and heuristic; in Lesson 6 α is BLX-α's blend width and β is SBX's spread factor; and in Lesson 10 the module textbook uses α and β as its own names for PSO's c₁ and c₂.

    Same letters, different algorithms — check which one you are in before you write “α controls exploration”.) A probability is still not a decision, so name the last step too: the ant picks by the same roulette wheel you met in Lesson 6 for parent selection, run over options instead of over individuals — draw one random number between 0 and the total score, then walk the options accumulating scores and take the one at which the running total first passes it.

    Bigger score, wider slice, likelier pick — but never a guaranteed pick, and that sliver of luck is the only reason two ants reading the same pheromone matrix ever return different solutions.

  • After all ants finish: deposit — better solutions add more pheromone to the decisions they used — and then evaporate, τ ← (1−ρ)τ, where ρ is the evaporation rate. Deposit-then-decay is the order his slides, the lab code and his own narration use (tidied from the recording: “once all individuals have completed the path, we'll update the pheromone… after that… we will apply the decay process”); plenty of textbooks do it the other way round, so use his.

    The concrete arithmetic, in the classic Ant System form due to Dorigo and used by most published work — the course reading gives the choice rule and no deposit rule at all — is Δτ = 1 / (length of the ant's route), added to every edge that ant walked: a shorter route is a bigger number, so good solutions reinforce themselves harder without anyone having to rank them. The module's own slide writes the deposit per-edge instead — second footnote below.

  • Elitist / rank-based variants let only the top ants deposit, which sharpens convergence at the cost of exploration. The module's ACO lab sets exactly this as an exercise — switch the deposit step from every-ant to best-ants-only and watch the trails settle faster — and then add a depreciation factor: a multiplier below 1 applied to the whole pheromone matrix each round, which is evaporation written as a decay rate rather than as a percentage removed.

    The module’s own notebook makes you write the evaporation line

    The starter notebook ships deliberately incomplete, and its own comments say so — “All ants update pheromone trails (no elitism)”, “Elitism???”, “Pheromone evaporation is not applied here.” — while the finished version settles on a decay multiplier of 0.5 and the top 10 of 50 ants depositing.

    Say in one clause why that matters: with no evaporation the trails only ever grow, so an early lucky route is reinforced permanently and the colony can never change its mind. Evaporation is the forgetting that makes the memory useful.

  • Then repeat — a fresh generation of ants over the updated matrix — for a fixed number of iterations or until nothing improves, and return the best solution any ant ever built. These five bullets in this order are the general-outline half of Q3: set up, construct, choose, update, repeat.

If the slides’ formula looks different — two footnotes

Footnote in case the lecture slides look different from the formula above: the slides write an ant's choice as pheromone·α·(1/d)·β, with α and β as plain multipliers, where the course reading (and the bullet above) writes τᵅ·ηᵝ with α and β as exponents. In class he corrected his own slide out loud — tidied from the recording: “there should be a plus here… add all that together, and it gives me a score” — that is, a weighted sum, score = ατ + β(1/d).

Reproduce the exponent form anyway: it is what the module's own ACO lab computes (score = (pheromone ** alpha) * ((1/distance) ** beta)) and what the reading prints. The one version to avoid is the slide exactly as printed, because with the two terms multiplied the weights cancel the moment the scores are normalised — (ατ/d) over the sum of all (ατ/d) is identical to (τ/d) over the sum of all (τ/d) — so they would change nothing at all. His sum and the lab's exponents both genuinely shift the balance; the printed product does not.

Second footnote, on the deposit step, where the slides and the classic form diverge again: the module's ACO slide deposits 1 / (distance between the two nodes) on each edge the ant walked, so every edge is rewarded for its own length; the Ant System form above deposits 1 / (total tour length) on every edge of the tour, so an edge is rewarded for the company it kept.

Both are standard ACO variants and no source in this module says one is preferred — the only thing that costs you a mark is leaving it ambiguous, so quote one and say in six words which you mean (“each edge scored by its own length” / “every edge scored by the whole tour”).

Watch ants find the short path

Ants choose between routes on a small graph. Line thickness = pheromone. Watch the short path win as evaporation starves the long one.

Applying ACO to a scheduling scenario (the Q3 skill)

Open with one sentence of pedigree and the 2 marks for “a sensible algorithm is named, linked to the structure of this problem” are banked, because it shows the choice was reasoned rather than reached for. The course reading gives ACO's standard published application list: routing optimisation in networks, vehicle routing, graph colouring, timetabling, scheduling, the quadratic assignment problem (assign n facilities to n locations so the total flow-weighted distance is smallest) and the travelling salesman problem.

Every scenario this module sets — exam timetabling, ship berthing, guard rostering — is a timetabling, scheduling or assignment problem, so it is already on ACO's home ground: “I propose ACO because assignment and timetabling problems of exactly this shape — allocate entities to resources in an order, under compatibility and exclusivity rules — are among its standard published applications.” Then stop; every mark after that sentence is in the applied half.

One ant builds one schedule: take the next unplaced entity (earliest release / highest priority first) → list only resources that are legal right now (compatible, free, within limits) → pick weighted by τ×η → repeat until complete. Then name η for this scenario out loud, because both walkthrough decks put it in the marked list and in the imperative: “you must also design the heuristic η — e.g. prefer the cheapest legal berth, or the emptiest yard”.

In a port problem η can be the lift rate of the fastest free crane, 1/handling cost for the cheapest legal berth, spare capacity for the emptiest yard section, or 1/waiting time for the earliest free slot. One sentence naming your η and why it is a sensible greedy hint scores better than another paragraph on pheromone.

Hard constraints are handled by construction: compatibility, occupancy, changeover can never be violated because illegal moves are never on the menu. No penalties, no repair.

Similarities: the decision variables, the fitness components and their weights, the hard-constraint list and the termination criteria are all exactly as in my GA answer, and both are population-based stochastic metaheuristics that learn only by sampling the fitness function. Encoding/decoding: there is no chromosome to design — construction replaces the decoder; pheromone lives on (decision → option) pairs, e.g. τ(ship, section). Evaluation: the fitness function is unchanged, but it now also drives pheromone deposit (better schedule ⇒ more pheromone on its choices). Implementation: parameters α, β, evaporation ρ, number of ants and number of iterations; needs a pheromone matrix and per-step legality checks — more bookkeeping than PSO, but constraint handling comes free. Judgement: I would prefer ACO when hard constraints are dense and interlocking, because feasibility is guaranteed by construction rather than penalties or repair.

Put numbers on those parameters, because “I would tune α and β” is half an answer

The mark row is implementation differences — parameters, and the same sentence carrying figures costs no extra time. His own two ACO notebooks, taken together, give you a defensible set: pheromone initialised uniformly at 0.5 on every edge (never zero); α between 1.5 and 4 and β between 3 and 5, with β above α in both of his runs, so the greedy hint outweighs the learned trail while the trail is still young; 40–50 ants; 200–1,000 iterations; evaporation coded as a decay multiplier of 0.5 applied to the whole matrix each round; deposit restricted to the top 5–10 ants.

His deposit is the per-edge Δτ = 1/d variant — the fork flagged in the second footnote above — so if you quote his numbers, quote his deposit rule with them. Then add the sentence that turns recall into judgement: these are starting points to be fixed by a handful of trial runs on a reduced instance, not constants derived from theory.

Bees, briefly (breadth insurance)

BCO / the Bees Algorithm (Bee Colony Optimisation) copies foraging. Mind the labels, because the module is loose with them: his bee deck is titled Bee Colony Optimisation, but its weekly outcome reads “describe the ABC optimisation algorithm” and its slides head the same algorithm “Proposed Bee Colony Algorithm (ABC)” — so treat BCO, the Bees Algorithm and ABC as one answer, not as cousins.

The course reading is stricter, splitting ABC (Artificial Bee Colony) into three named roles: employed bees (foragers working a known patch), onlooker bees (observers waiting in the hive) and scouts (searching at random). If a question says ABC, put those three names in your first sentence. Scout bees fly out at random; those that find a good patch return and recruit more foragers to it, while other scouts keep wandering off to look elsewhere. Exploitation and exploration are not two settings of one dial here — they are two job descriptions running simultaneously inside one hive.

Recruitment happens through the waggle dance, which carries exactly three pieces of information — a tidy factoid to quote: direction is the angle between the sun and the food patch, encoded in the angle of the dance; distance is how long the dance lasts; and quality is how often the bee repeats it.

Three channels, one dance. The third is the one that matters computationally: a better patch is advertised more insistently, which is the biological form of “better solutions get more search effort”.

If you ever do pick bees for Q3, the loop in steps: (1) send n scout bees to random positions; (2) evaluate every site they found; (3) keep the best m sites; (4) mark the top e of those as elite; (5) recruit more foragers to each elite site (nep bees) than to the other selected sites (nsp bees), each searching the neighbourhood of that site, a region whose size is set by ngh — and defining what “neighbourhood” means for your solutions is where the design work is; (6) keep only the fittest bee found in each patch; (7) send all remaining bees to fresh random positions; (8) repeat for imax iterations.

Parameters to name: n, m, e, nep, nsp, ngh, imax — and his own bee lab runs them at n 50, m 10–12, e 3–4, nep 10–12, nsp 5–6, ngh 2–3, imax 200–1,000, which is a defensible set to quote if a question asks you to set them. His deck describes ngh as the size of a patch around the site, which means nothing when a solution is a schedule rather than a point on a curve, so translate it once: in the module's own bee lab ngh is the number of swaps a recruited bee may make, between 1 and ngh of them, a swap being an exchange of two positions in the solution.

Patch size is therefore mutation intensity, which makes a bee's neighbourhood the same object as simulated annealing's further down this page. Strength: it locates good optima and escapes local ones, because random scouting never switches off. Weakness to admit in the same breath: that is a long list of parameters to set by trial and error — but finish the weakness, because half a weakness scores half.

The lecture names the mitigation alongside the flaw: those values “could be set by conducting a small number of trials”. So say what you would do — “its main cost is seven parameters, which I would fix by a handful of trial runs on a reduced instance rather than by theory” — rather than reciting a flaw and leaving it lying there.

The module's lab applied it to the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) — the classic benchmark in which a salesman must visit each city exactly once and return to where he started, minimising total distance. No resources to share and no compatibility rules; the only requirement is “visit everything once”, which is why it is the standard test-bench for route-shaped algorithms. One sentence on bees in Q3 shows breadth; don't spend more.

Artificial Immune Systems (AIS) — the name that scares people off past papers

AIS in three sentences — read once, then stop worrying

AIS is the immune-inspired member of the same evolutionary family: rather than copying breeding or foraging, it copies the way your immune system learns to recognise an invader. Its central mechanism is clonal selection — generate a diverse pool of candidate detectors (which are simply candidate solutions), measure how well each one matches the target, a score called its affinity, then clone them in proportion to that affinity — the better the match, the more copies it gets — and mutate those clones at a rate inversely proportional to affinity, so a poor match is scrambled hard (exploration) while a near-perfect match is only nudged (refinement).

Note the direction, because it is the whole trick and it is easy to get backwards: more clones and less mutation for the good ones. That affinity-driven hypermutation is the mechanism to name if you are ever asked how cells in an AIS construct a solution. The candidates that end up matching well are retained as memory cells, so that when a similar problem appears the system responds faster because it starts from what already worked instead of from scratch.

Why this box exists. AIS is never actually taught on this module. It is one bullet, with one sub-line, in the Week-1 overview of where CI ideas come from — “immune systems — recognising and adapting to new threats”, glossed “distinguish friend from foe; remember past invaders” — plus a short passage in the Week-1 reading, and no lecture, lab or tutorial goes near its mechanics.

It survives only in the wording of some past questions, which is precisely why three sentences are all you will ever need. Four past papers word Q3 restrictively — “…if you were to opt for another either ACO or AIS to address the above problem” — one older open-book paper says “either ACO or PSO”, and one asks you directly to “briefly outline either (a) how Ants in an ACO algorithm or (b) Cells in AIS, would go about constructing a solution”.

Read the wording on the day and obey it. The three most recent papers — 2025-06 and both 2026-01 versions, the format closest to Friday's — drop the named pair, and it is worth quoting them apart because they do not use the same words: 2025-06 asks for “another optimisation algorithm”, both 2026-01 papers for “another CI optimisation algorithm”.

Either wording is free choice, and the walkthrough that models Friday's paper agrees, “any sensible algorithm is acceptable”. But if the paper does name a pair, answer with one of that pair — writing PSO or simulated annealing into a question that said “either ACO or AIS” is off-question and risks the 2-mark “a sensible algorithm is named” row for no gain.

Either way you never have to write an AIS answer, because every pair a paper has ever named contains ACO, and this lesson has already given you ACO in full. Recognise the name, hold the three sentences above, choose ACO, and let the panic pass.

If a paper corners you anyway — how “cells in an AIS” would construct a solution. One paper (2023-07) asks precisely that, as option (b) against ACO's option (a), so this is your insurance policy and nothing more — option (a) remains the faster answer. Everything in this paragraph is our own extrapolation: it transplants the standard clonal-selection loop onto the running port scenario, because the module supplies no AIS mechanics of its own to quote.

A cell (or antibody) is one complete candidate schedule — the same object your Q1 chromosome encodes, so the encoding does not have to change. Its affinity is how well it matches the target, which here simply means your Q2 fitness read the other way up: lowest total cost and waiting = highest affinity, and you must say which direction you are using, because the whole algorithm is driven by it.

The loop, in five steps: generate a diverse pool of complete legal schedules; score every one with your unchanged fitness function to get its affinity; take the best few and clone each in proportion to affinity — the better the schedule, the more copies; hypermutate the clones inversely in proportion to affinity, so a weak schedule's clones get many edits (swap two ships between sections, move one ship to another legal section, shift a start slot) while the best schedule's clones get one or two; re-decode, re-score, keep the best of each clone family, and replace the worst cells outright with fresh random ones — the immune version of a restart, and the mechanism that keeps the pool from collapsing onto one answer.

The best-ever cells are kept as memory cells. Then hang it on the same three headings as everything else on this page: encoding/decoding unchanged, since a cell is your chromosome and your decoder still runs; evaluation unchanged except that fitness is now read as affinity and also sets clone count and mutation strength; implementation needs a pool size, a number of cells selected for cloning, a clone-count rule and a hypermutation rate schedule, replacing crossover and mutation probability. Write that and you have satisfied the question; you will still score more, faster, by writing ACO.

Grouping GA + local search (third Q3 option)

If your Q1 used the block chromosome: keep it identical (his deck's words: “Nothing changes at all. That is the argument for it.”), swap in block crossover (copy whole blocks parent→child, delete duplicates, reinsert missing entities at cheapest legal position) and add local search after crossover — swap two entities between groups, move one entity to a different legal group, or reorder two within a block, keeping the change only if fitness improves.

That acceptance rule is the whole definition: a GA carrying a local-search step is a memetic algorithm. Name both families in one line — “a grouping genetic algorithm with local search, i.e. a memetic algorithm” — because the deck says that single line signals you know where the problem sits in the literature.

Flag the cost in the same breath: fitness is now called far more often, since every trial move needs a score, so decoding speed suddenly matters. Most code of any option here, best fit for partition-shaped problems.

Simulated Annealing / Tabu Search (fourth Q3 option — the simplest defensible answer)

Every option so far has been a population method: many candidate solutions alive at once, competing or communicating. Simulated annealing (SA) throws the population away and keeps one solution, improving it by small edits. That sounds like a downgrade until you notice what it buys in an exam: no chromosome to design, no crossover to make permutation-safe, no mutation rate to defend, no operator that could break the encoding you spent Q1 justifying.

You carry the same encoding, decoder and fitness function across untouched, and change only how you move. The walkthrough deck endorses it outright — SA is its “Choice 3”, with a slide of its own — and the presenter's notes put it plainly: “SA is a perfectly good answer for a 10-mark outline. Its simplicity is a legitimate argument, not a weakness — as long as they say so.” Read the last clause twice: it is an instruction, not a reassurance.

Write the defence yourself, in one sentence — “I choose SA because it needs no new operators, so nothing in my Q1 encoding can be broken by the swap and my whole Q2 fitness function carries over untouched” — as a deliberate choice, never as an apology.

The neighbourhood, and when a worse move is accepted

“Moving” means defining a neighbourhood — the set of solutions that sit one small edit away from the one you hold. Three concrete moves cover almost any scheduling scenario, and naming them concretely is exactly what separates this from a textbook recital: swap two jobs in the service order; reassign one task to a different machine, berth or crane; shift one start time by a single slot. Each iteration you pick one at random, apply it, and re-evaluate the result with the fitness function you already wrote.

The clever part is what happens when a move makes things worse. Plain hill-climbing rejects every worsening move and therefore stops dead at the first local optimum — a solution better than everything one edit away, but not the best solution on the map. SA instead accepts a worsening move with probability exp(−Δ/T), where Δ is how much worse the neighbour is and T is a quantity called the temperature.

Read that formula as a mood rather than as mathematics: when T is large, exp(−Δ/T) sits close to 1 and almost anything is accepted, so the search wanders nearly at random and can walk straight out of a local optimum; as T falls, the same Δ becomes steadily less likely to be accepted, until near the end only genuine improvements get through.

The schedule by which T falls is the cooling schedule, and it is what the metallurgical name refers to — cool a metal slowly and its atoms settle into a low-energy arrangement; cool it too fast and they freeze into a bad one. The algorithm anneals from near-random early to near-greedy late: the exploration/exploitation dial of Lessons 6 and 10 as a single falling number.

Tabu search — the other escape mechanism

Tabu search is the same single-solution idea with a different escape mechanism. Rather than accepting worse moves by chance, it always takes the best neighbour on offer — even a worsening one — and prevents itself cycling by keeping a tabu list of recently made moves that are temporarily forbidden, so it cannot immediately undo what it just did and oscillate between two solutions forever.

The length of that list is the parameter to name. The refinement worth one extra sentence is the aspiration criterion: if a forbidden move would produce a solution better than anything seen so far, the ban is overridden — the list exists to stop cycling, not to refuse good news.

Similarities: the decision variables, the decoder, the fitness components and weights, the constraint-handling strategy and the termination criteria are carried over intact, and both SA and my GA are stochastic gradient-free searches that deliberately accept worse solutions to escape local optima — the GA through mutation and non-elitist selection, SA through the acceptance rule.

The structural difference to flag up front is that SA holds a single solution where the GA holds a population. Encoding/decoding: there is no chromosome to design, because there is nothing to breed — I keep the representation and decoder from Q1 exactly as they are and treat one instance as the current solution.

Evaluation: the fitness function is unchanged; the only new quantity is Δ, the fitness difference between the current solution and the neighbour under consideration, because acceptance is decided on Δ rather than on fitness directly.

Implementation: I define the neighbourhood as three moves — swap two jobs in the order, reassign a task to a different crane, shift a start time by one slot — and sample one each iteration; the parameters are the initial temperature T₀ and the cooling schedule (how fast T falls, how many moves per temperature), or for tabu search the tabu-list length plus the aspiration rule. Judgement: I would propose SA when implementation time is the binding constraint and my decoder already guarantees feasibility — by far the least code of any option here.

The weaknesses to state are that both follow a single trajectory and can still finish trapped in a local optimum if the cooling is too fast or the neighbourhood too narrow, and that neither returns diverse alternatives the way a GA or NSGA-II does: at the end you hold one answer, not a menu.

Similarities and differences — the half of Q3 nobody delivers

Two days before your test he put this structure on the whiteboard. His 12-Aug sketch writes Q3 as “Compare with another CI approach (ACO)” in exactly two parts: “Part A — differences GA vs ACO” (first row: GA evolves populations of solutions; ACO runs a population of 'agents') and “Part B — how ACO will be applied” — nodes taken from the scenario, options at each node, and “rules (ie filtering of options) as the ant moves from node to node”.

Part A is this section; Part B is the construction walk you built above. The board confirms both halves are still the marking shape this week.

His full-mark recipe for Q3 names two ingredients and then tells you nobody brings both: “you are talking about the differences… your genetic algorithm, and this other approach. Similarities and differences… and then you are giving a sort of an outline of how this approach will be applied… so to get full marks, those two things must be there. And so far, I've never got an answer that has those two things.” Everyone writes the differences, because differences feel like the new material.

He never says how the ten marks split between the two halves; he says an answer missing either one is not a full-mark answer. And the similarities take a third of the words and are strictly easier to write — you are not describing an algorithm at all, you are describing your own Q1 and Q2 answer and noting that it survives.

Write them first, under their own underlined heading word — Similarities — so the examiner cannot miss the row you are claiming. And note that this is not only an exam habit he wants: his ACO notebook ends with three exercises, and after “add a depreciation factor” and “only the top ants update the trail” the last one is headed “Task 3: Compare to GA and PSO”, with no answer supplied. The comparison below is the piece of work he set and left for you to do.

The shape below is reusable for every option on the menu — PSO, ACO, NSGA-II, bees, AIS, SA, tabu. Reproduce it as two short lists, or literally as a two-column table, which makes the mark rows impossible to miss. Fill the left column from your own script, not from memory: every entry is something you have already written earlier in the paper.

Carries over from my GA answer, unchangedWhat genuinely changes
The decision variables — the same choices still have to be made (which section, which crane, what order, what start time). Only the container they sit in changes.The representation, or the absence of one — a real-valued key vector (PSO), a partial solution being extended step by step (ACO), a single incumbent solution (SA / tabu), or the very same chromosome kept but ranked differently (NSGA-II).
The decoder — the phased procedure that turns a candidate into a real schedule runs untouched, and every hard rule it enforces by construction comes with it.How new candidates are produced — a velocity update then a re-decode, probabilistic construction over the currently legal options, or one small neighbourhood move, instead of selection + crossover + mutation.
The fitness function and every one of its components — same formulae, same units, same normalisation, same weights. Say this out loud rather than assuming it is too obvious to state: the walkthrough deck gives 2 of Q3's 10 marks to a row headed “Evaluation differences — you say what happens to the fitness function and to constraint handling.” Note the second half — the row wants both — and the deck answers it for you elsewhere: “the fitness function and the two-phase decoder carry over almost unchanged. That is the point worth making.”What memory the algorithm keeps — pbest and gbest vectors; a pheromone matrix on (decision → option) pairs that also evaporates; a tabu list and a temperature; a population plus its Pareto ranks and crowding distances.
The constraint-handling strategy — whichever mix of alphabet restriction, decoder enforcement, repair and penalty you argued for in Q2 still applies, for the same reasons. (ACO is the one that shifts it further toward construction; say so rather than pretending nothing moved.)Which parameters you must name and defend — ω, c₁, c₂ and swarm size; α, β, evaporation ρ and ant count; T₀ and a cooling schedule; tabu-list length. The GA's crossover and mutation rates simply stop existing.
The termination criteria — iteration limit, time budget, no improvement for k rounds, target fitness reached. Identical wording, identical justification.Whether the output is one solution or many — SA and tabu hand back a single schedule, PSO hands back gbest, NSGA-II hands back a whole front for a human to choose from.

Above every row of that left column sits the similarity students skip because it feels too obvious to be worth marks: both methods are stochastic, gradient-free metaheuristics — they need no derivative and no model of the objective, they treat your fitness function as a black box and only ever learn by sampling it, they search a space far too large to enumerate, they balance exploration against exploitation, and neither can prove that what it returns is optimal.

Both are also population-based, holding many candidate solutions at once — true of PSO, ACO, bees, AIS and NSGA-II, and the one place to swap the word is SA and tabu, where you write “single-solution” instead and score the same mark for spotting that the population is exactly what has gone.

The reusable opening sentence, so you never have to compose it in the hall: “[Algorithm] and my GA share the same decision variables, the same decoder, the same fitness components and weights, the same constraint-handling strategy and the same termination criteria — both are stochastic gradient-free metaheuristics that sample a search space too large to enumerate. What changes is the representation, how new candidates are generated, what memory the algorithm carries between iterations, and which parameters I have to set.” Four brackets to fill from the table, both halves of his recipe on the page, and you are into the applied outline in under a minute.

Choosing between the four when the clock is running

Q3 is 10 marks and roughly 20 minutes, so the choice itself should cost you seconds, not minutes. Read your own Q1 answer and let it decide. Did feasibility come from your decoder? Then PSO with random keys is the cheapest honest answer, because the decoder does the same work either way. Is the scenario a thicket of interlocking hard rules — compatibility, exclusivity, changeovers, certifications — that you ended up handling with penalties you weren't entirely happy about?

Then ACO, because construction never offers an illegal move. Is the problem shaped like a partition (items into groups, ships into sections) and did you use the block chromosome? Then grouping GA with local search, because nothing about your Q1 design has to change. Short of time, or is your encoding unusual enough that every operator would need re-explaining? Then simulated annealing: one solution, three moves, two parameters, done.

Whichever you pick, the marks are not in the algorithm. They are in the four or five sentences that tie it to this scenario — what an individual is here, what survives from your Q1 and Q2, which parameters replace which — and in the closing judgement sentence naming one thing your choice does better and one thing it does worse.

A slightly unfashionable choice, argued against the scenario's own features, outscores a flawless textbook description of the “right” algorithm every time. The No-Free-Lunch theorem from Lesson 1 is the formal version of that sentiment: averaged over all possible problems no algorithm beats any other, so the only defensible argument that exists is fit to the problem in front of you.

ACO in exactly the two sentences Q3 wants

“Foraging ants secrete a pheromone, a chemical trail. And so other ants have a choice or tend to follow that trail, but not every single ant will… if other individuals follow that trail, the pheromones get stronger and stronger. Whereas other paths, which are no longer as popular, the pheromone will dissipate and get weaker and weaker.”

Lesson 12 · ~30 min · the payoff

The Exam Method — D·E·D·D·F·O

Everything from Lessons 1–11 compressed into the exact procedure you'll run on Friday, mapped mark-by-mark onto the scheme.

Lesson 12 on one slide
  • The pipeline: D·E·D·D·F·O — Decisions → Encoding → Decoding → Data → Fitness → Other algorithm. Run it in order, label each block.
  • Q1's marks sit at 3 understanding · 4 representation · 4 decoding · 2 data · 2 justification — the chromosome drawing itself is only 4 of 15.
  • Three ceilings: a missed decision caps ~half · genes-with-no-decoder caps ~a third · one objective cannot pass Q2.
  • Draw the chromosome twice — one valid, one invalid with the broken rule named underneath.
  • First 15 minutes: read twice, list decisions, run the capacity sanity check (“very few students do this”).
  • There is no single right design — commit; the marks are in the justification, not the choice.
Tomorrow this buys you: the whole paper's shape — and the How to Write Answers page turns each of these lines into ready sentences.

The pipeline: Decisions → Encoding → Decoder → Data → Fitness → Others

Six stages, and they land on his mark scheme almost one row each. Q1 is the first four (problem understanding 3, chromosome representation 4, decoding process 4, data requirements 2, justification 2 — threaded through stages 1, 2 and 4). Q2 is stage 5. Q3 is stage 6. The fourth stage is the one students drop, and it is the cheapest two marks on the paper.

  1. D — Decisions. List every choice the scenario leaves open. Check for the sneaky ones: on/off activation, order, timing. Anything decidable must appear in the chromosome.

  2. E — Encoding. Pick ONE pattern (default: assignment vector + permutation). Draw it with the scenario's real numbers. State legal values per gene. Then name, in one line, the operators your choice forces: a permutation segment takes order crossover (OX) or PMX plus swap mutation, because one-point crossover there would duplicate some entities and lose others; an assignment segment takes uniform crossover and a mutation that resets a gene to another value from its own legal set, so children stay compatible by construction; a block chromosome takes a grouping-aware crossover plus a repair pass.

    And you never run one operator across both segments. The newest paper asks for exactly this in writing — “how the genetic operators will be applied” is a printed Q1 bullet — so it is a named deliverable, not a flourish. Two sentences vs a rejected alternative.

  3. D — Decoder. Numbered phases; why the order is forced.

  4. D — Data requirements. A grouped bullet list of the data you would need to run this — never prose. His deck calls it “the part most students forget” and scores it 2 marks, adding that they are “two easy marks lost every year”. Group it by the thing it describes (per entity, per resource, per site, per period, plus cost and policy rates), and say for each group where the data comes from and how often it changes.

    Include the data your own assumptions created: if you assumed a clearance rate or a changeover time, that rate is now a data requirement. On the port scenario that is: per ship — arrival time, container count, priority, physical restrictions; per crane — rate, power type, break and charging rules; per section — capacity, certifications, berth length; plus the cost and tariff rates and the drain rate you assumed.

  5. F — Fitness. Hard/soft table → constraint-tool table → components (formula + unit + purpose) → normalise → weights (cite the scenario) → Pareto alternative → critical awareness.
  6. O — Others. Q3: one alternative algorithm — PSO, ACO, grouping GA + local search, or simulated annealing — written in two halves. First a compact general outline of the algorithm itself (~5 marks), then similarities and differences against your GA and how it would be applied here, under the same three headings, closing on a judgement sentence.

The four deliverables hiding inside Q1’s single stem

One stage of those six is really four deliverables wearing one question number, and his walkthrough unpacks it for you. The Q1 stem reads “Explain the process of encoding, decoding and the representation of the solution as a chromosome for a genetic algorithm. Include all your data requirements.”, and his slide splits that single sentence into four numbered tasks: representation (what one chromosome looks like — length, gene contents, an example with real numbers), encoding (schedule → code), decoding (code → schedule, steps in order), and data requirements (every input the decoder and the fitness function need).

His note against the last of them is blunt — “The question says 'include all your data requirements'. Marks are waiting here.” — and his own speaker note tells the marker's side of it: “Easy marks. Tell students to bullet this section rather than write prose.” His verdict on the whole slide is worth carrying too: deliver all four parts and you are already in the pass band; detail and justification are what lift you past it.

So give each of the four its own visible heading, and lay the fourth out as Lesson 5 groups it — entity data · resource data · relationship data · policy data — rather than as a paragraph the examiner has to mine.

Encoding and decoding are two directions — write both

Say which way each arrow points. The question asks for “the process of encoding, decoding and the representation” — three things, and two of them are directions. Name them, one line each, before you describe either. Encoding is schedule → code: you take a real timetable you could draw on paper — SH1 in section A from 08:00, SH2 in B from 09:30 — and work backwards to the string of genes that would produce it. Decoding is code → schedule: you take an arbitrary legal string, run a fixed procedure, and land on a real timetable with clock times on it.

Most scripts describe only the second and call the whole thing encoding, which reads to a marker as a candidate who has not noticed there are two operations. Writing both directions costs fifteen seconds and does real work for you as well, because each direction is a test: can you encode a solution you invented by hand (if not, your encoding is incomplete and some real schedules are unreachable), and does any legal string decode to something real (if not, your decoder has a hole)?

Where the fifteen marks actually sit

Where Q1's 15 marks actually sit — and it is not where you think. Only about 4 of the 15 are for the chromosome itself. His walkthrough deck sets out all five scoring rows explicitly: problem understanding 3 (you identify the real decisions — who, order, when — and separate hard constraints from soft objectives), chromosome representation 4 (length, gene type, legal values, and a concrete worked example with real numbers, not just words), decoding process 4 (a clear ordered procedure that says exactly where each hard constraint is enforced), data requirements 2, and justification 2. That is 3 + 4 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 15.

Note what is on that list and is easy to forget — data requirements, which his deck calls “the part most students forget” and “two easy marks lost every year” — and note what is not a scoring row of its own: stating assumptions earns its marks through problem understanding and justification, not as a separate line.

A student who spends twenty minutes producing an ever more beautiful gene diagram is competing hard for four marks while eleven sit unclaimed on the page. Draw the chromosome once, clearly, with the scenario's real numbers written into the boxes — then move on to the parts carrying the weight.

The three grade ceilings

Three ceilings — and each one costs a whole grade. The walkthrough prices the common failures as caps rather than deductions, which means no amount of polish gets you past them. One. Leave a required decision out of the genes and Q1 “cannot score above about half marks, however well it is written”.

In the port version where you choose the berth, that decision is the section: encode only which crane and what time and you are capped near 7 or 8 of 15 before the marker has read a sentence of your prose. Two. Describe the genes and stop. An answer that says what each gene holds but never decodes, never lists the data and never justifies against an alternative is capped “at about a third” of Q1 — because representation alone is 4 marks of 15, and the decoding, data and justification rows sit unclaimed. Three.

“The scenario lists six aims. An answer with one objective cannot pass Q2 well.” One component fills part of one row and forfeits the aggregation and critical-awareness rows stacked behind it. Use those as a pre-flight check before you start writing: every decision sits in a gene, all four Q1 deliverables have a heading of their own, and at least five fitness components have names.

Q3’s real shape: half general, half applied

Q3's real shape: half general, half applied. He prices this question out loud — “you can pick up half those marks, the 10 marks, you can pick up half just by giving a bit of an outline of PSO. The rest of the marks, those five marks, are an outline of how we apply it.” So both halves are marked, and the first half is close to free.

Roughly five marks sit there for a clean, compact outline of the algorithm itself: what it is in one sentence, and then the sentence he dictated in class and told the room to write down — how its individual differs from a GA's. Tidied from the recording: “in a genetic algorithm, an individual is a solution. In PSO, an individual is a particle, an agent responsible [for] finding a solution… it's a position in my search space.” So: in a GA an individual is a solution; in PSO an individual is a particle whose job is to find one, and the solution is a position in the search space (in ACO, an ant is likewise not a solution but an agent that builds one, move by move).

Then the search space itself, because it is the second half of the same idea: its number of dimensions equals the length of your Q1 chromosome — his words, tidied, are “if the chromosome length is 10, same scenario, the dimensions will be 10” — so a 17-gene port chromosome means a 17-dimensional space and one particle is 17 real numbers.

That single sentence bolts the general half onto your own paper before the applied half has started. Then the metaphor in one line, the core update or construction rule that makes it work, and the parameters it forces you to set. Naming the originators (Kennedy & Eberhart, 1995 for PSO) is a cheap bonus, not a requirement.

Write that tightly — six or seven sentences, no code, no derivation — and bank it; do not skip it on the theory that the examiner already knows how PSO works, because he is marking whether you do. The other five are earned only by turning that machinery onto this paper: what an individual is in this scenario, how its position or its construction decodes into a schedule for these ships or these surgeries, which of your Q1 and Q2 artefacts survive the swap unchanged (Lesson 11's similarities table is the checklist), and which parameters replace which. The failure mode is writing only the general half and stopping — a flawless textbook recital of PSO with no ships anywhere in it caps you at about five out of ten.

So apply the old self-check to the second half only: if your applied paragraph would read identically on a completely different exam paper, it has not been applied yet. Note the verb, too. Every past paper words this question identically — “Provide an outline explanation of how addressing the above would differ (both in terms of encoding/decoding and implementation) if you were to opt for another CI optimisation algorithm…” — and outline means breadth, not depth, on both halves: a few sentences each on similarities and differences, encoding/decoding, evaluation, implementation and judgement. You are not being asked for a second full design, and building one costs you the time Q1 and Q2 were counting on.

How that squares with the deck's mark rows (2 / 3 / 2 / 2 / 1) on The Test, Decoded: it is the same ten marks cut a different way. Naming a sensible algorithm and linking it to the problem's structure (2), the implementation differences — parameters, operators, code effort (2) — and the closing comparative judgement (1) are the general half; the encoding/decoding row, how the key decision is represented here (3), and the evaluation row, usually “my fitness function carries over unchanged” (2), are the applied half.

Five and five. The exact internal split moves by a mark between deck versions and papers, so don't budget against it — the half-general, half-applied shape is the stable thing, and covering both halves makes every version of the split add up.

A first-fifteen-minutes move almost nobody makes: the capacity sanity check

Before designing anything, spend sixty seconds of the reading period asking whether the resources in the scenario are even capable of the work demanded — because the answer tells you what kind of problem you are actually holding. Worked on the running port scenario (four ships arriving across one shift to be unloaded, three yard sections to stack containers in, three quay cranes doing the lifting): the ships carry 630 containers between them, while the three cranes could shift roughly 1,037 — 155 an hour across an eight-hour shift is 1,240 at the stated rates, and that falls to about 1,037 once you take out the 30-minute break each crane owes after three hours' continuous running and the one-hour charge the two electric cranes owe per four hours worked (Lesson 3 has the crane-by-crane sum: 420 + 325 + 292.5).

The cranes are therefore comfortably fast enough — around 40% spare capacity — which means the difficulty in this paper is not throughput at all; it is the rules: berth compatibility, one ship per section at a time, 30-minute changeovers, crane break and charging requirements, buffer-zone limits. That single observation reframes the entire answer, and tells you your fitness function should be spending its effort on waiting, cost and clearance time rather than on squeezing out lifting speed.

It generalises to any scenario in about two lines of arithmetic: total work required versus total capacity available in the window. If capacity comfortably exceeds demand, say so and pivot the whole answer to constraint satisfaction. If capacity falls below demand, you have just discovered that no valid solution exists without relaxing something — which is a far more valuable thing to write down than another paragraph about crossover, and is exactly the kind of assumption the examiner wants stated. The walkthrough's own note against this move is “very few students do this”, which is precisely what makes the minute worth spending.

Then run the same check on storage, not just on speed

The check above compares work against throughput. Run it a second time against space, because in this scenario that is where the real trouble sits. The four ships carry 630 containers; the yard buffers behind sections A, B and C hold 200 + 250 + 150 = 600 between them.

If nothing ever left the yard, 630 containers could not be stored at all, and no schedule of any kind would be valid — the deck says so in as many words: “630 containers cannot sit in 600 units of buffer with nothing leaving.” The brief never says containers leave, so you must assume a clearance rate, and the walkthrough's is that trucks and trains remove 30 containers per hour from each zone, from 08:00. Write it down.

It is the single assumption the whole timetable rests on, and stating it converts every buffer from a running total into an occupancy level that rises and falls, which you then check at its peak, slot by slot. Get that distinction the right way round: “these two ships total 250 and the zone holds 200” is not a validity argument, because the zone drains while it fills.

The real cost of putting two ships in one section is that a section holds one ship at a time, so the second one waits.

When you cannot decide which design is right — commit. There is no single correct answer to Q1. The walkthrough opens by saying exactly that: marks come from a design that is complete, internally consistent and justified, not from matching a hidden model answer, and “the mark is for the reasoning, not the choice”.

The assignment-vector-plus-permutation and the block chromosome are both right, and so are the ship-level and job-level versions of either. A candidate who spends ten minutes weighing them has earned nothing in those ten minutes while the decoder, the data list and the justification sit unwritten. The procedure is: take the first pattern that can express every decision you listed in step D, write one sentence saying you chose it, and move.

Hedging is the only genuinely losing move — an answer that half-describes two encodings has one incomplete design instead of one complete one, can decode neither, and forfeits the justification marks as well, because comparing designs only scores when one of them is yours and finished. If you want the second design on the page, put it where it pays: in the Why this design and not another paragraph, as the rival you considered and rejected on a named trade-off.

Sentence templates (adapt, don't recite)

  • “I assume that [X], because the brief does not state it. Without this assumption, [Y] would be impossible.”
  • “[Decision] is not given, so it must be encoded. I represent it by [gene / block position / row].”
  • “[Entity] may only use [resources], so I restrict that gene's legal values to [set] — the violation cannot be expressed and the search space shrinks.”
  • “The chromosome has [N] genes: genes [a–b] represent [what]; genes [c–d] represent [what].”
  • “Because genes [a–b] are [an assignment segment / a permutation], I apply [operator] and [mutation] there and [operator] to [the other segment] — never one operator across both, because [reason].”
  • “The decoder first builds [phase 1], then [phase 2], because [2] cannot be determined until [1] is known.”
  • “A solution is valid if and only if it passes the following checks: …”
  • “These objectives conflict — improving [fᵢ] worsens [fⱼ] — so the weights express policy, not fact.”
  • “The component [fᵢ] measures [what it measures], in units of [unit].”
  • “Compared with [alternative design], my design is better at [X] but weaker at [Y].”
  • “This step is where the [name] constraint is enforced.”

The two-chromosome ritual. Whenever you draw your chromosome, draw it twice — once valid, once invalid, with the broken rule named underneath: “SH2 is assigned section A, but SH2 is too long for berth A. In my design this string cannot even be written, because A is not among that gene's legal values.” Get the reason right, because the two compatibility rules in this scenario have different causes and swapping them is exactly the misreading that loses marks: SH2 cannot use A because it is too long for that berth, while SH3 cannot use B because it carries hazardous cargo and B is not hazmat-certified.

It costs three lines and does two jobs at once: it proves your encoding is readable, and it proves you know your own validity rules, which is Q2's opening argument arriving early and for free. It also flushes out design flaws while there is still time to fix them — and if you find you cannot write an invalid chromosome at all, that is not a failure of the exercise, it is a sentence worth a mark: the rule is being enforced structurally by the encoding rather than by a penalty.

The nine mistakes that cost marks (his list, generalised)

  1. Missing a decision — “the commonest and most expensive error.” Activation decisions especially.
  2. Encoding per-task what happens once — a ship docks once; 13 genes doing 4 genes' work is wasted search. Say so.
  3. Ignoring compatibility — a design that lets ship 2 use berth A is invalid from birth.
  4. No exclusivity rule — two entities on one resource at one time must be a hard check.
  5. Inventing complexity — if the scenario doesn't mention holidays, leave them out.
  6. Unstated assumptions — they carry explicit marks; write them first.
  7. A fitness that can't see what you care about — the makespan trap; show the critical-awareness paragraph.
  8. Adding raw units — normalise before combining.
  9. Q1 overrun — 40 minutes maximum; it's 15 of 40 marks.

What full marks looks like (calibrate your ambition)

He is “allergic to giving students full marks” — the way to fight that is coverage of the scheme, not brilliance: every mark row in the scheme gets its own visible paragraph or table. An examiner can only award what they can find. Use headings matching the questions; underline component names; draw the chromosome.

It helps to picture the marking rather than the writing. Your script is one of a stack, read at speed, with a mark scheme beside it whose rows the examiner is trying to tick. Every heading you write is a signpost telling them which row they are currently on; every unlabelled paragraph is a row they must hunt for and may simply not find.

This is why “write more” is the wrong instinct and “write findable” is the right one: the same 600 words, cut into labelled blocks that echo the question's own wording — Assumptions, Decisions, Chromosome, Decoder, Validity checks, Fitness components, Weights, Critical awareness — will score higher than the identical content poured out as continuous prose, because nothing has to be searched for.

Underline the technical nouns you want credited (alphabet restriction, decoder, normalisation, Pareto front, construction heuristic); those are the words the scheme itself was written in, and a marker scanning for them should trip over yours.

Marking reality, in his own words

“So one of the first… area, I guess, where students lose marks is in this process, thinking about taking up the information, and can I get what's needed?” (verbatim from the recording; the ellipsis marks where the auto-transcript breaks his sentence in two. Keep “one of the first” — he is ranking a common failure, not naming the only one.) He is not talking about your prose.

He is asking whether your representation can hand back what the people who will use the schedule came for — his own example, from the same passage: “if it was an exam scheduling system, we want to know, as a student, which exam, on which day, in which…” (the recording garbles the last item; he means the room).

So run that test on your own chromosome before you defend it: name the two or three parties who will read the finished schedule, and show that decoding your design answers their questions — “decoding this chromosome yields, for each ship, its section, its crane and its start time”. It costs one sentence and it is the test he was applying live while marking.

The neighbouring point is about the scenario's own features, and he put a number on it while walking a scenario through in class — tidied from the recording: “when I mark these, I will tell you that 90% of students miss out constraints… it says here, master classes must not start before 10:30, so therefore your fitness, your evaluation must evaluate this, because it's a requirement.” Read that carefully, because it says where the constraint has to show up: not in a sentence acknowledging it, but inside the fitness function or the decoder, doing work.

Every feature the brief mentions — a buffer, a fee, a certification — must visibly appear somewhere in your answer, and the “please consider” bullets on the paper are a literal checklist the examiner wrote for you. Go through the brief line by line and put a tick against each rule once it has a home: a legal-value restriction, a decoder step, a hard-constraint check or a named fitness component.

Practice · the professor's own mock, condensed

The Port Walkthrough

In class he ran a mock — a port berth-and-crane scenario — then walked through the full model answer in 43 slides. This is that walkthrough, condensed and annotated. He said the real test is easier than this one.

The scenario

A container port has 3 quay sections (A, B, C), 3 cranes (C1–C3), and 4 ships arriving today. You must decide where each ship docks, which crane serves it, in what order, and when. Between them the ships carry 150 + 200 + 100 + 180 = 630 containers.

ShipETAContainersPrioritySpecial need
SH108:00150Highperishable — needs reefer power
SH209:30200Normallarge vessel — long berth
SH310:15100Emergencyhazardous — certified berth
SH411:00180Normalstandard

The three sections are not interchangeable, and the compatibility rule is derived from this table rather than announced. A buffer zone is the per-section storage area where unloaded containers wait for collection, and it has limited capacity; the three total 200 + 250 + 150 = 600 units.

SectionBerth lengthHazmat certifiedReefer powerBuffer capacity
AstandardYesYes200
BlongNoNo250
ClongYesNo150

Now read the rule off the table instead of memorising it. SH2 is a large vessel needing a long berth, so B or C and never A. SH3 is hazardous and needs a certified berth, so A or C and never B. SH4 carries no restriction. SH1 is the instructive one: it is legal in all three sections despite “needs reefer power”, because his own compatibility table gives the reason as “power is preferred, not required”.

Sort that correctly and you have the distinction the whole of Q2 turns on — a preference belongs in the fitness function, a requirement in the constraint list; mis-sort it and you either forbid legal plans or score illegal ones. The cranes are C1 at 50 containers/hour (electric), C2 at 60 (diesel), C3 at 45 (electric) — 155 an hour between them across the 08:00–16:00 shift, about 1,037 containers of capacity once breaks and charges are deducted, against the 630 that must move.

Raw capacity is therefore never the binding constraint; the rules are. Electric cranes need 1 h charging after 4 h work; all three need a 30-min break after 3 h. The berth-handling cost matrix in RM (ship × section) is printed in full in the fitness step below. Hard rules: compatibility (SH2 too long for A; SH3 needs certified ⇒ not B), one ship per section at a time, a changeover between ships at a berth — the rule is given, but the 30 minutes is a figure you supply, so declare it in your assumptions — no start before ETA, buffer zones must never exceed capacity, every container unloaded.

Sort those rules into two columns before you write a word — it is Q2's opening move and it costs ninety seconds. The paragraph above named the hard rules in passing; here is the complete split, both columns, laid out the way his own “sort the rules” step lays it out — nine hard rules against nine soft aims. Hard, because a plan that breaks one is not a schedule at all: ship–section compatibility (SH2 too long for A; SH3 hazardous, so not B); berth occupancy — at most one ship in a section at any moment; a 30-minute changeover between one ship leaving a berth and the next arriving; no job starting before its ship's ETA; at most one crane active in a section in any slot; a 30-minute break after three hours of continuous crane work; a one-hour charge once an electric crane reaches four hours worked; every zone inside its own capacity; all 630 containers unloaded.

Soft, because breaking one only makes the plan worse: keep total ship waiting low; serve emergency and high-priority cargo early; keep the cranes busy; keep energy cost low; finish before 16:00; stay well below buffer capacity; keep berth handling cost low; spread the load evenly across the three yards; clear the quay as early as possible.

Copy the shape onto any scenario — write the two headings, then walk the brief sentence by sentence and post each rule to one side. Nothing in a brief is decoration; every clause lands in one column or the other.

Three rules on each side exist only because you get to choose the section — say so, because that link is the mark. On the hard side they are compatibility, berth occupancy and changeover; his deck is blunt about what happens if you miss them — “If your answer omits them, your validity test is incomplete.” On the soft side they are berth handling cost, yard balance and quay clearance, none of which could be scored at all if the berths were fixed in advance: they would be constants, and, in his phrase, “a constant cannot be optimised”.

Write one sentence tracing all six back to the berthing decision and you have shown the marker that you understand why the objective set grows when the decision set grows, rather than having memorised a list.

Neither column says the part that earns the last mark: one quantity sits in both, and you should be the one to point at it. Buffer capacity is a hard check — no zone ever above its own cap, A 200, B 250, C 150 — and it is also a soft component, f₄ “buffer pressure”, scored as Σ over zones and slots of max(0, occupancy − that zone's capacity) in container-hours.

That is not double-counting. The hard check settles legality; f₄ measures how badly a plan overflows, so the search feels a slope rather than a cliff and can climb back out of an illegal region instead of being thrown off it. It is also why his own walkthrough deck handles this one constraint by penalty rather than by repair — a yard overflow cannot be edited out without wrecking the rest of the timetable, whereas compatibility goes in the encoding and berth occupancy, changeover and crane rests all go in the decoder. One clause pre-empting the apparent duplicate is a critical-awareness mark; leave it unexplained and it reads as a mistake.

Step through the model answer: each step below follows one stage of the professor's own 43-slide solution. Where we correct or extend his deck, the step says so in bold. Read a step fully before advancing.
From the same debrief — on fitness answers without weights

“You must have weights. Either you can have just equal hard constraints, soft constraints — all the hard are the same, all the soft are the same… Or you may interpret in terms of: this is very important, this is important, this is less important… the least important.”

Practice · the writing procedure

How to Write Each Answer

The three questions never change — only the scenario does. This page is the exact writing procedure for each one: what to write, in what order, with the sentence you open each block with. Every template is shown twice — once filled with the port scenario, once with the real March 2026 sitting — so you can see what stays constant and what the scenario swaps out.

Where the March 2026 answer comes from. Two days before your test he shared a complete submission from the March sitting of your own programme — scenario: an APU examination timetabling system (40 exams, 10 weekdays × 2 sessions = 20 time slots, 3 campus locations, 12 halls, 20 invigilators). It is a student's answer he chose to circulate, not his own model — treat its structure as endorsed, its details as good-but-not-gospel. Where this site's method goes further (worked arithmetic, normalisation), keep the site's version.

The clock, before anything else

2 hours, 40 marks: 3 minutes per mark. Fix this split before you enter the hall and spend the first 15 minutes on the scenario alone — reading it twice, listing every decision it leaves open, and running the capacity sanity check.

15 min read + assumptions → 40 min Q1 (15 marks) → 40 min Q2 (15 marks) → 20 min Q3 (10 marks) → 5 min check

In those first 15 minutes, write two lists on the question paper itself: every decision the scenario leaves open (these become genes) and every rule it states (these become constraints). Everything you write afterwards is built from those two lists.

Q1 — the chromosome 15

Eight labelled blocks, written in this order. Open every block with a bold label in the margin — the mark rows are problem understanding 3 · representation 4 · decoding 4 · data requirements 2 · justification 2, and a label puts each block in front of the right row without the marker hunting for it.

  1. Restate the decisions (3 marks live here)
