    Sentence template

    “For each ___ the scheduler must decide: ___ (which ___), ___ (when ___), and ___ (who / whether ___). These are the decision variables; everything else in the brief is either data or a rule about these decisions.”

    Port (site's spine)

    For each ship: which berth section (categorical), and in what order its unloading jobs are considered (sequence). The scenario's costs and rates are data, not decisions.

    Exam timetabling (Mar 2026)

    For each exam: which time slot (when), which hall — or two halls if split (where), and which invigilator(s) (who). Five decisions per exam.

  2. State your assumptions as a small table
    Sentence template

    “The brief does not fix ___, so I assume ___ — reasonable because ___.”

    The March answer gives this a whole slide — a three-column table (Component · Value · Why): 40 exams, 12 halls (4 per location), hall capacities 50–300, 20 invigilators (6 senior, 14 standard), ~30% high-priority. Three rows of that table cost ninety seconds and feed both problem understanding and data requirements. Never invent numbers silently — every number you use later must appear either in the brief or in this table.

  3. Draw the chromosome — layout first, then legal values
    Sentence template

    “One candidate solution is a string of ___ genes: ___ blocks of ___ genes, one block per ___. Gene ___ of block i holds ___, with legal values ___.”

    Port

    17 genes: segment A = 4 integer genes (one per ship, its section, alphabet restricted per ship so illegal berthings are unwritable), segment B = a permutation of the 13 unloading jobs.

    Exam timetabling

    200 genes: 40 blocks of 5 — SlotHall1Hall2Inv1Inv2 — Slot 1–20, Hall1 1–12, Hall2 0–12 (0 = no split), Inv1 1–20, Inv2 0–20 (0 = none).

    Then draw it twice: once with legal values, once with one gene deliberately illegal and the broken rule named under it (“SH2 in section A — invalid: SH2 is too long for berth A”). That pair is the cheapest proof on the whole paper that your encoding has boundaries.

  4. Worked example with the scenario's real numbers
    Sentence template

    “For example, the block [___] decodes as: ___.”

    The March answer writes [3, 3, 0, 2, 8] and reads it back: slot 3 → Day = ceil(3/2) = day 2, odd → morning; Hall 3 (capacity 200 fits 180 students); no split; invigilator 2 is senior — required because the exam is high-priority. One block, every gene interpreted, every value checked against a rule. Do exactly this with your scenario's numbers.

  5. Decoding as a numbered procedure (4 marks live here)
    Sentence template

    “To decode a chromosome into a real ___: Step 1 — ___ (this is where the ___ rule is enforced). Step 2 — ___ …”

    Port

    Phase 1: group ships by section, place sequentially — berth occupancy and 30-min changeover enforced here. Phase 1b: zone capacity. Phase 2: assign fastest legal free crane — eligibility, breaks, charging enforced here.

    Exam timetabling

    Extract each 5-gene block → map slot to day/session (ceil(Slot/2), odd = morning) → look up halls (capacity, split same-location) → look up invigilators (role vs priority) → build the day-by-day grid → validate against Q2's checks.

    The rule that earns the marks: every step names the constraint it enforces. A decoder that just “builds the timetable” scores half of one that says where each rule dies.

  6. Data requirements — bullets, not prose (2 easy marks)

    His own deck calls these “two easy marks lost every year”, and his note says to bullet them. Group them the way Lesson 5 does: entity data (per exam: duration, student count, priority, window), resource data (per hall: location, capacity; per invigilator: role, home site, mobility), relationship data (which students share exams — the overlap sets), policy data (rest rules, buffer minutes, travel time). Four labelled bullets and you have both marks.

  7. Justify against one named alternative (2 marks)
    Sentence template

    “I chose ___ encoding over ___ because ___. The alternative would ___, which in this scenario costs ___.”

    One honest comparison beats three vague virtues. Port: block integer + permutation over a flat time-grid, because the permutation makes double-booking unwritable. Timetabling: heterogeneous 5-gene blocks over one-gene-per-slot, because block boundaries let crossover cut at exam boundaries and never split one exam's genes.

  8. Optional lift — the search-space line

    If time remains, one sentence: “This space holds roughly ___ candidates (___), which is why enumeration is hopeless and a population search is justified.” It converts Lesson 1's argument into scenario-specific evidence.

Q2 — fitness and validity 15

Six blocks. The mark rows here reward components (multiple, named) · aggregation with weights · hard/soft separation · validity handling · critical awareness.

  1. Sort every stated rule into a two-column table first
    Sentence template

    “Hard constraints (a schedule violating one is not a worse schedule, it is not a schedule): ___. Soft objectives (violations are legal but cost quality): ___.”

    The March answer has 12 hard + 7 soft for timetabling; the port has 8 hard + 7 soft. The count doesn't matter — the visible sorting does. Do it before writing any formula, and check the brief again for aims it lists that you haven't placed (“the scenario lists six aims; an answer with one objective cannot score well”).

  2. Choose your aggregation form and say so

    Two standard shapes — both defensible, and naming your choice is itself worth a line:

    Penalty minimisation (Mar 2026)

    Fitness = 1000 × ΣHardViolations + Σ wᵢ · SoftViolationᵢ — minimise; perfect = 0. Use when your decoder can produce rule-breaking timetables: the 1000 makes any hard breach dominate every soft gain.

    Normalised weighted sum (site's port method)

    F = Σ wᵢ · fᵢ with every fᵢ scaled to [0,1] and pointed the same direction — use when the decoder already makes hard breaches unwritable, so fitness only ranks legal schedules.

    The bridging sentence to write

    “Because my decoder enforces ___ by construction, those constraints never reach the fitness function; the remaining rules are scored as weighted penalties.”

  3. Define each component as a counting function, then work one number
    Sentence template

    “f___ = ___ (counted on the decoded timetable). For the example above, f___ = ___.”

    One worked line is what separates “asserted” from “computed”. The March answer's congestion check is a model: count exams per programme per day; each one above 2 adds (excess × 50) to the penalty — a formula, a threshold and a weight in one sentence.

  4. Fix directions and units before adding

    Two sentences, both flagged in his five named Q2 mistakes: “Crane utilisation is a maximise quantity, so I add (1 − U) to keep every term a cost”, and “waiting minutes and ringgit are different units, so each component is normalised to [0,1] by its worst case before weighting”. Write both explicitly — silent unit-mixing is one of the graded failures.

  5. Weight table + the hierarchy sentence
    Sentence template

    “Weights: ___ . Rationale: feasibility outranks fairness to people, which outranks operational efficiency — so ___ carries the largest soft weight because the brief itself says ___.”

    The March answer's ladder: hard = 1000; workload balance 80 (staff complaints are in the brief); student congestion 50; priority-early 30; travel 25; period length 20; afternoon streaks 15; idle time 10 — every weight tied to something the scenario says, not taste. His recorded fallback if you can't rank: all-hard-equal, all-soft-equal, or a three-tier “very important / important / less important”.

  6. Validity, and what happens to invalid offspring
    Sentence template

    “A chromosome violating a hard constraint is invalid — not a poor solution but a non-solution. My design handles this by ___ (repair / penalty / rejection / unwritable-by-encoding), whose cost is ___.”

    The March answer's combination is worth copying whole: repair first for cheap deterministic fixes (swap standard→senior on high-priority exams, reset out-of-window slots, force split halls to one location), penalty for the rest (student clashes cascade when moved, so let 1000-weight selection evolve them away). Then name one cost of your choice — repair biases the search, penalties need the weight guessed right, rejection wastes evaluations.

Q3 — the alternative algorithm 10

This is the question he sketched on the whiteboard two days before your test (12 Aug). His own structure, verbatim from the board: “Part A — differences GA vs ACO” and “Part B — how ACO will be applied.” Five marks each, which matches what he said in the recorded debrief: half for the outline, half for applying it.

  1. Part A — differences, as a compact table or five contrast sentences (~5 marks)

    His board's first row: “GA: populations of solutions; ACO: population of 'agents'.” The March answer's table gives you the remaining rows — learn these seven contrasts and Part A writes itself for any pairing:

    AspectGAACO
    RepresentationFixed-length chromosome (here: 200 genes)No chromosome — solutions built step by step
    Solution creationRandom init + crossover + mutationAnts construct along a graph, guided by pheromone
    Constraint handlingRepair + penalties after buildingInvalid options filtered during construction
    Diversity controlCrossover & mutation ratesPheromone evaporation rate
    Memory of past searchThe population itselfThe pheromone matrix
    ElitismBest chromosomes copied overBest ants deposit extra pheromone
    Escaping local optimaMutation; risk without diversityEvaporation forgets stale trails
  2. Part B — application to this scenario (~5 marks)

    His board draws it as a row of boxes and a column of circles, and the recipe is three sentences long:

    1. Nodes come from the scenario — his board's words: “taken from the scenario (ie wards, slots, etc)”. Name the decision sequence: for timetabling, each exam is a stage and the ant chooses slot → hall → invigilator; for the port, each unloading job is a stage and the ant chooses its berth/crane.
    2. Options at each node — the legal values your Q1 genes had: 20 slots, 12 halls, 20 invigilators.
    3. Filtering — his board again: “we can apply rules (ie filtering of options) as the ant moves from node to node”. An ant never offers an option that breaks a hard constraint — a full hall, a clashing slot, an uncertified invigilator — so constraints are enforced during construction rather than repaired after. This one sentence is the entire ACO-vs-GA argument.
    Then close with parameters + carry-over + judgement

    “Choice probability P(option) ∝ pheromone^α × heuristic^β; after each iteration trails evaporate (e.g. ×0.7) and the best ants deposit. I would set ___ ants, α ___, β ___. My Q2 fitness function carries over unchanged to score each ant's finished ___. Compared with the GA, ACO produces fewer invalid solutions but needs a large pheromone structure and more parameters to tune.”

  3. The self-check

    If your Part B would read identically on a different exam paper, it has not been applied yet. It must name this scenario's stages, options and filters. And never skip Part A “because the examiner knows how ACO works” — he is marking whether you do, and it is the free half.

The whiteboard hint, honestly labelled

His 12-Aug node examples were “wards, slots” — wards is not a port word and not a timetabling word. Do not treat it as a leak; treat it as a reminder that the scenario family is allocate-things-to-slots-under-rules, and drill the templates above until the specific nouns don't matter.

Tonight's drill

Once through this page, then one rehearsal: invent a scenario you have never seen — hospital ward scheduling is the obvious candidate — and handwrite the Q1 skeleton for it in 25 minutes: decisions, three assumption rows, chromosome drawn twice, one decoded example, numbered decoder, four data bullets, one justification. If you can do it for a scenario you invented, tomorrow's scenario is just new nouns.

When you finish — or if you stall — mark yourself against the Solved Answer Papers page: three complete scripts written exactly the way these recipes say to write them, including one for a hospital ward roster.

Practice · the whole paper, solved

Solved Answer Papers

Three complete exam scripts — full Q1, Q2 and Q3, written from start to end the way you will actually write today: by hand, under the clock, following the How-to-Write recipes block by block. One scenario you have never seen, the real March 2026 paper, and the port. Same skeleton three times; only the nouns change.

The blue handwriting is the student's script — realistic full-marks volume for a two-hour paper, not an essay. The green ✎ notes are the examiner lens: why that block earns its marks. They are annotations, not part of the answer — never write them in the hall.

Script 1 — Hospital ward roster (the unseen scenario)

This is the drill scenario from the How-to-Write page, invented from nothing — proof that the recipes survive contact with nouns nobody has taught you. If tomorrow's paper is in the allocate-things-to-slots-under-rules family his whiteboard hinted at, this is the closest rehearsal on the site.

St. Anne's General Hospital — 7-day admission plan + nurse roster. Three wards: W1 General (8 beds), W2 Isolation wing (2 beds), W3 High-Dependency Unit (4 beds) — W3 keeps its own dedicated staff, rostered outside this problem. Six patients await admission; each has a type (emergency / urgent / elective), a special need (none / isolation / HDU), a length of stay (LOS) in 8-hour shifts, and days already waited:

PatientTypeSpecial needLOS (shifts)Already waited (days)
P1Elective—69
P2Urgent—83
P3ElectiveIsolation512
P4EmergencyHDU120
P5Urgent—92
P6Elective—48

Time runs in 8-hour shifts — Morning 07–15, Afternoon 15–23, Night 23–07 — over 7 days (21 shifts); admissions happen in morning shifts only. Isolation patients must go to W2; HDU patients must go to W3; every other patient may use W1 or W2. Emergencies must be admitted on day 1; urgent patients by day 2.

Nine nurses cover W1 and W2: N1–N3 senior, N4–N9 registered. Each ward-shift needs exactly one nurse; every ward-day needs at least one senior; a nurse works at most one shift a day, five shifts a week, and two consecutive nights. If no nurse is legal for a ward-shift, an agency nurse is hired at RM 400 per shift.

The hospital wants: waiting kept low · emergencies and urgent cases first · a fair spread of shifts — and of nights — across nurses · minimal agency spend.

Q1 — the chromosome 15

The decisions

For each patient the scheduler must decide which ward they enter (categorical, restricted by compatibility) and on which day they are admitted — admissions happen in morning shifts only. For the nurses, the scheduler must decide who covers each ward-shift on W1 and W2, but I make that a decoder decision fed by a priority permutation rather than a per-shift gene. Everything else in the brief — LOS, beds, days already waited — is data, not a decision. In the literature this is a patient-to-bed assignment plus nurse-rostering problem; the ward decision is the one that creates the W2 contention, the compatibility checks and the new data groups, exactly as a berth decision does in a port.

problem understanding — all decision variables named, and where each lives (3)

Assumptions

ComponentValueWhy
Time granularity8-hour shifts; admissions morning-onlya night admission needs a care team the brief does not roster
LOS mechanicswhole shifts; bed frees the shift after dischargethe brief gives LOS but not the discharge moment
W3 staffingown dedicated staff — rota covers W1, W2 onlystated in the brief
Agency rateRM 400 per shiftthe brief says “minimal agency spend” but names no figure — the number is mine, so I state it
Priority weights5 / 3 / 1 for emergency / urgent / elective; already-waited days tie-break electivesthe brief ranks types but gives no numbers

The chromosome

One candidate solution is a string of 21 genes in two segments. Segment A holds twelve integer genes — one WardDay block per patient. Segment B is a permutation of the nine nurses (N1–N9): the priority order the decoder consults when filling shifts. Ward genes: P1∈{1,2}, P2∈{1,2}, P3∈{2}, P4∈{3}, P5∈{1,2}, P6∈{1,2} — the alphabet is restricted per patient, so an incompatible admission is unwritable. Day genes: P4∈{1} (emergency — day 1), P2, P5∈{1,2} (urgent — by day 2), P1, P3, P6∈{1…7}.

Legal, and what it means: P123P222P321P431P512P614‖ N1 N4 N7 N2 N5 N8 N3 N6 N9 — P1 to W2 on day 3, P2 to W2 day 2, P3 to W2 day 1, P4 to W3 day 1, P5 to W1 day 2, P6 to W1 day 4; nurses considered in that order when shifts are filled.

The same drawing with one illegal gene: P411 — invalid: P4 needs an HDU bed and HDU patients go to W3 only; ward 1 is outside P4's alphabet. The second drawing is the cheapest proof on the paper that the encoding has boundaries.

representation — length, gene types, legal values per gene, worked example, compatibility handled by the alphabet (4)

Decoding — a numbered procedure

Phase 1, admissions. Step 1: read each patient block — ward and day genes already lie inside their legal alphabets, so compatibility and the admission windows are enforced here, before the decoder runs. Step 2: compute each patient's occupied shifts — from the morning of day d for LOS − 1 further shifts. Step 3: walk patients in day order; before committing one, test the ward's occupancy shift by shift — a level that falls when a patient is discharged, not a running total. Step 4: if any shift of the stay would exceed the ward's beds, repair: delay the admission to the next morning on which the whole stay fits. Step 5: mark the patient admitted; all six must be placed (completeness).

Phase 2, nurses. Step 6: walk the W1/W2 ward-shifts chronologically. Step 7: for each ward-shift take the first nurse in segment B who is legal: not already on duty that shift, under five shifts this week, not a third consecutive night. Step 8: prefer a senior while the ward-day still lacks one; if no nurse is legal, record an agency shift — priced in Q2's f₅.

Each step names the constraint it enforces: compatibility and windows in the alphabet (step 1), capacity in steps 3–4, completeness in 5, the nurse caps in 7, senior coverage and full coverage in 8.

decoding — ordered phases, and every step pinned to the constraint it enforces (4)

Genetic operators

Segment A: one-point crossover cutting between patient blocks — never inside a [Ward|Day] pair — and mutation that resets a gene to a random value inside its own alphabet. Segment B: order crossover (OX) and swap mutation, which keep a permutation a permutation. Both operators therefore preserve the alphabets, so they can never manufacture the illegal genes the encoding forbids.

Data required

  • Entity data — per patient: type, special need, LOS, days already waited.
  • Resource data — per ward: bed count and type; per nurse: grade (senior / registered).
  • Relationship data — the patient × ward compatibility table, which exists only because the ward is a decision.
  • Policy data — the shift grid, admission windows, nurse caps, the RM 400 agency rate, the 5 / 3 / 1 priority weights.

Every number my Q2 fitness uses is findable in this list or in the assumptions table — that is the mechanical test.

data requirements, grouped into four labelled bullets (2)

Justification

I chose heterogeneous [Ward|Day] blocks plus a nurse permutation over the two named alternatives. A flat bed-grid — one gene per ward per shift, 21 genes per patient — would be six times longer and would scatter one patient's decision across unrelated genes, so crossover could splice half an admission. One gene per nurse-shift (42 genes) would encode what the greedy decoder derives from a nine-gene permutation; the permutation is shorter and keeps every nurse rule in one place. The block boundaries are what make crossover safe, and the restricted alphabets are what make compatibility and the admission windows unwritable violations.

This space holds 2·7 × 2·2 × 1·7 × 1·1 × 2·2 × 2·7 = 21,952 legal admission plans times 9! = 362,880 nurse orders — roughly 8 billion rosters, with no gradient to follow because the objective is a decoded roster rather than a formula. That is why a population search, not enumeration.

justification against two named alternatives + the search-space line (2)

Q2 — fitness and validity 15

Sort the rules first — two columns

Hard — a plan that breaks one is not a roster: ① patient–ward compatibility (P3 only W2, P4 only W3, the rest W1 or W2) · ② admission windows (emergency day 1, urgent by day 2) · ③ ward capacity — for every ward and every shift, occupancy ≤ beds, counted as a level that falls at discharge · ④ every patient admitted exactly once · ⑤ a nurse on at most one ward-shift per shift · ⑥ at most five shifts a week · ⑦ at most two consecutive nights · ⑧ every ward-day on W1/W2 has at least one senior · ⑨ every ward-shift covered — by a rostered nurse, or by an agency nurse, because the policy allows agency cover at RM 400.

Soft — breakable, but each breach costs quality: keep waiting low · emergencies and urgent cases first · spread the shifts fairly across nurses · spread the nights fairly · keep agency spend low. Nothing in the brief is decoration; every clause lands in one column or the other.

One quantity sits in both columns, and I should be the one to point at it: check ⑨ is also f₅. That is not double counting — the hard check settles whether the roster is complete at all; f₅ measures how much cover we had to buy, so the search feels a slope instead of a cliff.

every hard constraint enumerated as a checkable test; the hard/soft split done visibly (3)

Validity — which tool for which rule

ChecksToolWhy
① ②Encoding alphabetthe illegal gene is unwritable, so it can never be born
③Decoder + repairthe decoder delays an overflowing admission to the next morning the whole stay fits — a bed overflow cannot be edited out without wrecking the rest of the roster
④Decodercompleteness — all six blocks walked
⑤ ⑥ ⑦Decoder countersthe greedy fill never assigns a nurse who is on duty, capped or on a third night
⑧Decoder preferenceseniors taken first while a ward-day still lacks one
⑨Decoder + penaltyif no nurse is legal the shift is covered by agency and f₅ prices it

Because my alphabet and decoder enforce ①–⑦ by construction, those constraints never reach the fitness function; the remaining rules are scored as weighted penalties. I name one cost of my choices: repair biases the search toward later admission days — accepted, because an overflow cannot be scored at all, and penalties need their weights guessed right, which is its own risk.

constraint handling reasoned — each rule routed to a tool, and a cost named (3)

The fitness — five components, formula + unit + purpose + one worked number

f₁ total waiting = Σ (admission day − 1), in day-waits — the core service metric. For the worked chromosome: 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 7; worst case 3 electives × 6 + 2 urgents × 1 + 0 = 20, so f₁′ = 7/20 = 0.35.

f₂ priority earliness = Σ weighttype × day with weights 5/3/1, in weight-days — urgent care first. Worked: 5·1 + 1·1 + 3·2 + 3·2 + 1·3 + 1·4 = 25; worst 5·1 + 3·2·2 + 1·7·3 = 38, so f₂′ = 25/38 ≈ 0.66.

f₃ shift balance = standard deviation of weekly shifts per nurse, in shifts — fairness, which the brief names. The finished week spreads 42 shifts as [5,5,5,5,5,5,4,4,4]: mean ≈ 4.7, σ ≈ 0.47; worst [5×8, 2] gives σ ≈ 0.94, so f₃′ ≈ 0.50.

f₄ night balance = standard deviation of night shifts per nurse, in nights — the same idea for the worst shift. Worked: 14 nights as [2,2,2,2,2,1,1,1,1] gives σ ≈ 0.50; worst [2×7, 0, 0] gives σ ≈ 0.83, so f₄′ ≈ 0.60.

f₅ agency spend = Σ agency shifts × RM 400, in ringgit — the hospital's last named aim. Worked: 0; normaliser 42 × 400 = RM 16,800, so f₅′ = 0.

each component: formula, unit, purpose, and one number actually worked on the decoded roster (4)

Directions, units, then weights

Every term is a cost — waiting, earliness, imbalance, spend are all “lower is better” — and every term is normalised to [0,1] against its own worst case before weighting, because day-waits, weight-days, shift counts and ringgit are different units and cannot be added raw. Weights: w₁ 0.30 · w₂ 0.25 · w₃ 0.20 · w₄ 0.10 · w₅ 0.15, summing to 1. Hierarchy sentence: care for patients (f₁, f₂) outranks fairness to staff (f₃, f₄), which outranks money (f₅) — the brief lists care first and agency spend last, so the weights follow the brief, not taste. Assembled: F = 0.30·f₁′ + 0.25·f₂′ + 0.20·f₃′ + 0.10·f₄′ + 0.15·f₅′ = 0.105 + 0.165 + 0.100 + 0.060 + 0 = 0.430 for the worked chromosome, lower is better.

normalisation before aggregation + weights stated and tied to the brief (2)

Critical awareness

The two cheapest moves fight each other: admitting everyone on day 1 would cut waiting but would fill W2 and force repair-delays for isolation patients while squeezing nurse legality toward agency shifts — so f₁ and f₅ are separate terms rather than one “goodness” number, and the weights are what pick the winner. That ordering is policy, not mathematics — a different hospital would swap them. And if a roster that feels wrong scores well, the missing-component test applies: a night-heavy nurse with a light week would score fine on f₃ alone, which is exactly why f₄ exists as its own term. Whatever appears in my Q1 chromosome has now reappeared in Q2, component by component.

conflicting objectives named, weights called policy, missing-component story told (3)

Q3 — the alternative algorithm: ACO 10

Part A — differences, GA vs ACO

AspectGA (Q1)ACO
Representationfixed-length chromosome (21 genes)no chromosome — solutions built step by step
Solution creationrandom init + crossover + mutationants construct along a graph, guided by pheromone
Constraint handlingalphabet + repair + penalties after buildinginvalid options filtered during construction
Diversity controlcrossover & mutation ratespheromone evaporation rate
Memory of past searchthe population itselfthe pheromone matrix
Elitismbest chromosomes copied overbest ants deposit extra pheromone
Escaping local optimamutation; risk without diversityevaporation forgets stale trails

a sensible named algorithm + the GA/ACO contrast written out (2 + part of 2)

Part B — how ACO would be applied here

Nodes come from the scenario. Each of the six patients is a stage, visited in a fixed construction order — emergency first, then urgent, then elective, each group tie-broken by days already waited; the construction order is itself a choice, so I state it.

Options at each node. The legal (ward, day) pairs for that patient — the same alphabets my Q1 genes had: P3 is only ever offered W2, P4 only W3, P2 and P5 only days 1–2.

Filtering as the ant moves. Before the ant chooses, I remove every option that would break a hard rule: a (ward, day) pair whose whole LOS would push the ward over its bed count in any shift is never offered — the same occupancy arithmetic the GA's decoder used, now applied during construction instead of after. This one sentence is the entire ACO-vs-GA argument.

Choice and pheromone. P(ward, day) ∝ τ(patient, ward, day)α × ηβ, with η = weighttype / admission day, so earlier and more urgent options smell better. After each iteration trails evaporate (× 0.7) and the best ants deposit extra. I would set 30 ants, α = 1, β = 2, ρ = 0.7.

What carries over. Once an ant has placed all six patients, the nurse roster is built by the same Phase-2 greedy decoder from Q1 — unchanged — and my Q2 fitness F scores the finished roster unchanged: the objective, the weights and the normalisation all carry over; the only new job is that F now drives pheromone deposits as well as selection.

encoding differences (3) + evaluation strategy (2) + implementation details with numbers (2)

Judgement

Compared with the GA, ACO produces far fewer invalid solutions — the filters make legality free — but it needs a pheromone structure (6 patients × 3 wards × 7 days ≈ 126 entries) and three extra parameters to tune. For this problem the GA's alphabet already achieves most of the same effect, so I would keep the GA as the primary design — and switch to ACO if the constraint web grew denser, because feasibility then comes free by construction.

one-sentence comparative judgement (1)

Script 2 — Exam timetabling (the real March 2026 paper)

The scenario the March 2026 cohort actually sat, answered here with the same structure the professor's circulated sample used — the 5-gene block, ceil(Slot/2) decoding, the 1000×HC fitness — compressed to what a hand can produce in two hours.

APU examination timetabling — the real March 2026 paper. The examinations office must timetable 40 exams over 10 weekdays × 2 sessions (09:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00) — 20 session-slots — across 3 campus locations. There are 12 halls (4 per location) with capacities from 50 to 300, and 20 invigilators: 6 senior and 14 standard, who may be asked to travel between locations.

Each exam has: a duration (1–3 hours), a student count, its programme, a priority (high or normal — roughly 30% are high), for some exams a permitted day-window (e.g. “days 2–4 only”), and student-overlap sets — which other exams share its students.

Rules: a hall hosts one exam per session; a large exam may split across two halls, but only at the same location and same session; consecutive exams in one hall need a 30-minute reset; no student may sit two exams in one session; a high-priority exam needs a senior invigilator; invigilators work at most 3 sessions a day.

Aims: high-priority exams early · fair invigilator workload · no student more than two exams a day · minimal inter-location travel · a compact exam period · avoid consecutive afternoons · low invigilator idle time.

Q1 — the chromosome 15

The decisions

For each exam the scheduler must decide: which time slot (when), which hall — or two halls if split (where), and which invigilator(s) (who). That is five decisions per exam, and one block of five genes carries them all. Everything else in the brief — durations, capacities, overlap sets — is data, not a decision. In the literature this is an examination timetabling problem, and naming the family is a credibility line.

all decision variables identified, and where each lives (3)

Assumptions

ComponentValueWhy
Split rulesplit = 2 halls, same location + same sessionthe brief allows splitting but does not say the two halls share a site — so I say it
Hall reset30 minutes between consecutive exams in one hallthe brief implies preparation but names no figure — the number is mine
Invigilator travelinter-site travel eats into the gap and is not restthe brief allows travel but does not say it is free
Large-exam staffinga second invigilator for exams over 150 studentsgives the Inv2 gene its meaning
Senior rulehigh-priority ⇒ invigilator 1 is seniorthe brief demands senior cover but not which gene carries it
Exam counts40 exams, ~30% high-priority; hall capacities 50–300; 6 senior + 14 standard invigilatorsthe brief's own figures, restated here so every number downstream is traceable

The chromosome

One candidate solution is a string of 200 genes: 40 blocks of five, one block per exam — SlotHall1Hall2Inv1Inv2. Slot ∈ 1–20; Hall1 ∈ 1–12; Hall2 ∈ 0–12 (0 = no split); Inv1 ∈ 1–20; Inv2 ∈ 0–20 (0 = none). Two alphabets are deliberately restricted: an exam with a day-window gets only that window's slots (window “days 2–4” ⇒ Slot ∈ 3–8), and a high-priority exam gets only seniors in Inv1 (∈ 1–6) — so the two rules that matter most are unwritable violations.

Legal block, read back: 33028 — see the worked example below.

The same drawing with one illegal gene: 33628 — invalid: a split must use two halls at the same location, and hall 6 is at a different site from hall 3. Drawing the boundary being broken is the cheapest proof that the encoding has one.

representation — length, gene types, legal values, worked example, key rules handled in the alphabet (4)

Worked example with the paper's own numbers

The block [3, 3, 0, 2, 8] decodes as: Slot 3 → Day = ceil(3/2) = day 2, and 3 is odd, so the morning session. Hall 3 — capacity 200, which fits the exam's 180 students ✓. Hall2 = 0 — no split. Inv1 = 2 — senior ✓, required because this exam is high-priority. Inv2 = 8 — a standard second invigilator, because 180 students exceeds my 150 threshold. One block, every gene interpreted, every value checked against a rule.

Decoding — a numbered procedure

Step 1: extract each 5-gene block in exam order. Step 2: map the slot gene — day = ceil(Slot/2), odd slots are mornings, even slots afternoons. Step 3: look up Hall1 and test capacity against the exam's student count — the capacity rule is enforced here; if Hall2 ≠ 0, test the split rule (same location, same session) — enforced here too. Step 4: look up Inv1 and Inv2; a high-priority exam must have a senior in Inv1 — enforced here (and already in the alphabet). Step 5: build the day-by-day grid and run Q2's validity checks over the finished timetable — clashes, reset buffers, invigilator caps are detected here, because they depend on the whole plan, not on one block.

Every step names the constraint it enforces: windows in the alphabet before decoding, capacity and the split rule in step 3, the senior rule in step 4, clash/reset/cap detection in step 5. A decoder that just “builds the timetable” scores half of one that says where each rule dies.

decoding, step by step, each step pinned to the constraint it enforces (4)

Genetic operators

One-point crossover cuts between blocks — always at a multiple of five — so it swaps whole exams and can never splice half of one exam's five genes. Mutation resets a single gene to a random value inside its own alphabet — a windowed exam's slot stays inside its window, a high-priority exam's Inv1 stays senior. Both operators therefore preserve the alphabets by construction.

Data required

  • Entity data — per exam: duration, student count, programme, priority, permitted window.
  • Resource data — per hall: location, capacity; per invigilator: role, home site.
  • Relationship data — the student-overlap sets: which exams share students, which is what the clash checks need.
  • Policy data — session times, the 30-minute reset, travel time, the senior rule, the 150-student second-invigilator threshold.

Every number my Q2 fitness uses is findable in this list or in the assumptions table.

data requirements, grouped into four labelled bullets (2)

Justification

I chose the heterogeneous 5-gene block over a one-gene-per-slot chromosome, because block boundaries let crossover cut between exams and never split one exam's five genes — the one-gene-per-slot design scatters one exam's decision across the grid, so a single cut can leave an exam with a hall but no slot. This space holds about (20 × 12 × 13 × 20 × 21)40 ≈ 10244 candidate timetables — no gradient, no enumeration — which is why a population search is the right tool at all.

justification against a named alternative + the search-space line (2)

Q2 — fitness and validity 15

Sort the rules first — twelve hard, seven soft

Hard — a plan that breaks one is not a timetable: ① every exam gets exactly one slot inside its permitted window · ② hall capacity respected — for a split exam, in both halls · ③ a hall hosts at most one exam per session (the split pair is the one exception) · ④ a split uses two halls at one location and one session · ⑤ 30-minute reset between consecutive exams in a hall · ⑥ an exam fits inside its 3-hour session — with a reset, duration + 0.5 h ≤ 3 h when a hall is shared · ⑦ no student in two exams in one session (the overlap sets) · ⑧ no invigilator in two places in one session · ⑨ an invigilator does at most 3 sessions a day · ⑩ a senior on every high-priority exam · ⑪ a second invigilator on exams over 150 students · ⑫ every exam has at least one invigilator.

Soft — breakable, but each breach costs quality: fair invigilator workload · no student more than two exams a day (congestion) · high-priority exams early · minimal inter-location travel · a compact exam period · few consecutive afternoons · low invigilator idle time.

One classification I make deliberately, because Q2 asks for the split by name: the paper lists “≤ 2 exams per student per day” under its aims and never calls a three-exam day impossible — so it is breakable at a price, and I classify it soft-with-penalty rather than hard. Classifying it hard is defensible; listing it in both columns without saying which is not.

the hard/soft split done visibly, twelve against seven, with the borderline case argued (3)

Aggregation — the penalty form, and why here

Fitness = 1000 × ΣHardViolations + Σ wᵢ · Softᵢ — minimise; a perfect timetable scores 0. I use the penalty form rather than a normalised weighted sum because my decoder can still produce a timetable that breaks the whole-plan rules — clashes, resets, caps depend on the entire grid, not on one block — so legality must live inside the fitness arithmetic. The 1000 is chosen so any single hard breach outweighs the entire soft ladder at its realistic worst: feasibility always outranks quality.

Validity — which tool for which rule, and what happens to invalid offspring

ChecksToolWhy
①Encoding alphabeta windowed exam's slot gene only ever holds a slot inside its window — unwritable
② ③ ④Decodercapacity and the split rule tested in decoder step 3; hall occupancy step 5
⑤ ⑥Decoderreset and session-fit tested while the grid is built
⑩Alphabet + decoderInv1 restricted to seniors; re-checked in step 4
⑪ ⑫Decoderthe 150-student rule and completeness in step 4
⑦ ⑧ ⑨Penaltydetected in step 5; each counts 1000 — clashes cascade when moved, so repair is the wrong tool for them

Repair first for the cheap deterministic fixes: swap a standard invigilator for a senior on a high-priority exam, reset an out-of-window slot to the nearest legal slot in the window, force a cross-site split back to one location. Penalty for the rest: a student clash cannot be edited out without moving an exam and creating a new one, so let the 1000-weight selection evolve it away. I name one cost of each choice: repair biases the search toward whatever the fixed version prefers; penalties need their weight guessed right.

every check routed to a tool, repair vs penalty reasoned, a cost named for each (3)

The seven components — formula + unit + one worked number

f₁ workload balance = standard deviation of weekly sessions per invigilator, in sessions — the brief names staff complaints first. About 60 invigilator-sessions over the week means a mean of 3; a timetable where every invigilator does exactly 3 scores f₁ = 0, and a spread of [4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 2] already scores ≈ 0.7.

f₂ congestion = count exams per programme per day; every day a programme goes above 2 adds (excess × 50), in weighted violations. Worked: programme IT has three exams on day 5 → (3 − 2) × 50 = 50.

f₃ priority earliness = Σ of the day index over high-priority exams, in weighted days. Worked: the twelve high-priority exams sit on days 1,1,2,2,2,3,3,4,4,5,6,7 → 40; a fully front-loaded plan (four per day on days 1–3) would score 24.

f₄ travel = Σ cross-site moves per invigilator, in moves. Worked: the example grid has six → 6.

f₅ period compactness = the last exam's day, in days. Worked: the last exam sits on day 9 of 10.

f₆ afternoon streaks = Σ over programmes of consecutive-afternoon runs, in runs. Worked: programme BA has afternoons on days 6 and 7 → 1 streak.

f₇ invigilator idle = Σ (hours on site − hours invigilating), in hours. Worked: a senior who covers one 3-hour session but must be on site for 6 is 3 idle hours.

each component: formula, unit, and one number worked on the example timetable (4)

Weights — the ladder, and every rung tied to the brief

Hard = 1000; then workload 80 (staff complaints are in the brief), congestion 50, priority-early 30, travel 25, period length 20, afternoon streaks 15, idle 10 — each weight tied to something the scenario says, not to taste. The hierarchy sentence: feasibility outranks fairness to staff, which outranks convenience to students, which outranks operational efficiency. If I could not rank them, the recorded fallback is all-hard-equal, all-soft-equal.

weights stated and justified against the brief (2)

Critical awareness

Two of my soft aims pull against each other: front-loading high-priority exams (f₃) squeezes them into mornings and leaves afternoons for everyone else, which is exactly the afternoon-streak pattern f₆ punishes — the weights are what pick the winner, and they are policy, not mathematics. The same tension runs through travel: cutting travel (f₄) locks invigilators to their home site and pushes the load onto whoever lives near the large halls, worsening f₁. And f₆ exists at all because the missing-component test caught it: a timetable with zero congestion could still chain every afternoon, and a fitness blind to that would disagree with intuition. Whatever appears in my Q1 chromosome has now reappeared in Q2, component by component.

conflicting objectives named, weights called policy, the missing-component story (3)

Q3 — the alternative algorithm: ACO 10

Part A — differences, GA vs ACO

AspectGA (Q1)ACO
Representationfixed-length chromosome (200 genes)no chromosome — solutions built step by step
Solution creationrandom init + crossover + mutationants construct along a graph, guided by pheromone
Constraint handlingalphabet + repair + penalties after buildinginvalid options filtered during construction
Diversity controlcrossover & mutation ratespheromone evaporation rate
Memory of past searchthe population itselfthe pheromone matrix
Elitismbest chromosomes copied overbest ants deposit extra pheromone
Escaping local optimamutation; risk without diversityevaporation forgets stale trails

a sensible named algorithm + the GA/ACO contrast written out

Part B — how ACO would be applied here

Nodes come from the scenario. Each exam is a stage, and the ant places the exams one at a time in a fixed construction order — high-priority first, then by descending student count, because the hard-to-place exams are placed while the board is still empty. The construction order is itself a choice, so I state it.

Options at each node. The legal values my Q1 genes had: a slot inside the exam's window, a hall — or a same-site hall pair if it must split — and invigilators.

Filtering as the ant moves. Before the ant chooses, every option that would break a hard rule is removed: a slot outside the window is never offered; a hall that cannot hold the exam is never offered; a slot that clashes with an already-placed exam from the same overlap set is never offered; a non-senior is never offered to a high-priority exam. Rules are therefore enforced during construction rather than repaired after — that one sentence is the entire ACO-vs-GA argument.

Choice and pheromone. P(option) ∝ τ(exam, option)α × ηβ, with η = priority weight / day index, so early slots and high-priority fits smell better. After each iteration trails evaporate (× 0.7) and the best ants deposit extra. I would set 40 ants, α = 1, β = 2, ρ = 0.7.

What carries over. My Q2 fitness scores each ant's finished timetable unchanged — the 1000 × ΣHard + Σwᵢ·Softᵢ sum, the weights and the ladder all carry over; the only new job is that the score now drives pheromone deposits as well as selection. Because the filters already killed most hard breaches, the 1000-weight term should rarely fire at all under ACO.

encoding differences + evaluation strategy + implementation with numbers

Judgement

Compared with the GA, ACO produces far fewer invalid solutions — the filters make legality free — but it needs a large pheromone structure (40 exams × 20 slots × 12 halls and more, with no fixed-length individual to index it) and three extra parameters to tune. For this paper the GA's block chromosome plus restricted alphabets achieves most of the same effect with a simpler machine, so I would keep the GA as the primary design — and switch to ACO if the overlap sets and hall windows grew dense enough that repair and penalties started doing real work.

one-sentence comparative judgement

Script 3 — The port (the site's spine)

The scenario every lesson on this site uses. The full Q1 page walks this answer in slow motion; here it is at exam speed, with the Q2 and Q3 scripts the walkthrough doesn't show.

A container port — berth, crane and buffer scheduling (the professor's own mock, condensed). Three quay sections — A (standard berth, hazmat-certified, reefer power, buffer 200), B (long berth, no hazmat, no reefer, buffer 250), C (long berth, hazmat-certified, no reefer, buffer 150). Three cranes: C1 50 containers/hour (electric), C2 60/hour (diesel), C3 45/hour (electric). Four ships arrive in the 08:00–16:00 shift (480 minutes):

ShipETAContainersPrioritySpecial need
SH108:00150Highperishable — needs reefer power
SH209:30200Normallarge vessel — long berth
SH310:15100Emergencyhazardous — certified berth
SH411:00180Normalstandard

Compatibility: SH2 is too long for A (B or C only); SH3 is hazardous and B is uncertified (A or C only). Cranes need a 30-minute break after 3 hours continuous work; the electric cranes additionally need a 1-hour charge after 4 hours of work. One ship occupies its section at a time, and a berth needs a changeover between ships. Every zone's buffer must never exceed its own capacity. Berth handling cost in RM (ship × section):

Cost (RM)ABC
SH1407090
SH2not allowed5080
SH360not allowed90
SH4705545

Aims: low waiting · priorities early · cranes kept busy · low energy cost · finish by 16:00 · stay below buffer capacity · low berth handling cost · balanced yards · clear the quay as early as possible.

Q1 — the chromosome 15

The decisions

Four things are genuinely open: which section each ship berths in, which crane serves each unloading job, the order the jobs are worked, and the clock time each begins. Two live in the chromosome — section and order — and two are derived by the decoder from the rules below. Everything else (ETAs, rates, the cost matrix) is data, not a decision. In the literature this is BACASP — Berth Allocation + Crane Assignment + crane Scheduling — and naming the family is a credibility line.

all decision variables identified, and where each lives (3)

Assumptions

ComponentValueWhy
Time granularity15-minute steps; crane time rounded up to the next stepa 10:15 ETA can be honoured exactly; rounding down would finish work not yet done
Changeover30 minutes between ships at one berththe brief implies preparation but names no figure — the number is mine
Buffer clearancetrucks drain 30 containers/hour per zonewithout it, 630 containers cannot pass through 600 units of buffer
Idle resets the clocka gap of 30 minutes or more counts as a breakthe one assumption that makes C2's 2½ h + 30-min gap + 3 h legal
Overtimeonly unloading past 16:00 counts — breaks and charges are freeso f₆ measures the last container, not the last crane activity
Energy tariffdiesel RM 120 / running hour; electric RM 45 / running hour, RM 30 / charging hourthe brief says “energy cost” but names no rate — so I state one

The chromosome

One candidate solution is a heterogeneous string of 17 genes in two segments. Segment A holds four integers, one per ship, giving its section, with the alphabet restricted per ship: SH1 ∈ {1,2,3}, SH2 ∈ {2,3} (too long for A), SH3 ∈ {1,3} (hazardous, B uncertified), SH4 ∈ {1,2,3}, where 1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C. Segment B is a permutation of the thirteen unloading jobs — T1–T3 are SH1's, T4–T7 SH2's, T8–T9 SH3's, T10–T13 SH4's, fifty containers each and thirty in the last, 630 exactly. Cutting ships into jobs is what lets two cranes share one large ship.

Legal, and what it means: SH11SH22SH33SH41‖ T2 T5 T1 T9 T13 T4 T7 T3 T11 T6 T12 T8 T10 — “1 2 3 1 means SH1 berths in A, SH2 in B, SH3 in C, SH4 returns to A once SH1 has left; the jobs are considered in that order, each placed at the earliest moment the rules allow, so position is priority, not start time.”

The same drawing with one illegal gene: SH21 — invalid: SH2 is too long for section A, and 1 is outside SH2's alphabet. Restricting the alphabet is deliberate: an incompatible berthing is unwritable, so compatibility never needs repairing.

representation — length, gene types, legal values, worked example, compatibility in the alphabet (4)

Decoding — phase 1, the berth plan

Read segment A; group the ships by section; order each group by ETA, ties broken by priority; lay the windows along the quay: each ship starts at max(its own ETA, the previous ship's departure + 30 minutes). Here A takes SH1 from 08:00 then SH4 from 11:00; B takes SH2 from 09:30; C takes SH3 at 10:15 — not a minute before it arrives. Berth occupancy, changeover and ETA are enforced in this phase, by construction.

Decoding — phase 2, the crane schedule

Walk segment B in order and give each job the fastest crane that is free, legal for that section and not due a rest, computing end = start + containers ÷ rate, rounded up to the next 15-minute step. Insert a 30-minute break after three hours of continuous work, and a one-hour charge once an electric crane reaches four hours of work. Each placement updates that zone's buffer level — rising by what the crane unloads, falling by the 30/hour drain — and records its peak, so capacity is checked slot by slot, as a level, not a total. The order is forced, not chosen: crane availability depends on where and when ships are berthed, which is why the berth plan must exist first.

Decoded, this chromosome puts C2 on SH1 (08:00–10:30, 150 ÷ 60 = 2½ h) and then on SH4 (11:00–14:00, 180 ÷ 60 = 3 h), C1 on SH2 (200 ÷ 50 = 4 h of work: 09:30–12:30, a 30-minute break, then 13:00–14:00), C3 on SH3 (10:15–12:30, 100 ÷ 45 ≈ 2 h 13 min → 2¼ h): quay clear at 14:00, no ship waiting, C1 charging 14:00–15:00 on its four hours of work.

decoding in two phases, each step pinned to the constraint it enforces (4)

How the operators apply

Segment A takes uniform crossover and a mutation that resets a gene to another value from its own legal set — children stay compatible by construction. Segment B takes order crossover (OX) and swap mutation, which preserve a permutation — one-point crossover here would duplicate and lose jobs. Tournament selection with k = 3, two elites, crossover probability 0.9, mutation about 1/17 per gene.

Data required

  • Per shift — each ship's ETA, container count, priority class, compatible sections.
  • Fixed reference data — section lengths and certifications, buffer capacities (A 200, B 250, C 150), crane rates and power types, break and charge rules, shift bounds 08:00–16:00, the 15-minute step, the 30-minute changeover, the 30/hour clearance rate.
  • Live data — current buffer occupancy per zone, since trucks drain the yard while cranes fill it.
  • Cost and policy data — the ship × section handling-cost matrix, the energy tariff, the overtime rate, the 5/3/1 priority weights.

data requirements, grouped — per-shift / fixed / live / cost (2)

Why this design and not another

I considered a grouping encoding — each section a block listing its ships in service order — and rejected it because it works at ship level, where one ship gets one crane start to finish, and SH2's two hundred containers are exactly the case where I want two cranes sharing the work. Encoding the section per job would be the trap to avoid — a ship docks once, so thirteen section genes would do four genes' work and widen the search for nothing. I also rejected a section × time-slot grid: it draws the timetable beautifully, but being indexed by section and time it has nowhere to put a crane's break or charge. The search space is 36 legal section assignments × 13! job orders — roughly 224 billion schedules, no gradient — which is why a population search, not enumeration.

justification against two named alternatives + the search-space line (2)

Q2 — fitness and validity 15

Sort the rules first — nine hard, nine soft

Hard — a plan that breaks one is not a schedule: ship–section compatibility (SH2 never A, SH3 never B) · berth occupancy — one ship per section at a time · 30-minute changeover at a berth · no start before ETA · one crane per section per slot · 30-minute break after three hours of crane work · one-hour charge after four hours for electric cranes · every zone inside its own capacity at every slot · all 630 containers unloaded.

Soft — breaking one only makes the plan worse: low waiting · priorities early · cranes busy · low energy cost · finish before 16:00 · stay below buffer capacity · low handling cost · balanced yards · early quay clearance.

One quantity sits in both columns, and I should be the one to point at it: buffer capacity is hard check 8 and soft f₄. Not double counting — the hard check settles legality; f₄, Σ over zones and slots of max(0, occupancy − capacity) in container-hours, measures how badly a plan overflows, so the search feels a slope instead of a cliff. It is also why this one rule is handled by penalty rather than repair: a yard overflow cannot be edited out without wrecking the timetable, whereas compatibility goes in the encoding and occupancy, changeover and crane rests go in the decoder.

the hard/soft split done visibly, and the dual-entry clause pre-empting the apparent duplicate (3)

Validity — nine checkable tests, each with a pass example

① Compatibility — every ship in an allowed section (SH3 not in B ✓). ② Berth occupancy — ≤ 1 ship per section per slot (A holds SH1 until 10:30, SH4 only from 11:00 ✓). ③ Changeover — ≥ 30 min between ships at one berth (out 10:30, in 11:00 ✓). ④ ETA — no start before arrival (SH3 not before 10:15 ✓). ⑤ Section exclusivity — ≤ 1 crane active per section per slot (A carries only C2 all morning ✓). ⑥ Continuous-work limit — no run over 3 h without a 30-min break (C1 works 09:30–12:30 then breaks ✓; C2's 2½ h + 30-min gap + 3 h is legal only because idle resets the counter). ⑦ Charging — electric cranes charge once 4 h of work is reached (C1 charges 14:00–15:00 ✓). ⑧ Buffer — every zone and slot ≤ its own capacity (A peaks at 150 against 200, B at 65 against 250, C at 33 against 150 ✓). ⑨ Completeness — every container unloaded (150 + 200 + 100 + 180 = 630 ✓).

Trace every check back to a decision — that link is the mark. Checks ① ② ③ exist only because I chose the section; his deck: “If your answer omits them, your validity test is incomplete.” The law runs both ways: f₇ and f₈ only exist as components because the section is a gene — a constant cannot be optimised — and two whole data groups (compatibility, the cost matrix) exist only because the section became a decision. One decision: three new checks, two new components, two new data groups.

nine checkable tests with pass examples, traced to the decision that created them (3)

Constraint → tool table

ConstraintToolHow
Ship–section compatibilityEncodinggene alphabet restricted {2,3} / {1,3} — unwritable
Berth occupancyDecodersequential layout per section — overlap never arises
Changeover 30 minDecoderauto-inserted between consecutive ships
ETA releaseDecoderstart = max(ETA, previous departure + 30)
Crane breaks / chargingDecoderinserted while building phase 2
Buffer capacityPenaltyf₄ = Σ max(0, occupancy − cap) × weight — degree matters

I name the cost of the one real choice: repair is wrong here because an overflow cannot be edited out without wrecking the timetable, and rejection wastes evaluations — so the buffer is the single penalty-handled rule, priced by degree.

The fitness — nine components, formula + unit + one worked number

f₁ waiting = Σ (berth start − ETA) in minutes; f₂ priority-weighted waiting = Σ w · waiting, w = 5 emergency / 3 high / 1 normal. Worked: 0 for both — no ship waits. They overlap by design, and I say so: f₂ carries the information f₁ cannot — whose waiting it is — so an hour of delay to SH3 costs five times an hour to SH4.

f₃ crane idleness = 1 − utilisation, a fraction. Utilisation is a maximise quantity, so I add (1 − U) to keep every term a cost. Worked: 11.75 crane-hours of work (C2 5½, C1 4, C3 2¼) over 3 × 8 = 24 available → f₃ = 1 − 0.49 = 0.51.

f₄ buffer pressure = Σ over zones and slots of max(0, occupancy − capacity), in container-hours. Worked: 0 — peaks 150 / 65 / 33 all stay under their caps.

f₅ energy = Σ running hours × rate + charging hours × rate, in RM. Worked: 5½ × 120 + 4 × 45 + 2¼ × 45 + 1 × 30 = 660 + 180 + 101.25 + 30 = RM 971.25.

f₆ overtime = Σ max(0, last unloading finish − 16:00), in minutes — measured on the last container moved, not the last crane activity, so C1's 14:00–15:00 charge costs nothing. Worked: 0.

f₇ berth handling cost = Σ matrix[ship, section], in RM. Worked: SH1→A 40 + SH2→B 50 + SH3→C 90 + SH4→A 70 = RM 250.

f₈ yard balance = standard deviation of peak zone occupancy, in containers. Worked: peaks 150 / 65 / 33 → mean 82.7 → σ ≈ 49 — one zone is carrying the yard while two sit half-empty.

f₉ makespan = when the quay is clear, in minutes from 08:00. Worked: 360. The component most answers drop — and the drop is expensive: without it the fitness can prefer a plan that drags the shift to 16:00 over one that finishes at 14:00.

nine components, each with formula, unit and a number worked on the decoded timetable (4)

Directions, units, normalise — then weights

Minutes, ringgit, fractions and containers are different units, so each component is normalised to [0,1] against its own justified range before weighting: f₁ 0→1,920 (4 ships × the 480-min shift) · f₂ 0→4,800 (10 weight-units × 480) · f₃ 0→1 · f₄ 0→500 · f₅ 500→2,000 · f₆ 0→240 · f₇ 195→330 (the matrix's own legal spread) · f₈ 0→100 · f₉ 240→600 — whose floor is not zero: the quay cannot clear before the fastest possible finish. Weights sum to 1: waiting 0.25 · priority 0.15 · idleness 0.05 · buffer 0.10 · energy 0.10 · overtime 0.05 · handling 0.10 · balance 0.10 · makespan 0.10. Hierarchy sentence: I weighted waiting above handling cost, because a berthed ship blocks the quay and the port is paid for turnaround — RM 30 of savings is not worth an hour of congestion.

Assembled: F = 0.05·0.51 + 0.10·0.314 + 0.10·0.407 + 0.10·0.49 + 0.10·0.333 = 0.0255 + 0.0314 + 0.0407 + 0.049 + 0.0333 ≈ 0.18, lower is better.

normalisation before aggregation + weights stated and defended (2)

Critical awareness

Read the cost matrix greedily and both SH1 (RM 40) and SH3 (RM 60) are cheapest in section A — exactly the congestion trap. Not because 150 + 100 = 250 “will not fit” a 200-unit buffer — it fits, because the zone drains while it fills and A's peak level stays in the low 90s — but because a section holds one ship at a time: SH1 occupies A until 10:30, the changeover runs to 11:00, and SH3, arrived at 10:15, sits off the quay. So f₇ pulls ships toward A while f₁ and f₄ push them away, and the weights are what settle that argument — they are policy, not mathematics. And if a plan that feels wrong ever scores well, the missing-component test applies: a fitness blind to makespan will keep passing plans that drag the shift to 16:00.

the matrix tension named, weights called policy, the missing-component story (3)

Q3 — the alternative algorithm: ACO 10

Part A — differences, GA vs ACO

AspectGA (Q1)ACO
Representationfixed-length chromosome (17 genes)no chromosome — solutions built step by step
Solution creationrandom init + crossover + mutationants construct along a graph, guided by pheromone
Constraint handlingalphabet + decoder + one penalty after buildinginvalid options filtered during construction
Diversity controlcrossover & mutation ratespheromone evaporation rate
Memory of past searchthe population itselfthe pheromone matrix
Elitismbest chromosomes copied overbest ants deposit extra pheromone
Escaping local optimamutation; risk without diversityevaporation forgets stale trails

a sensible named algorithm + the GA/ACO contrast written out

Part B — how ACO would be applied here

Nodes come from the scenario. Each of the four ships is a stage, visited in a fixed construction order — ETA order, ties broken by priority, exactly the order my GA's decoder already uses. The construction order is itself a choice, so I state it.

Options at each node. The legal sections for that ship — the same alphabets my Q1 genes had: SH2 is only ever offered B or C, SH3 only A or C.

Filtering as the ant moves. Before the ant chooses, every option that would break a hard rule is removed: a section whose buffer would overflow is never offered — the same slot-by-slot occupancy simulation my decoder runs, now applied during construction instead of after. That one sentence is the entire ACO-vs-GA argument.

Choice and pheromone. P(section) ∝ τ(ship, section)α × ηβ, with η = priority weight / handling cost, so cheap berths smell better to important ships. After each iteration trails evaporate (× 0.7) and the best ants deposit extra. I would set 40 ants, α = 1, β = 2, ρ = 0.7.

What carries over. Once an ant has berthed all four ships, the crane schedule is built by the same phase-2 decoder from Q1 — permutation order replaced by the construction order — and my Q2 fitness F scores the finished timetable unchanged: the nine components, the normalisation and the weights all carry over; the only new job is that F now drives pheromone deposits as well as selection. PSO with random keys — 8 real keys, banded per ship's legal sections — is the other defensible choice and would reuse the same decoder; ACO is the one I can apply node by node, which is why I picked it.

encoding differences + evaluation strategy + implementation with numbers

Judgement

Compared with the GA, ACO produces far fewer invalid plans — the filters make legality free, and the buffer penalty should rarely fire at all — but it needs a pheromone structure (4 ships × 3 sections, plus evaporation and deposit bookkeeping) and three extra parameters to tune. For this port the GA's restricted alphabet already achieves most of the same effect with a simpler machine, so I would keep the GA as the primary design — and prefer ACO if the compatibility and buffer rules multiplied, since the filters absorb them for free.

one-sentence comparative judgement

Practice · the finished artefact

A Full-Length Q1, Written Out

Everything else on this site is an outline, a table or a stepper — scaffolding. This is the building: one complete Q1 answer for the port scenario, written the way you would actually write it by hand in the hall. Read it for its shape first and its content second. The shape carries to any scenario; the port's numbers do not.

What you are looking at. About 1,150 words in eight short labelled paragraphs plus one drawn chromosome — deliberately more than you will write in the hall. At roughly 20 words a minute, which is what handwriting actually costs, that is nearer an hour, while the plan gives Q1's 15 forty minutes.

So read this as the full menu rather than the target: six hundred words that keep all eight labels is a strong answer and it fits inside the forty. The eight labels matter far more than the volume, because each one claims a mark band; where a paragraph runs long here it is showing you the extra clause that lifts a band from half marks to full, and you choose which of those clauses you have time for.

Every paragraph opens with a bold label so the marker finds the band without hunting. None of it is bullet fragments — the paper is handwritten prose plus diagrams, and a fragment the marker has to finish on your behalf earns nothing.

The small grey lines between the paragraphs are not part of the answer — they are my notes to you, naming the mark each block is claiming. In the exam you write only the dark text (and you draw the chromosome as a row of boxes, exactly as it appears below).

The scenario in full →

The answer

Assumptions. The brief leaves several things unstated, so I record them first. Time advances in 15-minute steps, so a 10:15 ETA can be honoured exactly. A berth needs a 30-minute changeover between ships: the brief implies preparation but names no figure, so that number is mine. A ship stays in its section until it has finished unloading — no re-berthing.

Any idle gap of 30 minutes or more counts as a rest and resets a crane's continuous-run counter. Trucks clear about 30 containers per hour from each zone, so a buffer holds a level that rises and falls, not a running total.

Why this block earns its marks: assumptions are not a band of their own — they are the insurance policy on all five. Each is one sentence and each is falsifiable. The rest rule and the truck rate are load-bearing: without them a legal crane rota and a legal yard become arguable, and the marker cannot tell which figures were given and which you invented.

Data required. I group the inputs four ways. Per shift: each ship's ETA, container count, priority class and compatible sections. Fixed reference data, loaded once: berth lengths, hazmat and reefer certification, buffer capacities (A 200, B 250, C 150), each crane's rate, power type, break and charging rules, the shift's start and end (08:00–16:00), the time granularity of 15 minutes, the 30-minute berth changeover, and the truck clearance rate of 30 containers per hour per zone.

Live: current buffer occupancy per zone, since trucks drain the yard while cranes fill it. Cost and policy data: the ship × section berth-handling matrix in RM, the energy tariff per crane-hour, the overtime penalty rate per minute past 16:00, and the priority weights that turn Emergency / High / Normal into numbers — I use 5 / 3 / 1. The last four groups of figures are the ones my assumptions created; they belong here precisely because I invented them.

2 Data requirements, grouped. The grouping is the mark. A flat list of nouns reads as a brain-dump; per-shift / fixed / live / cost reads as a specification, and it costs one extra clause per line. His own data slide is explicit that the list must include the data your assumptions create — granularity, changeover, clearance rate, overtime rate, priority weights — and the test is mechanical: every number that appears in your Q2 fitness must be findable in this paragraph, or that component cannot be computed.

The decisions. Four things are genuinely open: which section each ship berths in, which crane serves each unloading job, the order the jobs are worked, and the clock time each begins. Two live in the chromosome — section and order — and two are derived by the decoder from the rules stated below. Every decision is therefore accounted for: none silently dropped, none encoded twice.

3 All decision variables identified, and where each lives. Note the last sentence: naming a decision as decoder-derived claims the mark just as well as giving it a gene, and it keeps the chromosome short. The section is the one students forget; it is also the decision that makes berth handling cost and yard balance optimisable at all.

The chromosome. The space this searches is 36 legal section assignments × 13! job orderings, about 224 billion schedules, with no gradient to follow because the objective is a decoded timetable rather than a formula — which is why a population search rather than enumeration or a greedy rule. Seventeen genes in two segments.

Segment A holds four integers, one per ship, giving its section, with legal values restricted per ship: SH1 ∈ {1, 2, 3}, SH2 ∈ {2, 3} because it is too long for A, SH3 ∈ {1, 3} because it is hazardous and B is uncertified, SH4 ∈ {1, 2, 3}, where 1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C. Segment B is a permutation of the thirteen unloading jobs: T1–T3 are SH1's, T4–T7 are SH2's, T8–T9 are SH3's and T10–T13 are SH4's, fifty containers apiece and thirty in the last — 630 exactly. Cutting each ship into jobs is what lets two cranes share one large ship. A worked example, in the scenario's own terms:

SH11SH22SH33SH41‖ T2 T5 T1 T9 T13 T4 T7 T3 T11 T6 T12 T8 T10

— read as “1 2 3 1 means SH1 berths in A, SH2 in B, SH3 in C, SH4 returns to A once SH1 has left; consider the thirteen jobs in that order, each placed at the earliest moment the rules allow, so position is priority, not start time.” The map runs both ways: to encode a finished berth-and-crane plan I read segment A straight off the quay — whichever section a ship is berthed in becomes its gene — and build segment B by listing the thirteen jobs in the order the decoder must have considered them to produce that plan.

The map is deliberately many-to-one: two jobs that never compete for a crane or a berth can be considered in either order, so several strings decode to one timetable. Restricting the alphabet is deliberate too: an incompatible berthing is unwritable, so section assignments fall from 81 to 36 and compatibility never needs repairing.

4 Representation. Length, gene types, legal values per gene, a worked example using the scenario's real ships, and compatibility handled explicitly — five things, one paragraph. Draw the boxes. A described chromosome is worth less than a drawn one. That opening clause converts “the question said GA” into “I chose a GA”, and the both-ways sentence is the deliverable most answers drop: the question names encoding, decoding and representation, and encoding is the backwards arrow — schedule → string.

Decoding, phase one — the berth plan. I read segment A, group the ships by section, order each group by ETA with ties broken by priority, and lay the windows along the quay: each ship starts at max(its own ETA, the previous ship's departure + 30 minutes). Here A takes SH1 from 08:00 then SH4 from 11:00; B takes SH2 from 09:30; C takes SH3 at 10:15 — not a minute before it arrives.

Decoding, phase two — the crane schedule. I then walk segment B in order and give each job the fastest crane that is free, legal for that section and not due a rest, inserting a 30-minute break after three hours of continuous work and a one-hour charge after four hours for the electric cranes.

Each placement updates that zone's buffer level and records its peak, so capacity is checked slot by slot rather than as a total. The order is forced, not chosen: crane availability depends on where and when ships are berthed. Decoded, this chromosome puts C2 on SH1 and then on SH4, C1 on SH2 and C3 on SH3, clearing the quay at 14:00 with no ship waiting; C1 breaks at 12:30 on three hours' continuous work and charges 14:00–15:00 on four hours' total.

Those clock times are the timetable his own worked example reaches from this section vector — a job order that handed the fastest crane to the wrong ship would still decode, just to a slower legal plan, which is exactly what searching over the order is for.

4 Decoding, step by step, and why the order is forced. Two phases, each stated as an algorithm you could hand to a programmer, plus the one sentence that says why they cannot be swapped. The final clause matters most: the decode lands on real clock times, which proves the decoder exists rather than merely being promised.

How the operators apply. Segment A takes uniform crossover and a mutation that resets a gene to another value from its own legal set, so children stay compatible by construction. Segment B takes order crossover (OX) and a swap mutation, both of which preserve a permutation — one-point crossover here would duplicate and lose jobs. Tournament selection with k = 3, two elites, crossover probability 0.9, mutation about 1/17 per gene: one changed gene per chromosome on average.

The newest paper adds this as a sub-bullet, so budget three sentences for it. The marks are for operators that fit your encoding — naming OX and saying why one-point crossover fails is worth more than listing every operator you know.

Why this design and not another. The alternative I considered seriously is a grouping encoding: each section is a block listing its ships in service order — six genes instead of seventeen, section and order in one structure so they cannot contradict, and an idle berth stated on purpose rather than by accident.

I rejected it for two reasons, one mechanical and one about this port. Mechanically it needs a block-aware crossover and a repair pass, where my two segments run on standard operators at a fixed length. Substantively, it works at ship level: a block says which ships a section takes and in what order, so a ship is served by one crane from start to finish — and SH2's two hundred containers are exactly the case where I want two cranes sharing the work.

Recovering that means going back to job-level genes, which is where I already am. Neither design is redundancy-free: several block strings encode the same partition, just as two of my job orders can decode to the same timetable. I also rejected a grid of sections against time slots: it draws the timetable beautifully, but being indexed by section and time it has nowhere to put a crane's break or charge. What indexes your chromosome decides what it can say.

2 Justification against an alternative. One rival compared properly on a named trade-off, one dismissed in a sentence. Never “I chose this because it is simple” — say what the other design buys, what it costs, and which side of that trade you took.

Imitate the shape, not the sentences

Eight labels, in this order, work on every scenario this module has ever set: Assumptions · Data required · The decisions · The chromosome · Decoding phase one · Decoding phase two · How the operators apply · Why this design and not another. Write the eight labels down the margin in your first two minutes, then fill them. You will never lose a mark band to panic, and a marker scanning for the scheme finds all five bands without reading a word.

What it costs in time

Five minutes planning (decisions listed, chromosome sketched), thirty minutes writing, then stop — even mid-flourish. Q1 is 15 of 40 marks; his own warning was not to spend too long here and “miss out on everything else”, and working the mock live in class he stopped after an hour and a bit to point out that only “50 minutes left to finish two more questions” remained — 25 of the 40 marks, still untouched.

Practice · real + fresh

Sample Papers

The two real 2026 papers (your cohort's siblings), plus two fresh scenarios written in exactly the same style — with full model answers. Attempt before peeking; the answers are folded shut on purpose.

Real paper 1 — April 2026 (Full-time) · “Clustered Exam Scheduling”

Scenario — a faithful condensation of the real paper. Every element the three questions depend on is reproduced below; you need nothing else to attempt it. APU has moved exams to a “Clustered Resource Model” across three sites — Meranti, TPM Main, Satellite South — for a 14-day exam period. You are the AI consultant designing the scheduling system.

  • Written vs lab-based exams; labs split into advanced-workstation vs GPU-enabled needs. Satellite South is cheapest (RM2,500/session) but has zero GPU labs; TPM Main is fully equipped at RM10,000/session — “variable activation”: opening a building for a session costs a flat fee.
  • Chain modules: theory (written) + practical (lab) pairs needing a minimum 48-hour gap, both within the 14 days.
  • 10% seating buffer: every hall keeps 10% vacancy — usable capacity is 90%.
  • Front-loading: high-priority exams (resits, final-year, accreditation) in the first 5 days; chain rule still applies.
  • Congestion: no student may have more than 2 exams in a day.
  • Traffic: inter-site commute 15 min, but a 45-min penalty during the 12:00–2:00 PM window; a transfer is physically impossible if travel exceeds the break.
  • Invigilators: juniors must pair with a senior; workload within ±35% of cohort average; seniors mandatory for high-priority and technical labs.

Tasks: the standard three questions (chromosome incl. Building Activation Status and written/lab distinction; penalty vs repair for infeasible schedules; cost–capacity trade-off; slot-dependent traffic in the fitness; senior-invigilator coverage).

What was left out, and why it costs you nothing: only the cover-page boilerplate (CLO tag, academic-integrity notice, timing block) and the original's connective prose. The paper itself never states how many exams there are, how many seats each hall holds, or how many invigilators exist — those figures are yours to assume and state, which is exactly where the assumption marks live. Nothing above has been simplified away.

Model answer outline — open after attempting

Real paper 2 — March 2026 (PT-ODL) · “Two-week Exam Timetable”

PT-ODL = the part-time, open & distance learning cohort — same module, same three questions, different scenario.

  • 2 weeks × 5 weekdays, two sessions/day (09:00–12:00, 14:00–17:00).
  • Exams: duration 1–3 h, intake size, programme + level, priority (high/normal), permitted day-window (e.g. days 2–4), student-overlap sets (exams sharing students).
  • Halls: per-site, capacity, 30-min reset buffer between consecutive exams, max 3 sessions/hall/day; large exams may split across halls in the same site+session.
  • Invigilators: shared across sites; senior / standard / part-time; 6-h daily max; mandatory rest rules.
Model answer outline — open after attempting

Fresh scenario A · “St. Meridian Hospital — Operating Theatres”

St. Meridian Hospital runs 4 operating theatres (T1–T4) over a 5-day week with three daily blocks (morning / afternoon / evening). 28 surgeries await scheduling. Each surgery has: an ID, a duration (1–4 blocks… assume 1 for simplicity or state otherwise), a specialty (orthopaedic, cardiac, general, neuro), a priority (emergency / urgent / elective), and a lead surgeon.

  • Only T1 and T2 are equipped for cardiac; only T4 has the neuro-navigation rig. General and orthopaedic can use any theatre.
  • A theatre needs a 45-minute sterilisation turnaround between surgeries; assume one surgery per block plus turnaround inside the block boundary unless you argue otherwise.
  • Emergency surgeries must be scheduled within the first 2 days. No surgeon may operate more than 2 blocks per day or in two theatres in the same block.
  • Each theatre activated for an evening block incurs an RM3,000 out-of-hours staffing fee; T3 is the cheapest theatre to run generally, T1 the most expensive.
  • Anaesthetists are a shared pool of 6; each covers exactly one theatre-block; at least 2 must remain unassigned per day as emergency cover.
  • The hospital wants: minimal elective waiting (days from listing), fair workload across surgeons, minimal out-of-hours fees, priorities served early.

Your task — printed with sub-bullets, the way both 2026 papers print theirs, because a printed sub-rubric is a mark scheme you have been handed. In addition to the above, please consider: your assumptions about the underlying data structures and resource availability; how your chromosome represents the evening-activation decision and the specialty-restricted vs unrestricted theatre split; whether infeasible schedules are handled by penalty or by repair during decoding; and the cost–capacity trade-off between out-of-hours fees and the anaesthetist cover floor.

  1. Explain in detail the process of encoding, decoding and the representation of the solution as a chromosome, assuming a genetic algorithm.
