Consider: the structure of the chromosome · the meaning of each gene · how key scenario requirements are represented · how a chromosome is decoded · the data required to support encoding and decoding · how the genetic operators will be applied. 15
  2. Discuss in detail how fitness and validity will be determined. Address: hard vs soft constraints · how invalid solutions are detected and handled · each component of the fitness/objective function · justification of penalty weights and prioritisation. 15
  3. Outline how the above would differ — in encoding/decoding and implementation — if you used another CI optimisation algorithm, covering encoding and representation, evaluation strategy, and practical implementation considerations. 10

The operators bullet in Q1 is the full-time paper's; the PT-ODL paper drops it and adds “explain how fairness and priority are incorporated” to Q2 instead. Rehearse both — you get one of the two.

Fresh scenario B · “SwiftFleet — Drone Delivery Depot”

SwiftFleet operates 6 delivery drones from one depot serving 20 delivery jobs in a morning window (08:00–12:00). Each job: ID, package weight, destination distance, customer tier (premium / standard), and an earliest-dispatch time.

  • Drones differ: 2 heavy-lift (any package), 4 standard (≤5 kg only). Battery: a drone must recharge 20 min after every 2 consecutive jobs.
  • Each job's flight time = distance-based; only one drone may occupy the launch pad per 5-minute slot (single pad).
  • Premium jobs promise delivery before 10:00. Wind advisory: flights beyond 8 km are forbidden after 11:00 (hard).
  • Costs: energy per km (heavy-lift drones cost 1.6×); a late-delivery goodwill voucher RM25 per missed premium promise (the company treats promises as breakable at a price — is that hard or soft? Decide and justify).
  • Objectives: minimise total lateness, energy cost, voucher spend; balance jobs across drones.

Your task, printed with sub-bullets as both 2026 papers print theirs. In addition to the above, please consider: your assumptions about data structures and resource availability; how your chromosome represents the drone-assignment decision and the heavy-lift vs standard drone compatibility split; whether infeasible plans are handled by penalty or by repair during decoding; and the temporal logic — the 8 km wind ban and the 10:00 premium promise both depend on the slot a job lands in, so the fitness must vary with time, not just with distance.

The question bank — every scenario since 2021

All ten distinct past papers, condensed: the scenario, the twist that made it interesting, and how you'd attack Q1 + Q2. Read these for pattern recognition — after five, you'll notice you're reading the same paper in different clothes. Paper codes = year-month of the intake + cohort: 2601FT = January 2026 intake, full-time; 2308PT = August 2023, part-time (the sitting itself can land a little later — 2601FT's paper ran in April).

Worth knowing

The 2410 paper was a verbatim re-run of the 2402 paper — same warehouse scenario, same three questions, and the 2410 file still carries the old “(APU|DF2402)” header (the paper that actually sat in October 2024 was 2408, the nurse-placement one). Scenarios get recycled — every entry below is a live candidate for Friday.

And the format has only ever gotten more standardised toward the Q1/Q2/Q3 scheme: “they've got a little bit more difficult since then” (his words) means richer scenarios with more constraints, never new question types.

Insurance: the two historical odd-ball Q3 styles

Twice in history Q3 drifted implementation-ward: 2308PT asked for DEAP specifics and one 2111 variant asked for skeletal code. If that ghost returns, three sentences suffice: “In DEAP you define the fitness and individual via creator.create, register genes/operators (mate = cxOnePoint or cxOrdered, mutate = mutUniformInt or mutShuffleIndexes, select = selTournament) on a Toolbox — picking the operator to match the segment: cxOnePoint/mutUniformInt on an integer segment, cxOrdered/mutShuffleIndexes on a permutation segment, and cxTwoPoint/mutFlipBit(indpb=…) if the chromosome is a plain bit string, which is the pair the module's own binary labs register — then run algorithms.eaSimple with pop, cxpb, mutpb, ngen (crossover probability, mutation probability, number of generations). The custom work is exactly the encoding and fitness you designed in Q1/Q2 — DEAP supplies the loop.” That paragraph is full marks for an implementation-flavoured Q3.

If a paper ever does say “snippets”, six lines is all a 10-mark outline needs — and note that the only paper ever to ask for actual code was the open-book 2111 variant, before the format settled (2308PT asked only for an outline explanation of DEAP, which the paragraph above already answers):

creator.create("FitMin", base.Fitness, weights=(-1.0,))
creator.create("Individual", list, fitness=creator.FitMin)
tb = base.Toolbox()
tb.register("individual", tools.initRepeat, creator.Individual, gene, n=N)
tb.register("evaluate", evaluate)   # = decode() then the Q2 fitness
tb.register("mate", tools.cxUniform, indpb=0.5)      # cxOrdered if permutation
tb.register("mutate", tools.mutUniformInt, low=1, up=K, indpb=0.05)
tb.register("select", tools.selTournament, tournsize=3)
algorithms.eaSimple(pop, tb, cxpb=0.8, mutpb=0.2, ngen=300)

One line worth knowing the alternative to. tools.initRepeat builds an individual by calling one gene generator over and over, which is right for a fixed-length string of same-shaped genes. When your chromosome is not that — nested segments, a per-individual variable length, blocks of different types — you register your own builder instead: the module's Acme scheduling lab writes tb.register("individual", tools.initIterate, creator.Individual, acme.create_individual), where create_individual is a function you wrote that returns one whole legal chromosome. initRepeat then still builds the population out of those individuals.

One sentence naming that split — repeat a gene generator for a flat chromosome, iterate over your own builder for a structured one — shows you understand that the library has to be bent to your encoding rather than the other way round.

Annotate three lines — why that alphabet, why that crossover for your encoding, why that penalty weight — and you have converted a code question back into the encoding-and-fitness argument you already wrote.

Multi-objective DEAP, one breath more (2308PT asked exactly this): weights=(-1.0,-1.0,-1.0) means minimise all three — the weights control direction (MAX vs MIN), not scaling. Mixed signs are legal: (+1.0, -1.0) maximises the first objective while minimising the second. One correction to the guard lab, because it is the trap most people copy: that notebook declares weights=(-10.0, -1.0), but its evaluation function returns a one-element tuple (return guard.getCost(individual),), so DEAP only ever reads weights[0] and the −1.0 is dead.

The ×10 that genuinely makes hard violations outrank soft ones lives inside the cost function instead — the object is built as Guard(10) and getCost returns 10 × hardViolations + softViolations as a single number. Write the rule down: the weights tuple must carry exactly one entry per objective your evaluation returns, and a weight sets direction (maximise or minimise), not priority — prioritising hard over soft is arithmetic you do inside the fitness.

Then swap the machinery: tools.selNSGA2 as selection (“the heart of NSGA-II”), algorithms.eaMuPlusLambda(mu, lambda_) as the loop, and tools.ParetoFront() as the hall of fame so the whole trade-off front survives, not just one best.

The Cram Sheet

If you remember only this page, you pass. If you can write this page from memory, you're chasing full marks.

Test contract

Fri 14 Aug · 2:30 PM (hall 2:30–5:00) · 2 h · closed book · 40 marks · Q1 15 / Q2 15 / Q3 10
Time: 15 read+assume → 40 Q1 → 40 Q2 → 20 Q3 → 5 check

Pipeline: D · E · D · D · F · O

Decisions → Encoding → Decoder → Data requirements → Fitness → Others (alternative algorithm)

Q1 (3 · 4 · 4 · 2 · 2)

  • Decisions: assignment · order · time · on/off activation — anything the scenario leaves open
  • Encodings: Binary Integer Real Permutation Tree (Grid = bonus 6th pattern) — permutation needs OX/PMX + swap
  • Encoding properties: Completeness · Non-redundancy · Connectedness (locality) · Feasibility (validity bias) · Simplicity (easy to code)
  • Patterns: ① vector+permutation (default) ② blocks+separators ③ direct heterogeneous (reject) ④ grid (reject)
  • Compatibility → restrict the alphabet (violation unwritable, search space shrinks)
  • Chromosome drawn with real numbers · legal values stated · decoder in 2 phases + why forced · justified vs 1 alternative
  • Data requirements in 4 groups — per-shift entity data · fixed resource specs · live state · cost-and-policy figures — 2 marks, the row most people drop, and it must include the numbers your own assumptions invented
  • Mar 2026 sample shapes to reuse: assumptions as a 3-column table (Component · Value · Why) · block encoding 5 genes/exam [Slot, Hall1, Hall2, Inv1, Inv2] with 0 = “not needed” · slot decode Day = ceil(Slot/2), odd = morning · crossover cuts only at block boundaries · Q2 penalty form 1000×ΣHC + Σwᵢ·SCᵢ, weights ranked feasibility > fairness > efficiency

GA settings you can quote (the module's own labs)

If a question asks what you would set, do not wave at ranges — give a configuration and say it is a starting point you would tune. The guard-rota, moth and Acme labs all run the same one: population 100, crossover probability 0.9, mutation probability 0.1, tournament selection with k = 3, a Hall of Fame of 3 (DEAP's archive of the three best-ever individuals, so a champion can never be lost), and 100 generations in the moth and Acme labs, 500 in the guard rota.

The feature-selection lab runs a leaner variant — population 50, crossover 0.9, mutation 0.2, 50 generations, Hall of Fame 5, tournament k = 2 — which is the shape you use when one fitness evaluation is expensive.

The distinction that catches people out. The mutation probability above (0.1 or 0.2) is the chance that an individual is handed to the mutation operator at all. The chance that any single gene then flips is a second, much smaller number — DEAP calls it indpb. The feature-selection lab sets it to 1 ÷ chromosome length (1/16 on its 16-gene string), so a mutated individual expects about one changed gene; the guard and moth labs simply pin it at 0.01 per bit. Quote both numbers and say which is which, and “mutation rate 0.1” stops being ambiguous.

What convergence looks like, in one sentence you can write. Best fitness climbs steeply for a few generations, then plateaus while the average keeps creeping up toward it. In the feature-selection run (fitness maximised there) the best went 0.972 → 0.980 by generation 1, reached 0.985 by generation 16 and never moved again through generation 50, while the average drifted from 0.880 to roughly 0.98. Flat best plus rising average is a converged run — and it is the moment a “no improvement for k generations” stopping rule fires.

Q2 (3 · 3 · 4 · 2 · 3)

  • Validity = numbered checks: capacity · exclusivity · release · buffers/gaps · compatibility · pairing · limits
  • Tools, cheapest first: Encoding > Decoder > Repair > Penalty > Rejection
  • Components (formula+unit+purpose): waiting · weighted-waiting (5/3/1) · 1−utilisation · overload · cost+activation · overtime · allocation cost · balance (std-dev) · MAKESPAN
  • Normalise f′=(f−min)/(max−min) → weights sum to 1 → lower better · or NSGA-II Pareto menu
  • Critical: objectives conflict · weights = policy · missing-component (makespan) story · slot-dependent terms per assignment
  • Penalty shape: (hardViolations)×BIG + softMisses

Q3 (2 · 3 · 2 · 2 · 1) — two halves: ~5 general + ~5 applied

His 12-Aug whiteboard skeleton (memorise this shape): Part A — differences GA vs ACO: solutions vs agents · chromosome vs step-by-step construction · repair/penalty after vs filtering during · mutation/crossover rates vs evaporation · population memory vs pheromone matrix. Part B — how it applies here: nodes from the scenario (exams / ships / wards) → options at each node (slots, halls, staff) → filtering rules as the ant moves node to node → parameters with numbers → “my Q2 fitness scores each finished ant unchanged” → one judgement sentence.

Open with the general half: a compact outline of the algorithm itself, before you compare anything. Write it — the examiner is not reading to learn how PSO works, he is marking whether you know, which makes this the closest thing to free marks on the paper. Then the applied half: how that algorithm runs on this scenario, set out under the three difference headings — Encoding/Decoding · Evaluation · Implementation — with Similarities given its own underlined heading beside them, since his recipe asks for overlaps as well as differences.

Tidied from the automatic transcript, his own statement of what a full-mark Q3 contains: “Similarities and differences where there are overlaps and where there are key differences… and then you are giving a sort of an outline of how this approach will be applied. So to get full marks, those two things must be there. And so far, I've never got an answer that has those two things… mostly it's the first thing.” Read that last clause carefully: the piece almost every script omits is the applied outline, not the textbook description.

  • PSO: real-vector particles · random keys (banded per legal set = compatibility; sort = order) · v←ωv+c₁r₁(pb−x)+c₂r₂(gb−x) · decoder+fitness unchanged · no operators · params ω c₁ c₂
  • ACO: no chromosome — ants construct, only legal moves offered ⇒ feasibility free · P ∝ τᵅηᵝ · evaporation ρ · fitness unchanged + lays pheromone · params α β ρ #ants · elitist: top ants deposit
  • Grouping GA + LS (LS = local search): Q1 blocks unchanged · block crossover copy→dedupe→reinsert · + local search swaps, kept only if fitness improves — that acceptance rule is what makes it a memetic algorithm, so name the family · cost: every move needs its own fitness call, so decoding speed starts to matter
  • SA/Tabu: single solution, no population · neighbourhood moves (swap jobs / reassign crane / shift start slot) · SA accepts worse with exp(−Δ/T), params T₀ + cooling · Tabu bans recent moves (list length + aspiration) · “a perfectly good 10-mark answer”
  • Judgement: PSO = least effort · ACO = dense constraints · GGA = partition quality · SA = simplicity (a legitimate argument)
  • NFL theorem: averaged over all problems, all algorithms tie — so justify fit to this scenario, never a textbook dump

ACO magnitudes, so you never write “α and β are set appropriately”. Two settings from the module's own ACO runs are quotable as they stand: α = 1.5, β = 3, 40 ants, 200 iterations on a 10-city problem, and α = 4, β = 5, decay 0.5, 50 ants with only the top 10 depositing, 1,000 iterations on a 15-city one.

The lecture says plainly that α and β “can be arbitrarily assigned”, so nobody expects a derivation — they expect a number and a reason, and the reason is the easy half. β set above α leans each choice on the greedy heuristic η, which is the sensible bias while the pheromone has learned nothing yet; raising α leans it back onto what the colony has since learned.

A decay of 0.5 halves every trail each iteration, which forgets fast enough that one lucky early route cannot own the run. And ant count is set exactly like a GA population — enough to sample the space, small enough to afford the fitness calls.

NSGA-II one-liner

Combine parents+children (elitism) → non-dominated sort into fronts → fill by rank → crowding-distance tiebreak keeps the front spread out.

Traps

Missing decision (activation!) · per-task genes for one-off choices · unstated assumptions · raw-unit sums · “X twice as important as Y” ⇒ wₓ=2wᵧ, cite it · don't invent complexity · Q1 ≤ 40 min · consume every scenario feature visibly.

His pacing warning — Q3's 10 marks are the cheapest on the paper

“You got two hours, you got three questions. The more you spend here, the less time you're going to have down here… now you haven't got enough time to work on question three, where there are full 10 marks to get. And so you're sacrificing time spent here to pick up a couple of marks here.”

To a student panicking about memorising code

“How many times do I have to write it repeatedly so we can memorise it? — You don't need to memorise it. You just need to be able to do.”

Glossary — every term on this site, one line each

Open the glossary (folded shut so the printed cram sheet stays one clean page)

If any word or abbreviation anywhere on this site stops you, it's here — alphabetical, one exam-usable line each.

Terms

TermMeaning
Activation (opening cost)A yes/no decision to switch a resource on for one period, carrying a flat fee the moment it is used at all — opening a building for an exam session (Satellite South RM2,500, TPM Main RM10,000), running an evening theatre block, powering a quay section. It is the decision most often missed, because the scenario hides it inside a cost sentence instead of an instruction. Give it a gene — one on/off bit per resource per period — and let the fee enter the fitness only when that bit is 1. Missing a decision is “the commonest and most expensive error”, and activation is the usual victim.
AffinityAn AIS's word for fitness: how well an antibody (candidate solution) matches the antigen (the problem).
AlleleOne particular value a gene currently holds — “section = B” is an allele of the section gene.
AlphabetThe set of legal values a gene may take; restricting it makes some violations literally unwritable.
Aspiration criterionTabu search's override: a banned move is allowed anyway if it produces the best solution seen so far.
Binary encodingEncoding type 1 of 5. Every gene is 0 or 1 — in/out, on/off, take/leave. Knapsack (1 = pack this item), feature selection, facility opening, activation bits. Chromosome length = number of decisions; search space = 2length, so the 336-bit guard rota has 2336 ≈ 10101 candidates. Operators: one-point, two-point or uniform crossover with flip-bit mutation — the pair the module's own binary labs register.
Buffer zonePer-section storage area where unloaded containers wait for collection — limited capacity, checked as peak occupancy slot by slot.
ChangeoverThe idle gap a berth needs between one ship leaving and the next arriving, enforced in decoder phase one as start = max(the ship's own ETA, the previous ship's departure + changeover). His walkthrough fixes it at 30 minutes and puts it in the decoder rather than in a penalty — “Add 30 minutes to the earliest legal berth time for the next ship at that section” — but no printed brief names the figure, so declare yours in your assumptions. “Forgetting changeover time” is an entry on his own list of expected mistakes, glossed “Ships do not teleport.”
ChromosomeOne complete candidate solution written as a string of genes — the thing the GA copies, cuts and mutates.
Clonal selectionAn AIS's engine: clone the best-matching detectors and mutate them in inverse proportion to their affinity (better ⇒ smaller changes).
Combinatorial explosionWhy brute force is not an option: options multiply instead of adding, so n exams into k slots gives kn schedules — 40 exams and 20 slots is roughly 1052. Naming it is the standard one-line justification for reaching for a CI method at all.
CompletenessEncoding property: every legal solution must be writable as some chromosome, or the optimum is unreachable.
Connectedness (locality)Encoding property: a small gene change should cause a small change in the decoded solution, so the search can walk instead of teleport.
Constraint (hard / soft)See Hard constraint and Soft constraint (soft objective). Hard ones decide whether a candidate is a solution at all; soft ones decide how good it is. Sorting every clause of the brief into those two columns is Q2's opening move and costs ninety seconds.
Construction graphWhat replaces the chromosome in ACO: the network of legal partial choices — (ship, section, crane), or (job, crane, position) — that an ant walks one step at a time, offered only legal moves and depositing pheromone τ on the arcs it used. There is no separate decoding step, because construction is the decoding; that single sentence is the sharpest thing you can write in an ACO Q3.
Continuous / discreteProblem axis. Continuous variables take any real value (angles, weights, dosages) and yield to calculus and gradient methods; discrete or combinatorial ones are choices, orders and assignments — every scenario in this module — and need combinatorics, graph theory and search. Mixed problems have both.
Cooling scheduleSimulated annealing's temperature plan (e.g. T ← 0.95T each step) — it sets how quickly the search stops accepting worse moves.
CrossoverThe operator that builds children by recombining two parents — his decks also call it recombination; the GA's main engine of progress, so pc is high. Three basic forms: single-point, where one random location (the crossover point or cut point) is chosen and everything to its right is swapped; two-point / k-point, which swaps the middle segment; and uniform, which decides each gene independently from one parent or the other and so mixes hardest. Permutations need OX or PMX instead, because these three duplicate and lose items.
Crowding distanceNSGA-II's spread score: sum of neighbour gaps per objective; front endpoints get ∞ and are always kept.
DEAP API namesThe identifiers the module's labs print — worth recognising, because one past paper's Q3 is entirely about them. creator.create builds the fitness class (FitnessMin, negative weights = minimise) and the Individual class; base.Toolbox() is where you register the gene generators and the four hooks — evaluate, mate, mutate, select; algorithms.eaSimple is the plain generational loop; algorithms.eaMuPlusLambda is the elitist loop used for NSGA-II, same arguments plus mu (survivors) and lambda_ (children per generation), with tools.selNSGA2 as selection and tools.ParetoFront() as the hall of fame. You are never asked to write working code, only to say which hooks you would swap.
Death penaltyConstraint handling by rejection: an invalid solution is discarded (or scored worst) outright.
Decision variableIngredient one of any optimisation problem: something you are free to change. His Week-2 deck puts it plainly — “Decision variables are the things you can change. They define the ‘shape’ of any candidate solution.” Every one must end up either as a gene or as a quantity the decoder derives from the genes, and Q1 pays 3 marks for identifying all of them and saying where each lives. Anything the brief fixes is data, not a decision — and a constant cannot be optimised, so it earns no fitness component either.
DecoderThe fixed routine that turns a chromosome into the real schedule; a well-built one repairs as it constructs.
DetectorAn AIS's candidate solution, by analogy with an antibody: a pattern that either matches something or does not. How well it matches is its affinity, which is the AIS word for fitness.
DominanceA dominates B when A is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on at least one.
ElitismCopying the best individual(s) unchanged into the next generation so progress is never lost.
Encoding / decodingTurning a real solution into a chromosome, and the fixed routine that turns it back into a schedule — you design both, in Q1.
Evaporation (ρ)ACO's forgetting rate. After each iteration every trail is reduced, τ ← (1 − ρ)τ, before the new deposits land, so a route that stops being reinforced fades away. Without it the first lucky path owns the run; the module's own ACO code uses a decay of 0.5, which halves every trail each iteration. ρ is the third ACO parameter alongside α and β.
Exploration / exploitationTrying new regions vs refining known good ones (textbooks: diversification / intensification).
Feasibility (validity bias)Encoding property: prefer a representation in which most — ideally all — chromosomes decode to legal solutions.
Fitness functionThe routine that scores a decoded solution; here, a normalised weighted sum of components with lower = better.
Fitness landscapeFitness plotted over the whole search space, like terrain — peaks, valleys, plateaus.
Fitness scalingRescale raw fitness with a linear scaled = a × raw + b before spinning the roulette wheel. His worked example maps a raw range of 4–45 onto 50–100, which solves to a = 1.22, b = 45.12; after it the best individual is only twice as likely to be picked as the worst, instead of more than eleven times. That fixes both of roulette's failure modes: one huge individual dominating the wheel early, and a late population whose fitnesses are so alike that selection stops discriminating.
GeneOne position in the chromosome, carrying one decision — e.g. “the section for SH2”.
GenerationOne full cycle of select → crossover → mutate → replace; runs are measured in generations (DEAP's ngen).
Genotype / phenotypeThe encoded chromosome vs the real-world solution it decodes into.
Giant tour with delimitersThe vehicle-routing name for the block chromosome: one long sequence of entity IDs cut by separator genes, so which block an entity falls into is its assignment and its position inside the block is its order. Same family as Falkenauer's grouping GA. Dropping the name costs one line and reads as distinction-level.
Global optimumThe genuinely best solution in the whole search space — the tallest mountain in the landscape, not merely the top of the hill you happen to be standing on. Do not confuse it with PSO's gbest, which is only the best position the swarm has found so far.
Grid encodingThe bonus sixth pattern: a resource × time table, one cell per slot, each cell naming what is happening there. Exclusivity becomes structural — one cell holds one entry, so a collision is literally unwritable — but the chromosome is huge and mostly empty, and anything not indexed by the two axes (a crane's break, its charge) has nowhere to live. The clearest picture and the worst chromosome: draw it to explain your answer, do not run your GA on it.
Hall of FameDEAP's archive of the best individuals ever seen, kept outside the population so a champion can never be lost. Note what it does not do on its own: eaSimple replaces the population wholesale with the offspring each generation and merely calls halloffame.update(), so the archive records but does not reinsert. Elitism is the extra step — select population_size − n individuals and drop the n hall-of-fame members into the remaining slots — and it is not in any of his four eaSimple labs, which is exactly why he set “making use of Elitism” as a homework exercise.
Hard constraintA rule that cannot be broken — physically, legally or contractually. Breaking one does not make a schedule bad, it makes it not a schedule. Capacity limits, exclusivity, release times and compatibility are the usual family. Hard constraints define validity, and you can enforce them in four places: in the encoding (restrict the alphabet), in the decoder (never place an illegal job), by repair afterwards, or — as a last resort — by a penalty term added to the objective, which is why a hard rule does sometimes appear in the fitness arithmetic.
Heterogeneous / homogeneous chromosomeHis own vocabulary, drawn on his Lab-1 whiteboard as two labelled strips. Heterogeneous representation: segments of different gene types — segment A an integer section per ship, segment B a permutation of jobs — each segment getting its own crossover and mutation, and never one operator run across both. Homogeneous representation: one uniform gene type from end to end (his board's example is a guard rota where equal blocks of the strip simply are the shifts of a day) with a smarter decoder doing the structural work. Heterogeneous is the default for these scenarios; say which you chose and why.
HeuristicA rule-of-thumb that finds good-enough answers with no optimality guarantee.
HypervolumeMulti-objective quality measure: how much objective space your Pareto front dominates against a fixed reference point — bigger is better.
Ideal pointThe (usually unattainable) corner where every objective sits at its individual best; the Pareto front bends toward it.
Inertia decayShrinking PSO's ω over the run: explore early, settle late.
Integer encodingEncoding type 2 of 5. Each gene is a whole number naming a choice from a list — which section, which theatre, which hall, how many. The port's segment A is four integers with 1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C, so gene 3 = 2 means ship SH3 → section B. Restrict each gene's legal set and an incompatible assignment becomes unwritable. Operators: uniform or one-point crossover, plus a mutation that resets a gene to another value drawn from its own legal set.
Knapsack problemOne of the module's two named benchmarks (with the TSP): a bag with a weight limit and a list of items, each with a weight and a value — choose the subset of greatest value that still fits. The flagship binary-encoding example, 1 = take it. Capacity can be handled several ways: the module's own lab decoder simply skips any item that would push the bag over the limit, but repair, a graded penalty or worst-fitness are all legitimate — say which you chose and why (Lesson 7).
Local optimumBetter than every neighbouring solution, but not the global optimum — where naive search gets stuck.
Local search (LS)Improving one solution by repeatedly trying small moves in its neighbourhood — swap two jobs, move one entity to another group, shift a start slot. On its own it is a hill-climber and stops at the first local optimum. Bolted onto a GA after crossover, keeping a move only if fitness improves, it makes the algorithm memetic. Simulated annealing is local search that sometimes accepts a worse move; tabu search is local search that refuses to undo its recent ones.
LocalitySee Connectedness — small gene change ⇒ small change in the decoded solution; the property crossover and mutation depend on.
MakespanWhen the last job finishes; total schedule length. A port is paid for turnaround.
Memetic algorithmA GA with a local-search step bolted on: after crossover and mutation, try small improving moves on each child (swap two ships between sections, shift one start slot) and keep the change only if fitness improves. Evolution explores, local search polishes. Naming the family — “a grouping genetic algorithm with local search, i.e. a memetic algorithm” — costs one line and signals you know where the problem sits in the literature; the cost to admit in the same breath is that every local-search move needs its own fitness evaluation, so decoding speed suddenly matters.
Memory cellAn AIS's long-lived survivor of a successful clone — it makes the response to a similar problem faster next time.
MetaheuristicA higher-level search strategy mixing randomness with local search — GA, PSO and ACO all are.
Multimodal / unimodalA fitness landscape with many peaks vs one. On unimodal problems exploitation wins and a hill-climber would do; on multimodal ones — every scheduling scenario here — exploration earns its cost, which is the argument for a population, for mutation, and for niching.
MutationThe operator that randomly alters a gene to inject new material and keep diversity alive; pm stays small (≈1/length, per gene). His named forms: flip-bit (binary), swap two positions, inversion of a slice, scramble/shuffle of a slice, and Gaussian for real genes. Swap, inversion and scramble keep a permutation legal; flip-bit has no meaning on one.
Negative selection (self / non-self)From the module's Week-1 reading: the immune system learns to tell self (normal, acceptable) from non-self, and detectors that match self are destroyed before deployment, so the survivors fire only on anomalies. Name it as the second AIS mechanism alongside clonal selection if Q3 offers you AIS — but do not oversell it as constraint handling: screening out illegal candidates is ordinary rejection, which any algorithm here can do.
Niching / fitness sharingThe diversity mechanism from his GA Breakdown deck: individuals crowded together in the search space have their fitness reduced (the classic implementation is fitness sharing), so the population spreads across several peaks instead of collapsing onto one — and you finish with several genuinely different good plans rather than three near-copies. The third answer to premature convergence, after lowering k and raising mutation. Worked in full in Lesson 6.
Non-redundancyEncoding property: avoid many different chromosomes decoding to the same solution — redundancy inflates the search space for nothing.
NormalisationRescaling each component to 0–1 with f′ = (f − min)/(max − min) so minutes, ringgit and containers can legitimately be added.
Objective functionThe same thing as the fitness function, said in the language of optimisation rather than of evolution: the number a candidate solution is scored on. Papers use the two words interchangeably, and so may you. Every optimisation problem is decisions + objective(s) + constraints; naming all three in your opening paragraph banks the framing marks.
OffspringThe children produced by crossover and mutation in one generation, before replacement decides which survive. In DEAP's eaSimple the offspring replace the population wholesale each generation — which is precisely why elitism has to be added on purpose.
OperatorsThe GA's moves: selection, crossover, mutation.
Pareto frontThe set of mutually non-dominated trade-off solutions; report the whole front, not one point.
PenaltyA fitness deduction per broken rule, sized so the worst legal solution still beats the best illegal one.
Permutation encodingEncoding type 4 of 5. The chromosome lists every item exactly once and the ordering is the solution — routes, sequences, service orders. Search space = n!, so thirteen jobs is 13! ≈ 6.2 billion. The rule everyone misreads: position = priority, not time — gene 1 is considered first by the decoder, not started first. Needs permutation-safe operators (OX or PMX, with swap, inversion or scramble mutation), because one-point crossover would duplicate some items and lose others.
PopulationThe set of chromosomes held at once (typically 50–200) — searching many points in parallel is what makes a GA a GA.
Premature convergenceThe population collapses around one (usually local) optimum before anything better is found.
PurserA cabin-crew rank in charge of the cabin on a flight — its own category alongside junior and senior, not simply a senior. Both crew-rostering papers (2307 and 2308PT) state that “Each flight must have 1 purser to oversee the cabin”, so a roster that leaves one out is invalid rather than merely poor: it is a hard constraint, and the count belongs in your Q2 validity checklist next to capacity and exclusivity.
Quay / berthQuay = the dock wall ships tie up along; berth = one ship-sized slot on it.
Random keysOne real number per item, sorted ascending to give the sequence — how PSO expresses an ordering without leaving real-valued space (see SPV). Band the range per item and compatibility comes free.
Rank-based selectionRoulette run on rank position instead of raw fitness. Useful when a few individuals have far larger fitness than the rest — ranking eliminates the large differences, so those few cannot take over the next generation — and equally useful when everyone is nearly equal, since ranking spreads them apart and restores a clear advantage for the better ones.
Real-valued encodingEncoding type 3 of 5. Each gene is a real number — continuous parameters such as angles, weights and speeds. It is also PSO's native space, which is why random keys exist: sort the reals and their rank order gives you an ordering without leaving real-valued space. Operators: BLX or SBX crossover, Gaussian mutation.
Reefer / hazmatRefrigerated container needing shore power / hazardous cargo needing a certified berth.
Release timeThe earliest moment an entity becomes available — a ship's ETA, a job's arrival.
RepairA post-operator fix-up that edits an invalid chromosome back to validity.
SchemaA gene pattern shared by good solutions; crossover preserves schemas, mutation disrupts them — why pc is high and pm tiny.
Search space / solution spaceEvery chromosome the encoding can write / every real solution they decode to. A good encoding keeps both small and mostly legal.
SelectionChoosing which parents breed — the pressure toward fitness, not a source of new material: selection never opens the chromosome. His five methods are roulette wheel (slice ∝ fitness), stochastic universal sampling (one spin, N evenly spaced pointers), rank-based, fitness scaling and tournament (best of k drawn at random — the labs' default, k = 3).
Selection pressureHow strongly selection favours the fittest; too much causes premature convergence.
Separator gene (delimiter)The ‖ in a block chromosome. It carries no value of its own — its position is the information: move one separator a place to the left and a ship changes section; swap two IDs inside a block and their order changes. Cheap to draw, and it is exactly what forces a block-aware crossover.
SimplicityEncoding property: it must be quick to code and cheap to decode — an elegant design you cannot implement scores nothing.
Single- / multi-objectiveProblem axis: one goal to optimise, or several that genuinely conflict (and, separately, constrained or unconstrained). Tick each axis in your opening paragraph — continuous or discrete, static or dynamic, single- or multi-objective, constrained or not — after you have named the decisions, objective and constraints.
Soft constraint (soft objective)A preference or a cost. Breaking it makes a solution worse but still legal, so it becomes a weighted component of the fitness function rather than a validity test.
StagnationGenerations passing with no noticeable improvement in the best fitness. It is both a stopping signal and a diagnosis: a flat best with a rising average is healthy convergence; a flat best with a flat average, early, means the population has collapsed and you should cut selection pressure or raise mutation.
Standard deviation (σ)The spread of a set of numbers around their mean — the statistic that carries every fairness or balance component (f₈). Small σ means the load is even, large σ means one resource is carrying the shift. Two lines of arithmetic — peak occupancies 150 / 65 / 33 → mean 82.7 → σ ≈ 49 — turn the phrase into a measurement you understand; do them, then give the unit and say what the component buys.
Static / dynamic / adaptive penaltyPenalty coefficient fixed once / rising on a schedule with the generation counter / reacting to how infeasible the population currently is.
Static vs dynamic problemProblem axis: does the data stand still while you optimise, or change under you — a ship arriving late, an invigilator calling in sick? Every class-test scenario is a static snapshot; say so as an assumption, and add the one clause that a live port would re-run the search on each disruption.
StigmergyIndirect communication through the environment — ants coordinating via pheromone, not messages.
Stochastic / deterministicUses randomness, so two runs can differ (every CI method here) / same input always gives the same output (classical exact methods).
Stopping condition (termination criterion)A GA cannot recognise the optimum, so you must tell it when to stop. His two: a maximum number of generations has been reached, or there was no noticeable improvement over the last few generations. Worth one sentence in any answer — “run for G generations or until no improvement for k” — and it is the natural place to mention your evaluation budget.
Tabu listTabu search's short memory of recent moves, which it forbids reversing; the list length is its key parameter.
Tabu searchSingle-solution local search that always takes the best neighbouring move but bans recently reversed ones, so it can climb out of a local optimum.
Topology (star / ring)Who a PSO particle listens to: star = everyone follows one gbest (fast, converges early); ring = each follows its neighbours' lbest (slower, keeps diversity).
Tournament size (k)How many individuals are drawn at random for each tournament; the fittest of them becomes a parent. The larger k, the likelier the best individuals are in the draw and the smaller a weak one's chance of slipping through — so k is the selection-pressure dial. His own words on the trade-off: a very small k gives “a very good chance of picking weak solutions”, a very big one “a very big chance of just picking the best solution”. k = 2 is gentle, k = 3 is the common default and what the labs and his live demo run, k ≥ 5 is harsh. Justify your k by that trade-off rather than quoting a number.
Tree encodingEncoding type 5 of 5. The chromosome is a tree rather than a string — internal nodes are operators or functions, leaves are values — and it is what genetic programming evolves: formulas, rules, programs. Named on his list of five and examinable as a name; no scheduling scenario in this module wants it.
Valid (feasible)A candidate that passes every hard constraint. There is no “a bit valid”: the answer is yes or no, and a schedule that fails is not a bad solution but a non-solution. Do not confuse it with Feasibility (validity bias) above, which is a property of the encoding — what proportion of the chromosomes it can write decode to legal solutions — rather than a verdict on one schedule.
Velocity clampingCapping a PSO particle's step size so it cannot overshoot the search space.
Waggle danceThe bee algorithms' recruitment metaphor: a successful forager advertises its patch, so more bees are sent to the better patches.
Weighted sum (scalarisation)Combining several normalised objectives into one score, F = Σ wᵢ·f′ᵢ with the weights summing to 1, so that any two candidates can be ranked. The alternative is to keep them separate and return a Pareto front.

Abbreviations

Abbrev.Stands for / means
ABC / BCOArtificial Bee Colony / Bee Colony Optimisation — bee-foraging search: scouts find patches, recruits exploit the best.
ACOAnt Colony Optimisation — ants build solutions move by move, guided by pheromone (τ) and desirability (η).
AHAArtificial Hummingbird Algorithm — the fifth swarm method on his Lab-1 whiteboard (“PSO / ACO / ABC / GWO / AHA”). Named in the module, not taught in it: know it is a swarm method and that it is his.
AISArtificial Immune System — immune-inspired: generate diverse detectors (candidate solutions, scored by affinity), clone and mutate the best in inverse proportion to affinity, keep the winners as memory cells. Its second mechanism is negative selection: detectors matching “self” are destroyed before deployment.
alpha / beta (α, β)ACO's two exponents, in P ∝ ταηβ: α weights the pheromone (what the colony has learned) and β the heuristic desirability η (what looks good right now). The lecture says plainly they “can be arbitrarily assigned”, so give a number and a reason — β above α leans on the greedy heuristic while the pheromone knows nothing; raising α leans back on what has been learned. Nothing to do with the α/β/δ ranks in GWO.
BLXBlend Crossover (real genes) — child sampled from a widened interval around the two parents.
CIComputational Intelligence — the nature-inspired toolkit (evolution, swarms, fuzzy, neural) this module lives in.
CLO / PLOCourse Learning Outcome (his slides head the same outcome text “Module Learning Outcome”) and Programme Learning Outcome — the accreditation tags on the cover page, e.g. “CLO1: Evaluate the encoding and decoding of a computational intelligence algorithm (C5, PLO2)”. The bracketed C-number is the Bloom level (C2 = understand, C5 = evaluate): on a C5 paper, judgement and comparison score, transcription does not.
cxpb / mutpb / indpb / ngenDEAP's run knobs, and the distinction that catches people out. cxpb = probability a parent pair is crossed (his labs: 0.9). mutpb = probability an individual is handed to the mutation operator at all (his labs: 0.1; the zoo lab 0.2). indpb = probability each gene is altered once that individual is being mutated (his labs: 0.01; the zoo lab uses 1/length). The 1/chromosome-length rule below is about indpb. ngen = number of generations.
DEAPDistributed Evolutionary Algorithms in Python — the module's lab library.
EAEvolutionary Algorithm — umbrella term for evolution-inspired methods, GA included.
ETAEstimated Time of Arrival — a ship's earliest possible start, and the port scenario's release time (SH1 08:00, SH2 09:30, SH3 10:15, SH4 11:00). “No job starts before its ship's ETA” is a hard constraint, and it is the one every decoder enforces first.
FPSFitness-Proportionate Selection — roulette wheel's textbook name; slice size proportional to fitness.
FT / PT-ODLFull-Time cohort / Part-Time, Open & Distance Learning cohort — the two paper streams.
GAGenetic Algorithm — evolves a population of encoded solutions with selection, crossover, mutation.
GGAGrouping GA (Falkenauer) — the chromosome is built from groups/blocks rather than fixed positions, so crossover must move whole blocks, not single genes.
GWOGrey Wolf Optimizer — pack hierarchy (alpha, beta, delta) steers the hunt toward prey. These α and β are wolf ranks and have nothing to do with ACO's exponents. It appears on his Lab-1 whiteboard list of swarm methods but in none of his slide decks, so name it as a swarm family, not as something the module taught.
HoFHall of Fame — DEAP's container for the best-ever individuals. See the Terms table: it archives, it does not reinsert, so it is not elitism by itself.
IGD+Inverted Generational Distance (plus) — average distance from a reference front to yours; smaller is better, and it scores closeness and coverage at once.
MOEA/DMulti-Objective EA by Decomposition — splits one multi-objective problem into many single-objective sub-problems solved in parallel.
NFLNo-Free-Lunch theorem — averaged over all possible problems, every algorithm ties; so tailor to the problem.
NSGA-IINon-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II — rank into Pareto fronts, tiebreak by crowding distance.
OX / PMXOrder / Partially-Mapped Crossover — the permutation-safe crossovers (no duplicated genes).
pbest / gbest / lbestPSO's three attractors: a particle's own best position / the whole swarm's best / the best inside its ring neighbourhood — the pull terms in v ← ωv + c₁r₁(pbest − x) + c₂r₂(gbest − x).
pc / pmCrossover / mutation probability. pc is high — typically 0.7–0.9. The common default for pm is one expected mutation per chromosome, i.e. pm ≈ 1/chromosome length: ≈0.003 for the 336-bit guard rota, ≈0.06 for a 17-gene port chromosome, up to ~0.1 for a very short string. Quoted textbook ranges like 0.01–0.1 assume short chromosomes — quote 1/length and let the decimal fall where it falls.
PSOParticle Swarm Optimisation — particles fly through real-valued space, pulled by personal best and global best.
RMMalaysian ringgit — the currency in every costed scenario.
SASimulated Annealing — one solution, neighbourhood moves, accepts worse with probability exp(−Δ/T) as temperature T cools.
SBXSimulated Binary Crossover (real genes) — children spread symmetrically around the parents; parents' average preserved.
SISwarm Intelligence — “any attempt to design algorithms or distributed problem-solving devices inspired by the collective behaviour of social insect colonies and other animal societies” (Bonabeau, Dorigo & Theraulaz, 1999). The last five words are what let one definition cover ants (ACO), birds (PSO), bees (ABC/BCO) and wolves (GWO). Full citation and how to unpack it: Lesson 11.
SPVSmallest Position Value — sort a real vector; the rank order of positions is the permutation (PSO→ordering bridge).
SUSStochastic Universal Sampling — N evenly spaced pointers around the roulette wheel; one spin picks all N parents.
TSPTravelling Salesman Problem — visit every city exactly once and return home, minimising total distance.
VRPVehicle Routing Problem — TSP with a fleet: split the stops across vehicles, then order each route.
Built from CT099-3-M past papers (2021–2026), the class-test walkthrough deck, lecture slides, and class recordings. Verify test-day logistics against your professor's latest announcement. Good luck — you've earned the calm.
